Q1293
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
At 18 months of age, a child develops a comitant esotropia that measures 20 prism-diopters (Δ) in primary position at near and distance. The child is not hyperopic and shows no lateral incomitance. What is her most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. basic acquired esotropia
Rationale
Basic acquired esotropia develops in children after 6 months of age, and the amount of hyperopia is not significant. It may be precipitated by disruption of binocular fusion (such as due to hyphema, preseptal cellulitis, ptosis, or patching for amblyopia).
Patients with accommodative esotropia typically have hyperopia, with onset from 6 months to 7 years. Infants with esotropia, by definition, have onset prior to 6 months of age. Cranial nerve VI palsy would cause an incomitant esotropia.

Q1294
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the principal reason that patients with oculocutaneous and ocular albinism have decreased vision?
Correct answer: C. foveal hypoplasia
Rationale
Albinism refers to a group of various conditions involving the melanin system of either the skin and eye (oculocutaneous albinism, OCA) or the eye alone (ocular albinism, OA). All types of albinism have foveal hypoplasia or aplasia, iris transillumination from decreased pigmentation, and a characteristic deficit of pigment in the retina, especially peripheral to the posterior pole (figure). The figure shows: A. Transillumination of iris in albinism, right eye. B. Fundus in albinism, right eye, demonstrating complete lack of pigment and macular agenesis. C. Child with oculocutaneous albinism type 2 (OCA2). Note white hair, eyebrows, and lashes, and light-colored irides and freckles.
Decreased vision is due to foveal hypoplasia resulting in nystagmus. If a child has significant foveal hypoplasia, nystagmus will begin at 2–3 months of life. The severity of the visual defect tends to be proportional to the degree of nystagmus and foveal hypoplasia. Iris transillumination is a key diagnostic feature but is not visually significant.
Optic nerve hypoplasia (ONH), which appears clinically as a pale or gray and smaller-than-normal optic nerve, can result in visual field defects and a range of visual acuities (normal to no light perception). Children with bilateral ONH can have sensory nystagmus, and those with unilateral ONH may have sensory strabismus. ONH is not associated with albinism, but is associated with midline central nervous system abnormalities such as septo-optic dysplasia (de Morsier syndrome), which is ONH with the absence of the septum pellucidum and agenesis of the corpus callosum.

Q1295
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 6-year-old girl presents for her annual eye examination and glasses update. Retinoscopy demonstrates a spherical equivalent of -12.00 in both eyes. She and her mother both had cleft palates at birth, and her mother reports a history of retinal detachments in both eyes. What underlying genetic condition most likely is present?
Correct answer: C. Stickler syndrome
Rationale
The abnormalities described are suggestive of Stickler syndrome. Ophthalmic findings of Stickler syndrome include high myopia, optically empty vitreous, congenital glaucoma, cataracts, and retinal detachment. Associated systemic findings include flat midface, progressive hearing loss, Pierre Robin sequence (a series of anomalies caused by abnormal descent of the tongue, including cleft palate, glossoptosis, micrognathia, and respiratory problems), mitral valve prolapse, and progressive arthropathy. The most common type of Stickler syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by a mutation in COL2A1, the gene that encodes for type II procollagen.
A mutation in OPA1 is the most common cause of dominant optic atrophy, which is characterized clinically by a gradually progressive loss of visual acuity. A mutation in the mitochondrial genome at the 11778 position is the most common cause of Leber hereditary optic neuropathy, which usually presents with acute or subacute, bilateral, sequential vision loss with central or cecocentral scotomas. A mutation in WFS1 may cause Wolfram syndrome (aka DIDMOAD: diabetes insipidus, diabetes mellitus, optic atrophy, deafness).

Q1296
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 12-month-old boy presents with a slowly growing mass on the lateral orbital rim. On examination, it is a painless, mobile mass. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) shows a well-circumscribed mass fixed to the periosteum. What treatment is recommended?
Correct answer: C. complete surgical excision
Rationale
The question describes the classic presentation of an orbital dermoid cyst that is painless and most commonly located at the superotemporal orbital rim. These cysts can extend into the bony suture line. To prevent rupture of the cyst, which causes an acute inflammatory reaction, surgical excision is recommended. Radiation is not indicated. The lesion is not infectious, so antibiotics would not be effective. Percutaneous drainage would likely cause an inflammatory reaction, and without removal of the cyst lining, the lesion would recur.

Q1297
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the most common cause of pseudopapilledema in children?
Correct answer: C. optic disc drusen
Rationale
Pseudopapilledema can usually be differentiated from true papilledema by the absence of disc hyperemia, retinal hemorrhages, or exudates and by the lack of any systemic findings that are associated with increased intracranial pressure. The most common cause of pseudopapilledema in children is optic disc drusen (figure). Pseudopapilledema from disc drusen is associated with anomalous branching of the large retinal vessels. The drusen can appear within the first or second decade of life, as demonstrated in the second figure. Although some patients with drusen can be identified by funduscopic evaluation, occasionally it is difficult to tell for certain that drusen are responsible for the swollen disc appearance. B-scan ultrasonography can be helpful in this situation as shown. Computed tomography can also detect these drusen. Uveitis also causes disc edema, but not papilledema, as there is uncommonly elevation of the intracranial pressure. The presence of an intracranial mass or idiopathic intracranial hypertension results in papilledema, not pseudopapilledema.

Q1298
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the most likely mode of inheritance for the condition pictured?
Correct answer: C. autosomal dominant inheritance
Rationale
Craniosynostosis is characterized by the premature closure of cranial suture lines. This can occur as an isolated abnormality or as a genetic syndrome with systemic abnormalities. The most common craniosynostosis syndrome is Crouzon syndrome, which is the only syndrome that does not have the hallmarks of syndactyly and brachydactyly. Typical ophthalmic features include exophthalmos, proptosis, globe luxation, corneal exposure, strabismus, and amblyopia. The most common inheritance pattern of the craniosynostosis syndromes is autosomal dominant.

Q1299
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 4-year-old patient has new esotropia of a similar angle at distance and near. His refractive error is +4.00 D. When he wears glasses with the full correction, his vision is good in both eyes and his eyes are straight. What type of esotropia is this?
Correct answer: B. refractive accommodative esotropia
Rationale
Refractive accommodative esotropia occurs in the setting of uncorrected hyperopia with accommodative convergence with insufficient fusional divergence, leading to an esotropia. The angle is approximately the same at distance and near fixation and is generally between 20 and 30 prism diopters. The average amount of hyperopia in refractive accommodative esotropia is +4.00 D.
In high AC/A ratio accommodative esotropia, patients have an excessive convergence response for the amount of accommodation required to focus. The deviation is only present at near or is much larger at near. In divergence insufficiency, the deviation is greater at distance than at near. A sensory esotropia would apply if the vision in one eye were poor.

Q1300
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A patient with a near esodeviation greater than 10 prism diopters more than the distance deviation is considered to have what type of strabismus?
Correct answer: A. high accommodative convergence to accommodation ratio (AC/A) esotropia
Rationale
A patient with an esodeviation and a high AC/A ratio has more esotropia at near than at distance. A patient with divergence insufficiency would have more esodeviation in the distance than at near. Convergence insufficiency would also have less esotropia at near.

Q1301
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
When does gonococcal conjunctivitis typically manifest in neonates?
Correct answer: B. 3 to 4 days after birth
Rationale
Neonatal gonococcal conjunctivitis usually presents as bilateral conjunctival injection and discharge 3 to 4 days after birth. Initially, the discharge can be serosanguineous with copious purulent exudates developing later. Corneal ulceration and possibly corneal perforation can occur if the infection is not treated. Treatment requires systemic ceftriaxone with topical saline irrigation.
Typically, chemical conjunctivitis is seen within 24 hours of birth. Chlamydia typically appears 1 week after birth. Herpes simplex virus (HSV) is typically seen 2 weeks after birth.

Q1302
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the most common type of leukemia in children?
Correct answer: B. acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL)
Rationale
Acute leukemias tend to have the most severe manifestations, with a rapid onset and course. Leukemia in childhood is acute in 95% of cases and is more commonly lymphocytic than myelocytic. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is the most common malignant disease of childhood. It is responsible for 30% of all cancer cases. In the US, there are 4000 new cases per year. The most common ocular manifestation of leukemia is leukemic retinopathy; however, all ocular structures can be affected. Ocular involvement is highly correlated with central nervous system (CNS) involvement.

Q1303
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What optic nerve anomaly is most likely to be associated with a basal encephalocele?
Correct answer: B. morning glory disc anomaly
Rationale
Morning glory disc anomaly (top [1st] photo) typically appears as a funnel-shaped excavation of the posterior fundus that incorporates an enlarged optic disc with elevated surrounding retinal pigment epithelium and an increased number of blood vessels looping at the edges of the disc. It is sometimes associated with a basal encephalocele, PHACE (posterior fossa malformations, hemangiomas, arterial lesions, cardiac and eye anomalies) syndrome, and moyamoya disease.
Optic nerve hypoplasia (2nd photo) is associated with pituitary abnormalities and septo-optic dysplasia, not basal encephalocele. An optic nerve pit (3rd photo) represents herniation of dysplastic retina into a collagen-lined pocket extending posteriorly, often into the subarachnoid space, through a defect in the lamina cribrosa. Nevertheless, an optic nerve pit is not associated with encephalocele. Optic nerve coloboma (4th photo) is associated with CHARGE (coloboma, heart defects, choanal atresia, mental retardation, genitourinary abnormalities, and ear abnormalities) syndrome, but not encephalocele.

Q1304
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the natural course of an eyelid hemangioma in a newborn?
Correct answer: C. growth for several months, followed by regression
Rationale
Hemangiomas (previously termed capillary or strawberry hemangiomas) are congenital lesions that become evident after the first few weeks of life. Treatment is indicated if the lesion involves the visual axis or causes some other amblyopic circumstance, such as significant astigmatism. The natural course of a capillary hemangioma is to increase in size until approximately 1 year of age, followed by involution over the next 4-5 years. It does not typically recur or regress immediately after birth.

Q1305
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A child is diagnosed with orbital rhabdomyosarcoma. What is the most likely finding on examination?
Correct answer: B. proptosis
Rationale
Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common primary pediatric malignancy of the orbit, and is thought to originate from undifferentiated mesenchymal cells. The patient usually presents with rapidly progressing painless proptosis, globe displacement, and eyelid/conjunctival swelling. Proptosis is the most common feature, present in 80%-100% of cases. A palpable mass and pain are less common features, present in 25% and 10% of cases, respectively.

Q1306
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the best test of binocular alignment to identify the presence of a tropia?
Correct answer: B. cover-uncover test
Rationale
Cover-uncover testing is the most important test to reveal a tropia. Alternate cover testing will measure both a tropia and a phoria. Worth 4-dot testing best measures suppression. The Lancaster red-green test is used for incomitant strabismus. Double Maddox rod testing precludes fusion and therefore does not differentiate between heterophorias and heterotropias.

Q1307
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the essential feature of monofixation syndrome?
Correct answer: A. presence of peripheral fusion with the absence of bifoveal fusion, due to a central scotoma
Rationale
Monofixation syndrome is a sensory state in strabismus where there is the presence of peripheral fusion with the absence of bifoveal fusion, due to a macular scotoma. Thus amblyopia may be present in the deviated eye, along with a reduction of stereopsis. Because of peripheral fusion and anomalous retinal correspondence, the Worth 4-dot test demonstrates suppression at distance, but fusion at near.

Q1308
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
An ophthalmologist examines the retina of this 5-year-old patient who presents with a failed vision screening in the left eye. Fundus findings are shown in the figure. For what systemic manifestation should the ophthalmologist be concerned?
Correct answer: A. intracranial arteriovenous malformation
Rationale
Wyburn-Mason syndrome (racemose angioma) is a rare sporadic disorder that is typically discovered in childhood. It is characterized by an arteriovenous malformation (AVM) of the retina (racemose angioma), as shown in the figure. Children present with decreased vision depending on the size of the retinal AVM, or proptosis from an intraorbital lesion. Seizures or intracerebral hemorrhage can occur because of an intracranial AVM that may bleed. Thus, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) is recommended in all patients. Other complications include neovascular glaucoma and intraocular hemorrhage.
Meningiomas are associated with neurofibromatosis type 2, optic pathway gliomas with neurofibromatosis type 1, and renal cell carcinoma with von Hippel-Lindau disease (angiomatosis of the retina and cerebellum).

Q1309
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
After attempted but unsuccessful treatment of his convergence insufficiency with orthoptic exercises, a 35-year-old man is unwilling to try adding prism to his glasses. What surgical procedure is most likely to improve his function?
Correct answer: C. medial rectus muscle resection
Rationale
Surgical treatment of convergence insufficiency is intended to improve ocular alignment primarily at near with reduction of the patient's exodeviation. This can be accomplished by lateral rectus recession or medial rectus resection, with no strong data suggesting one procedure is better, but medial rectus resection is more commonly chosen. Anterior transposition of the inferior oblique muscle can be used to treat dissociated vertical deviation. Recession/resection of all 4 rectus muscles can be used to treat congenital nystagmus in some patients. Posterior fixation of the lateral rectus muscles can be used for improvement of strabismus in high myopes.

Q1310
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A patient is found to have A-pattern exotropia with compensatory head posture. What is the most likely head posture?
Correct answer: C. chin-down
Rationale
In an A-pattern exotropia, the misalignment is more exotropic in downgaze and less exotropic in upgaze. Therefore, the patient may adopt a chin-down position to decrease or eliminate the misalignment. A chin-up position would worsen the alignment. A-pattern strabismus does not typically have lateral incomitance, so left and right face turns will not improve or worsen the alignment.

Q1311
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the most common cause of visual loss in infants with abusive head trauma (previously called shaken baby syndrome)?
Correct answer: A. cortical visual impairment
Rationale
Intracranial injury in shaken infants almost always includes subdural hematoma over the cerebral convexities or in the interhemispheric fissure. Cerebral parenchymal damage is evident on neuroimaging as edema, ischemia, or contusion, and in later stages as atrophy, which leads to cortical visual impairment.
The most common ocular manifestation is retinal hemorrhage involving the preretinal, deep retinal, or subretinal layers. Sometimes the retinal tissue becomes disrupted, leading to full-thickness perimacular folds in the neurosensory retina and traumatic retinoschisis. Full-thickness retinal breaks and detachments are rare. Cataract formation and hyphema may develop secondarily to direct trauma to the eye, but not primarily from the shaking itself.

Q1312
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What laboratory test is most likely to determine the etiology of anterior uveitis in a child?
Correct answer: B. antinuclear antibodies
Rationale
The most common identifiable etiology of anterior uveitis in a child is juvenile idiopathic arthritis, which occurs in 15%–47% of cases. Antinuclear antibody positivity is typically present in these children; rheumatoid factor is typically negative. Although juvenile spondyloarthropathies are associated with anterior uveitis in children, they are less common; thus, HLA-B27 testing is less likely to be beneficial. Infectious etiologies of anterior uveitis in children are less common, and results of serologic testing are less likely to reveal the etiology in these patients.

Q1313
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 1-year-old patient is diagnosed with pseudoesotropia. Cycloplegic retinoscopy is +2.00 OU. What is the most appropriate management?
Correct answer: A. reexamination of ocular alignment in 6-12 months
Rationale
The illusion of pseudoesotropia is commonly associated with prominent bilateral epicanthal folds. Because no real deviation exists, results of corneal light reflex testing and cover testing are normal. The appearance of pseudoesotropia changes with growth of the nasal bridge and does not require surgical correction. The amount of hypermetropia measured in this child is age-appropriate. However, due to the hypermetropia and pseudoesotropic appearance, re-evaluation should be done to rule out the development of an accommodative esotropia in the future.

Q1314
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What long-term refractive change is expected in the surgical eye of a 1-year-old child after an intraocular lens (IOL) is implanted?
Correct answer: C. increasing amounts of myopia
Rationale
Because the child's eye continues to elongate throughout the first decade of life, the selection of IOL power is complicated. Thus, if a child is made emmetropic at age 1 with an IOL and the eye continues to grow, the result would be an increasing amount of myopia. These factors need to be taken into consideration when choosing IOL power.

Q1315
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
Wilms tumor may develop in 30% to 50% of children with what congenital disorder?
Correct answer: D. sporadic aniridia
Rationale
Sporadic aniridia is associated with the WAGR complex (Wilms tumor, aniridia, genitourinary malformations, and mental retardation).
Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome is usually autosomal dominant, and 50% of cases develop glaucoma. Ocular findings in Goldenhar syndrome can include Duane syndrome, microphthalmia, upper eyelid coloboma, iris abnormalities, and corneal hypoesthesia. Weill-Marchesani syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive or autosomal dominant disease. Its ocular manifestations include microspherophakic lenses, severe myopia, and ectopia lentis.

Q1316
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
An 18-month-old child demonstrates an asymmetric, high-frequency, small amplitude ("shimmering") nystagmus, associated with head nodding. Neuroimaging is normal. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
Correct answer: D. observation
Rationale
Spasmus nutans is an idiopathic, asymmetric, high-frequency, small amplitude ("shimmering") nystagmus, associated with head nodding. It manifests during the first 2 years of life. The natural history is for the nystagmus and head nodding to diminish by 3-4 years of age. Spasmus nutans is a benign disorder in most cases, and management includes observation. Notably, because spasmus nutans-like nystagmus has been seen in the setting of chiasmal tumors, neuroimaging should be considered in these cases.
A Kestenbaum procedure is a surgery for nystagmus involving a recession-resection on both eyes. Vigabatrin is used to treat difficult-to-control seizures in tuberous sclerosis, and carbamazepine is used to treat superior oblique myokymia.

Q1317
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What surgery would most benefit an 18-month-old child with a V-pattern infantile esotropia and bilateral dissociated vertical deviations?
Correct answer: A. bilateral medial rectus recessions and bilateral inferior oblique recessions
Rationale
Children with infantile esotropia commonly have a V-pattern strabismus due to inferior oblique overaction. Inferior oblique recessions will address a V pattern and dissociated vertical deviation (DVD). Superior rectus recessions are done for DVD without inferior oblique overaction. Anterior oblique transposition is done to enhance the effect of the inferior oblique recession in these cases.
Unilateral recess and resect will not address the pattern or the DVD. Bilateral lateral rectus resections would address the esotropia, but a V pattern would be addressed by supraplacement, and this would not address DVD or inferior oblique overaction.

Q1318
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 4-month-old girl is brought for evaluation because her "eyes cross." Her cycloplegic refraction is +1.00 sphere in each eye. She has 40 prism diopters of constant esotropia in all directions of gaze. Using a toy for fixation, the ophthalmologist notes bilateral abduction deficits that resolve with patching each eye. No nystagmus is noted. What is the most appropriate long-term management for this patient to prevent the development of amblyopia?
Correct answer: C. strabismus surgery
Rationale
This patient has infantile esotropia. Pertinent clinical features of infantile esotropia include a deviation characteristically greater than 30 prism diopters, overelevation in adduction, dissociated vertical deviation (DVD), and low hyperopia (1.00-2.00 diopters). Equal visual acuity is common, and an apparent abduction deficit may result from cross-fixation. The infant’s ability to abduct can be elicited by the doll’s head maneuver, spinning the infant to stimulate the vestibulo-ocular reflex, or by observation with either eye patched. These patients usually have full abduction unless there is secondary medial rectus muscle restriction. Hyperopia or astigmatism greater than +2.50 diopters suggests a refractive strabismus. Deviation in primary position of less than 30 prism diopters is uncommon in infantile esotropia.
Deviations greater than 30 diopters are unlikely to resolve and will probably require surgical intervention; ocular alignment is rarely achieved without surgery in early-onset esotropia. The belief is that the eyes should be aligned by 2 years of age, preferably earlier, to optimize binocular cooperation. The Congenital Esotropia Observational Study showed that when patients present with constant esotropia of at least 40Δ after 10 weeks of age, the deviations are unlikely to resolve spontaneously. Smaller angles can be monitored, as they may improve spontaneously. Full cycloplegic refraction should be prescribed, but because there is minimal refractive error, this is unlikely to fully resolve the esotropia (ie, minimal accommodative component).

Q1319
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the preferred laboratory testing for a child with a unilateral congenital cataract?
Correct answer: A. no testing (typically none is needed)
Rationale
Unilateral cataracts are not usually associated with occult systemic or metabolic disease; laboratory tests are therefore not warranted. It is important to note that bilateral cataracts can have significant asymmetry, however, so deferring laboratory tests should be done with caution.
In cases of bilateral cataracts, multiple components of the history and physical examination, rather than a battery of tests (a "shotgun" approach), can be useful for directed laboratory investigations. Part of the evaluation of pediatric cataracts should focus on cataract morphology (eg, nuclear, lamellar, anterior polar, posterior lenticonus, etc.). Family history is useful in some cases (isolated inherited cataracts are usually autosomal dominant). Other features that could suggest a need for directed testing include external appearance (eg, many craniofacial syndromes are associated with cataracts, as are chromosomal abnormalities such as Down syndrome, trisomy 13, and trisomy 18), history of renal disease (eg, Alport syndrome or Lowe syndrome), or history of metabolic disorders (eg, diabetes mellitus, Fabry disease, Wilson disease, etc). TORCH titers can also be useful in certain circumstances.

Q1320
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
The 3-step test for cyclovertical muscle function is a useful diagnostic test for what class of vertical strabismus?
Correct answer: B. paralytic strabismus
Rationale
The 3-step test is used to identify which paralytic muscle is causing a cyclovertical strabismus. The 3-step test involves determining: (1) the hypertropic eye with distance fixation, (2) whether the misalignment is worse in left or right gaze, and (3) whether the misalignment is worse in left or right head tilt.
This test does not work with patients who have had previous strabismus surgery, have a restrictive disease (such as thyroid eye disease), or have Brown syndrome.

Q1321
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
For a patient with dissociated vertical deviation (DVD), what motility anomaly accompanies the upward movement?
Correct answer: D. extorsion of the globe
Rationale
Patients with dissociated strabismus can have accompanying extorsion and exodeviation (not esodeviation) of the elevating eye. Typically there is no hypodeviation of the fellow eye on cover testing, due to an apparent violation of Hering's law of motor correspondence. DVD is usually seen in infantile strabismus. In this form of strabismus, any associated nystagmus is of the latent variety, which has a horizontal vector.

Q1322
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
After laser surgery, a child with retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) demonstrates a 30 prism diopter (∆) right exotropia on Hirschberg testing. When the left eye is covered, the right eye does not move medially. What is the most likely reason for this finding?
Correct answer: B. positive angle kappa
Rationale
Angle kappa is the angle between the visual axis and the anatomical pupillary axis of the eye. The fovea is usually slightly temporal to the pupillary axis, making the corneal light reflection slightly nasal to the center of the cornea. This is termed positive angle kappa. A large positive angle kappa (eg, from temporal dragging of the macula in cicatricial retinopathy of prematurity [ROP]) can simulate exotropia.

Q1323
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
How is dissociated horizontal deviation (DHD) typically treated?
Correct answer: C. lateral rectus recession
Rationale
Dissociated strabismus can contain vertical, horizontal, and torsional components. When the dissociated abduction movement is predominant, it is called dissociated horizontal deviation (DHD). Treatment of DHD usually consists of unilateral or bilateral lateral rectus recession in addition to any necessary oblique or vertical muscle surgery. Base-out prisms and orthoptic exercises can be used to treat convergence insufficiency. Refractive correction of myopia can help control intermittent exotropia; however, DHD is not a true exotropia.

Q1324
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the defining clinical feature of monofixation syndrome?
Correct answer: A. evidence of peripheral sensory fusion without central fusion
Rationale
Monofixation syndrome describes peripheral fusion with the absence of bimacular (or central) fusion. The patient usually has a small deviation, usually less than 8 prism diopters of esotropia, which results in a central scotoma. Motor fusion is a vergence movement that is intended to cause retinal images to fall on corresponding retinal areas. This movement is present in monofixators, but central fusion is lacking as a result of the presence of a central scotoma.

Q1325
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A child with cognitive impairment, seizures, and hypomelanotic macules presents for routine eye care. What intraocular finding is most likely to be observed?
Correct answer: A. astrocytic hamartoma
Rationale
The classic triad of tuberous sclerosis (known as Vogt triad) includes cognitive impairment, seizures, and facial angiofibromas. Facial angiofibromas are not usually present in young children, but hypomelanotic macules called "ash-leaf spots" are. The most frequent and characteristic ocular manifestation of tuberous sclerosis is retinal phakoma, or astrocytic hamartoma. Phakomas are usually located near the posterior pole and involve the retina and/or optic nerve.
Capillary hemangioblastomas are associated with von Hippel-Lindau disease. Choroidal hemangiomas are the most significant retinal anomaly associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome. Incomplete peripheral retinal vascularization and subsequent proliferative retinal vasculopathy can occur in incontinentia pigmenti (Bloch-Sulzberger syndrome) and closely resembles that of retinopathy of prematurity.

What eye movement abnormality can occur in healthy infants in the first months of life?
Correct answer: D. intermittent esotropia
Rationale
In the first few months of life, episodes of intermittent strabismus are common. Constant strabismus is not normal, even at this early age. Vertical nystagmus and ocular flutter are also abnormal.

Q1327
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What feature of morning glory disc anomaly differentiates it from optic disc coloboma?
Correct answer: C. increased number of blood vessels coming off the disc
Rationale
Morning glory disc anomaly (MGDA) is the result of abnormal development of the distal optic stalk at its junction with the primitive optic vesicle. The anomaly is typically unilateral and is more common in girls. A morning glory disc anomaly appears clinically as a funnel-shaped excavation enveloping the optic disc. There is an increased number of blood vessels coming off the disc, and a white tuft of glial tissue may be observed in the center of the optic disc cup. Morning glory disc anomaly is typically unilateral. Morning glory disc anomaly is associated with basal encephalocele and midface anomalies. It is also associated with moyamoya disease. Moyamoya disease typically presents with constriction of the internal carotid arteries as they enter the skull base and join the circle of Willis. Blood vessel constriction often leads to recurrent strokes, and patients may be started on antiplatelet therapy. Therefore, all patients with morning glory disc anomaly should have a brain MRI/ MRA to rule out these 2 conditions.
Optic disc coloboma arises from an incomplete closure of the embryonic fissure. Colobomas vary in appearance from small excavations that resemble glaucoma to widespread excavation. The defect typically extends inferonasally and may extend to the uvea. It is usually bilateral but may be asymmetric in appearance. Complications include retinal detachment. Visual acuity can vary from 20/20 to very poor. Ocular coloboma may be associated with systemic findings and a number of syndromes, including CHARGE syndrome: Coloboma, Heart (tetralogy of Fallot), choanal Atresia, mental Retardation, Genitourinary abnormalities, and Ear abnormalities.

Sickle cell testing must be performed in all African American patients with hyphema. Because of sickling of the red blood cells in the anterior chamber, sickle cell trait or disease can result in elevated intraocular pressure, even in the presence of a small hyphema.

Four weeks after bilateral medial rectus muscle recession, a patient presents with a new exotropia of 15 prism diopters. On examination, there is limited adduction of the right eye. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. slipped muscle
Rationale
Limited adduction is evidence that the medial rectus muscle has reattached too far posteriorly to be effective as an adductor of the eye. Anterior-segment ischemia does not typically limit rotation and would not be expected after operation on only one extraocular muscle per eye. Adherence syndrome causing restriction would arise from adherence created on the opposite aspect of the globe, and the lateral rectus muscle was not included in the procedure. Conjunctival scarring over the medial rectus muscle would, if anything, limit abduction.

What clinical feature best distinguishes Apert syndrome from Crouzon syndrome?

Rationale
Crouzon and Apert syndromes have similar clinical appearances. However, Apert syndrome is associated with an extreme amount of syndactyly. Q1334
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the leading cause of vision loss in the world, as well as a leading cause of visual impairment?
Correct answer: C. cataract
Rationale
Cataract is the leading cause of vision loss in the world. The World Health Organization (WHO) has estimated that more than 20 million people are blind due to cataract and that the condition causes 51% of blindness worldwide. The majority of cases (up to 90%) of blindness due to cataract are found in developing areas. Cataract is also the leading cause of visual impairment, with 33% of the world’s population experiencing decreased vision because of this disorder; only refractive error has a greater impact in this regard.
As the leading cause of irreversible blindness in the world, glaucoma also poses significant public health problem. It has been estimated that by 2020, approximately 80 million people worldwide will have glaucoma, with 11.2 million bilaterally blind as a result. A meta-analysis estimated that the global prevalence is about 3.5%.

Children with glaucoma typically demonstrate other findings, including corneal clouding, corneal enlargement, hydrops, epiphora, and photophobia. Congenital endothelial dystrophy causes edema, not breaks in Descemet membrane.

Monocular elevation deficiency is an incomitant strabismus where there is deficient elevation in all horizontal orientations of the eye. Depression is typically normal in this syndrome. Elevation deficit in adduction only is suggestive of an inferior oblique paralysis. Elevation deficit in abduction only is suggestive of a superior rectus paralysis.

Correct answer: C. insulin-like growth factor I (IGF-1)
Rationale
Younger gestational age and lower birth weight are the risk factors most strongly associated with higher risk of developing ROP, and are related. A complex interaction between vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and insulin-like growth factor I (IGF-I) is believed to underlie abnormal angiogenesis. Low levels of serum IGF-I are reflective of poor overall growth and also appear to correlate with more severe ROP.

Q1338
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
An ophthalmologist is asked by the neonatal department to evaluate a premature infant for a possible embryogenetic defect. If the child has bilateral anophthalmia, at what stage did embryogenesis fail?
Correct answer: D. The optic vesicle did not grow out from the cerebral vesicle.
Rationale
The first step in ocular embryogenesis is the formation of the optic vesicle, which evaginates from the forebrain toward surface ectoderm. If this step fails, anophthalmia (also termed anophthalmos) results. The remaining choices describe progressive developmental steps in ocular formation. Failure of any particular step results in specific developmental abnormalities that are seen clinically.
Failure of embryonic fissure closure results in coloboma formation of the optic nerve head.
Branchial cleft abnormalities typically present as surface deformities defined by the Tessier system, with cleft palate and lip being the most common examples on the face. Multiple clefting patterns may occur in the periocular region; Goldenhar and Treacher Collins syndromes are good examples of periocular clefting abnormalities.
The choroidal fissure emanates from the ventral aspect of the optic stalk. It is most easily described as an anterior extension of the optic cup. Failure of choroidal fissure closure manifests as an iris coloboma.

Q1339

A 14-year-old girl has 10 prism diopters of exodeviation in upgaze and 10 prism diopters of esodeviation in downgaze. Examination of her extraocular movements is most likely to reveal overaction of what extraocular muscles?
Correct answer: D. inferior oblique muscles
Rationale
In a V-pattern strabismus, the horizontal deviation is more convergent in downgaze than in primary position and more divergent in upgaze than in primary position. It is often associated with overaction of the inferior oblique muscles. An overaction of the superior oblique muscles is associated with an A-pattern strabismus. Both the superior rectus and inferior rectus muscle actions are normal in V-pattern strabismus.

Correct answer: D. chloroma

Q1341
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 5-year-old child presents for evaluation of the lesions shown in the photo. Ophthalmologic examination also is significant for nystagmus and ocular motor apraxia. What is the most likely underlying condition?
Correct answer: B. Louis-Bar syndrome
Rationale
Ataxia-telangiectasia (AT; Louis-Bar Syndrome) is an autosomal recessive disorder from a genetic mutation of the ATM gene on chromosome 11 that results in defective repair of DNA breaks. Children develop early-onset ataxia between 1 and 5 years of age. It is associated with cutaneous telangiectasia and visceral telangiectasias that can bleed. Patients characteristically have difficulty initiating saccades, with preservation of vestibular-ocular movements (ocular motor apraxia). Strabismus and nystagmus also may be present. Other associated features include immunologic deficiency with increased risk of infections, malignancy, and coarse hair and skin.
Oculodermal melanocytosis (nevus of Ota) is a combined ocular and dermal pigmentation. In 10% of the patients, glaucoma occurs in the affected eye. Malignant melanoma can develop in the skin, conjunctiva, uvea, or orbit. The lifetime risk of uveal melanoma is 1:400.
Wyburn-Mason syndrome (racemose angioma) is a nonhereditary arteriovenous malformation of the eye and brain.
Von Hippel-Lindau disease (angiomatosis of the retina and cerebellum) is characterized by capillary hemangioblastomas of the retina and the brain (often the cerebellum).

Q1342
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What structure maintains the position of the extraocular muscles relative to the orbit?
Correct answer: B. fibroelastic pulleys
Rationale
The muscle pulleys are fibroelastic pulleys that maintain the position of the extraocular muscles in the orbit. The pulleys consist of collagen, elastin, and smooth muscle, enabling them to contract and relax. Dynamic MRI studies show that, in some cases, the pulleys act mechanically as the rectus muscle origins. The pulleys may also serve to stabilize the muscle path, preventing sideslipping or movement perpendicular to the muscle axis. Anterior, the pulleys merge with the intermuscular septum, which fuses with the conjunctiva 3 mm posterior to the limbus.

Q1343
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
During examination, a child is noted to have a compensatory face turn associated with an esotropic Duane syndrome, as shown. In an effort to improve this face turn, what surgical procedure is recommended?
Correct answer: C. recession of the medial rectus muscle on the left eye
Rationale
Duane syndrome is considered to be one of the “congenital cranial dysinnervation disorders,” which also includes Mobius and congenital fibrosis syndromes. Exposure to environmental agents that may affect fetal development in the first 6 weeks of gestation are risk factors for esotropic Duane syndrome. No surgical approach will normalize motility. However, for esotropic Duane syndrome, recession of the medial rectus muscle on the involved/inturning side has been the procedure most often recommended to correct the oculomotor deviation in primary position and reduce or eliminate the face turn. Deviations greater than 20 prism diopters may require adding recession of the opposite medial rectus, but that is not the best answer, given the small deviation pictured and the fact that recession of the medial rectus on the involved side is essential. Because of the risk of aggravated globe retraction, most surgeons do not favor resection of the lateral rectus muscle in esotropic Duane syndrome.

Q1344

A 4-year-old girl is newly diagnosed with iridocyclitis. She has had swelling of the left knee in the past, and the antinuclear antibody (ANA) titer is positive. In addition to corticosteroid eyedrops, what type of topical medication should be started?
Correct answer: D. mydriatic
Rationale
The patient has juvenile idiopathic arthritis with iridocyclitis. The inflammation in this condition is chronic, bilateral, and nongranulomatous. Posterior synechiae are very frequent and, when extensive, can lead to pupillary block and acute secondary angle closure. A mydriatic helps to break posterior synechiae and decrease the risk of this complication.
Miotics are contraindicated in active inflammation. NSAIDs and oral corticosteroids can be considered in moderate and severe disease but are not typically used for initial treatment. Typically, methotrexate is initiated if the disease severity warrants this, and there is recent evidence supporting the use of adalimumab as well. Given the systemic symptoms, this patient would be a great candidate for methotrexate concurrent with her topical therapy.

Q1345

A 12-month-old child is brought to the office with recurrent unilateral "pink eye" despite numerous courses of antibiotics, as well as lacrimal sac massage. What would be the preferred treatment?
Correct answer: A. probing and irrigation of the nasolacrimal system under general anesthesia
Rationale
Nasolacrimal duct obstruction is present in 5%-20% of newborns. It is most commonly caused by a persistent membrane at the valve of Hasner. It can resolve spontaneously in the first 9 to 12 months of life. Early treatment consists of lacrimal sac massage and antibiotic usage.
For nonresolving nasolacrimal duct obstructions, probing and irrigation is very successful. For recurrent obstruction after failed probing procedure, balloon catheter dilation and/or insertion of stents can be performed under general anesthesia.

For pediatric patients with presumed retinoblastoma, why are magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and ultrasonography the preferred imaging modalities instead of computed tomography (CT) scan?
Correct answer: D. CT scan subjects the child to radiation.
Rationale
Unlike MRI and ultrasonography, a CT scan subjects patients to radiation. Children with heritable retinoblastoma are at high risk for secondary radiation-induced tumors, so any additional radiation should be avoided if possible.

Q1347
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
How do ductions differ from versions?
Correct answer: D. ductions are monocular movements; versions are binocular
Rationale
Ductions are monocular rotations of the eye. Adduction is movement of the eye nasally; abduction is movement of the eye temporally. Supraduction is an upward rotation of the eye, while infraduction is a downward rotation of the eye.
Versions are binocular eye movements when the eyes move in the same direction.
Vergences are binocular eye movements when the eyes move in opposite directions. Convergence is movement of both eyes nasally to a given starting position, while divergence is movement of both eyes temporally to a given starting point.

Correct answer: C. systemic corticosteroids
Rationale
Lymphatic malformations of the orbit may present with sudden proptosis caused by spontaneous intralesional hemorrhage. Exacerbations tend to occur during upper respiratory tract infections and can be managed with a short course of systemic corticosteroids. Surgical intervention is deferred unless vision is affected. Systemic workup and systemic antibiotics are not indicated in this disorder. Complete surgical excision is often difficult, and attempts are reserved for cases where there is a threat of permanent vision loss.

Q1349
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the most appropriate approach to a left hypertropia occurring after a left orbital floor fracture without entrapment?
Correct answer: B. Observation for 6 months
Rationale
A patient with a left hypertropia after a left orbital floor fracture without entrapment most likely has weakness or palsy of the left inferior rectus. Initial management should be observation, as the weakness may improve with time.
If recovery is not complete within 6–12 months of the injury and there is at least a moderate degree of active force, resection of the affected muscle can be performed. If the hypertropia is large, the procedure can be combined with recession of the ipsilateral superior rectus muscle or recession of the contralateral inferior rectus muscle, with or without the addition of a posterior fixation suture (fadenoperation). Transposition of the ipsilateral medial and lateral rectus muscles to the inferior rectus muscle (inverse Knapp procedure) may be necessary for treatment of complete, chronic inferior rectus muscle palsy or when a crippling amount of recession has been necessary to relieve restriction.

Microcornea is defined by a horizontal corneal diameter at birth of less than or equal to what measurement?
Correct answer: C. 9 mm
Rationale
In the newborn, the corneal diameter is normally 9.5 mm to 10.5 mm. By the time the child is 2 years old, the cornea has reached its adult diameter, which averages 12.0 mm. A corneal diameter that is 9.0 mm or less at birth, or less than 10.0 mm when the child is more than 2 years old, is considered microcornea.

Stargardt disease is the most common hereditary macular dystrophy. It is bilateral, symmetric, and slowly progressive. Visual acuities level off at about between 20/50 and 20/200. Vision begins to slowly deteriorate between the ages of 8 and 15 years. Both photopic and scotopic vision is eventually affected.

Q1355
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 2-year-old child presents with a 30° right head turn. The patient cannot abduct the right eye, and there is narrowing of the palpebral fissure on adduction. Dilated funduscopic exam is normal. What is the most appropriate management?
Correct answer: D. right medial rectus recession
Rationale
The patient described has type 1 Duane retraction syndrome. A medial rectus recession on the affected side would correct the head turn and centralize the field of binocular vision. While limited abduction may be a result of a sixth nerve palsy, globe retraction causing narrowing of the palpebral fissures is diagnostic of Duane retraction syndrome. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is thus not necessary for further evaluation of a sixth nerve palsy; aberrant regeneration from a compressive lesion is unlikely in a 2-year-old, and if associated with the third nerve would result in widening of the palpebral fissure with or without miosis rather than narrowing of the palpebral fissure. A lumbar puncture to check for elevated intracranial pressure, which may be indicated in the presence of a sixth nerve palsy, is also not indicated, especially with a normal dilated fundus exam. A muscle biopsy for strabismus is used in cases of suspected chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO) to evaluate for ragged red fibers or mitochondrial DNA changes. A child with CPEO would be expected to present with ptosis and limitation of eye movements but not globe retraction.

Q1356

What initial therapy is used to treat the condition shown in this 7-day-old infant with Giemsa stain showing intracytoplasmic inclusions?
Correct answer: C. systemic erythromycin
Rationale
The photograph demonstrates a hyperacute conjunctivitis with purulent discharge in a newborn infant. This is neonatal conjunctivitis due to chlamydia, as evidenced by a Giemsa stain showing intracytoplasmic inclusions from a conjunctival scraping. The recommended treatment of chlamydial ophthalmia neonatorum is systemic erythromycin (oral or intravenous), even though inclusion conjunctivitis in the newborn usually responds to topical erythromycin or sulfacetamide. Systemic treatment can cover Chlamydia-associated infections, such as pneumonitis and otitis media, which can accompany inclusion conjunctivitis. Topical 1% silver nitrate solution and 0.5% erythromycin ointment are used for prophylaxis of infectious neonatal conjunctivitis (gonococcal and chlamydial disease). Erythromycin ointment is favored because topical silver nitrate solution can cause a chemical conjunctivitis. Originally, 2% silver nitrate was used as prophylactic treatment of gonorrheal ophthalmia neonatorum. However, it is not effective against C trachomatis and has largely been supplanted by agents that are effective against both N gonorrhoeae and C trachomatis, such as erythromycin and tetracycline ointments and 2.5% povidone-iodine solution.

Q1357
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 62-year-old woman developed horizontal binocular diplopia while driving 3 weeks ago. She has a 15 prism diopter right esotropia, which increases in right gaze. She refuses forced ductions. Saccades are evaluated. What finding supports the diagnosis of a right microvascular sixth nerve palsy over a restrictive right abduction deficit?
Correct answer: D. slower saccade of the right than left eye in right gaze
Rationale
Microvascular cranial nerve palsies render the affected extraocular muscle weaker. Observing a slower saccade in the direction of muscle action suggests a paretic muscle rather than a restrictive process, seen in this case as slower abduction of the right lateral rectus compared to the adduction of the left medial rectus on right gaze. Classically, restriction from a tight medial rectus or other orbital connective tissue involvement would produce a similar saccade speed but shorter amplitude than that of the contralateral eye, indicating that the muscle, while functionally shorter, is still strong.
Slower saccade of the left eye than the right eye in right gaze is incorrect because it suggests weakness of the left eye's medial rectus, a pattern common in left internuclear ophthalmoplegia.
Shorter saccadic amplitude is incorrect because it does not differentiate paretic from restrictive processes.

Q1358
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 17-year-old girl presents with congenital nystagmus associated with a null zone in right gaze and a preferred position in left face turn. She is orthotropic. What is the preferred surgical management to improve this patient's head posture?
Correct answer: B. recession of right lateral rectus, resection of right medial rectus, recession of left medial rectus, resection of left lateral rectus
Rationale
Extraocular muscle surgery can be performed to improve the head posturing in nystagmus by bringing the null point closer to the primary position. This involves rotating the eyes away from the null point. In this case, the procedure to be done is recession of right lateral rectus, resection of right medial rectus, recession of left medial rectus, resection of left lateral rectus. The other choices would have the following results:
  • Recession of right medial rectus, resection of right lateral rectus, recession of left lateral rectus, resection of left medial rectus would move the eyes in the other direction.
  • Recession of both medial recti, resection of both lateral recti would create exotropia.
  • Recession of both lateral recti, resection of both medial recti would create esotropia without adjusting the null point.

Q1359

What clinical test is most useful for measuring heterotropia separate from any underlying heterophoria?
Correct answer: C. simultaneous prism and cover test

Tests of ocular alignment can measure either the heterotropia or the combined heterotropia and heterophoria. The simultaneous prism-cover test measures the actual heterotropia separate from the heterophoria during binocular viewing and is especially useful in cases of monofixation syndrome.
The Lancaster red-green test, alternate prism-cover test, and double Maddox rod test all disrupt fusion and measure the combined heterotropia and heterophoria.

Q1360
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
In neonates, what is the most likely transmission method of Chlamydia trachomatis?
Correct answer: C. direct exposure during birthing
Rationale
Chlamydia trachomatis is an obligate intracellular bacterium that causes infections in infants and adults. Neonatal Chlamydia is typically transferred via direct contact with infected vaginal secretions during the birthing process. Trachoma, a chronic conjunctivitis in children and adults, is transmitted by direct contact with other infected people, insects, or fomites. Adult chlamydial conjunctivitis is sexually transmitted disease. Chlamydia is not typically transmitted transplacentally.

Q1361
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
Botulinum toxin injection for strabismus would be most effective for what condition?
Correct answer: B. acute, paralytic strabismus
Rationale
Botulinum toxin injection for strabismus is most effective for small to moderate horizontal misalignments. Botulinum toxin is also useful for postoperative residual strabismus, acute paralytic strabismus, and as a supplement to rectus recession for large-angle misalignments. It is not as effective for large deviations, A or V pattern strabismus, or secondary strabismus with an over-recessed muscle.

Q1362
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
An object that is projected onto a noncorresponding retinal point is seen singly. What is this called?
Correct answer: C. Panum's area
Rationale
If the horopter includes all points in space that stimulate corresponding retinal points, double vision would be expected when the target does not lie on the horopter. However, the visual system can combine slightly disparate points within a limited area surrounding the horopter, called Panum’s area of single binocular vision. Objects within Panum’s area do not result in diplopia. Objects outside Panum’s area stimulate widely disparate retinal points, resulting in physiologic diplopia. If an object is distal to Panum’s area, uncrossed physiologic diplopia will result; if an object is proximal to Panum’s area, crossed physiologic diplopia will result.

Q1363
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What has been shown regarding the adverse effects and visual outcomes for infants age 1 to 6 months who undergo cataract surgery with versus without intraocular lens placement?
Correct answer: D. IOL implantation in infants age 1 to 6 months is associated with a higher rate of adverse events requiring further surgery and no better grating acuity at 1 year.
Rationale
The Infant Aphakia Treatment Study Group showed that compared with contact lens rehabilitation in aphakic patients, IOL implantation in infants aged 1 to 6 months is associated with a significantly higher rate of adverse events requiring further surgery, but not associated with a significant difference in grating acuity at 1 year. Also, aphakic infants who had mild persistent fetal vasculature cataracts treated with contact lenses had a higher incidence of adverse events after lensectomy, compared with children with other forms of unilateral cataract. However, both groups had similar visual outcomes 1 year after surgery.

For a patient with sporadic aniridia, what is the most important associated extraocular condition that requires evaluation?
Correct answer: D. Wilms tumor
Rationale
In patients with sporadic aniridia, the presence of Wilms tumor must be excluded with renal ultrasonography, which must be repeated until molecular genetic analysis rules out an 11p13 deletion and confirms an intragenic PAX6 mutation. Iris abnormalities that are associated with systemic abnormalities include neuroblastoma in patients with Horner syndrome, Lisch nodules in patients with neurofibromatosis, and heterochromia in patients with Waardenburg syndrome.

What information does preferential-looking testing provide?
Correct answer: B. quantitative visual acuity in children who cannot cooperate for subjective visual acuity testing
Rationale
Teller Acuity Cards are used in a preferential looking test and can provide a quantitative visual acuity. The test relies on the observer noting at which image, when presented with a choice, the child prefers to look. It does not equate with Snellen acuities and has many false negatives and false positives. Other methods, such as LEA symbols or a Snellen chart should be used as soon as the child is capable.

A 7-year-old boy is diagnosed with mild exacerbation of orbital lymphatic malformation (orbital lymphangioma) in the right eye during an upper respiratory infection. Examination reveals normal visual acuity, normal optic nerve function, and 2 mm of right eye proptosis. What is the most appropriate initial management?
Correct answer: A. cold compresses and corneal lubricants
Rationale
Exacerbations of orbital lymphatic malformations (lymphangiomas) tend to occur with upper respiratory infections and can typically be managed conservatively if vision is not being threatened. A course of systemic steroids can be used in cases of marked ptosis or decreased vision. Surgical decompression may be done for acute orbital symptoms, but complete resection is not possible, due to the infiltrative nature of this type of lesion. There is no role for topical corticosteroids. Newer treatments include oral sildenafil and intralesional injection of sclerosing agents.

A 5-week-old boy presents with stable esotropia, bilateral sixth nerve palsies, and bilateral seventh nerve palsies since birth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: D. Möbius syndrome
Rationale
Möbius syndrome is a rare condition characterized by both sixth and seventh nerve palsies. Although they can present with esotropia, Duane syndrome and congenital fibrosis syndrome are not typically associated with seventh nerve palsies. Congenital myasthenia gravis is seen in the setting of a child born to a mother with myasthenia gravis and resolves rapidly.

Q1368
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
Intoxication with what class of eye drop would cause fever, flushing, dry mouth, and delirium?
Correct answer: A. cycloplegics
Rationale
Cycloplegic agents are competitive antagonists of the muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. Systemic intoxication includes fever, dry mouth, flushing, rapid pulse, nausea, dizziness, delirium, and erythema. A common mnemonic used to describe the physiologic manifestations of atropine overdose is "hot as a pistol, blind as a bat, dry as a bone, red as a beet, and mad as a hatter."
Adverse effects of pilocarpine (a cholinergic) administration include miosis, retinal detachment, headache, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Beta blockers can cause bradycardia and bronchospasm. Alpha agonists can result in fatigue, hypotension, and headache.

Q1369
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 25-year-old man is diagnosed with a right superior oblique palsy based upon his sensorimotor examination, which is shown. What historical and/or clinical findings would corroborate that he has an acquired superior oblique palsy?
Correct answer: A. recent head trauma, absence of facial asymmetry, and a larger deviation on left gaze
Rationale
Recent head trauma, absence of facial asymmetry, and a larger deviation in left gaze are consistent with a recently acquired superior oblique palsy. Whether acquired or congenital, patients present with a hypertropia worse in contralateral gaze and worse in ipsilateral (and not contralateral) head tilt. Childhood photographs documenting an oblique deviation suggest congenital onset. Unilateral superior oblique palsies are usually congenital, traumatically acquired or idiopathic. Traumatically acquired ones typically occur following closed head trauma. Microvascular disease or, rarely, tumors can also result in rare acquired or cryptic idiopathic unilateral superior oblique palsy, which is the most common isolated cyclovertical muscle palsy. Patients with acquired cases of superior oblique palsy may also complain of or demonstrate a torsional component on examination. Neuroimaging is usually recommended upon diagnosis of acquired superior oblique palsy.

Q1370
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 2-week-old infant with leukocoria is suspected of having persistent fetal vasculature (PFV).  Anatomically, what globe size strongly supports a diagnosis of PFV over retinoblastoma?
Correct answer: B. microphthalmia
Rationale
Persistent fetal vasculature (PFV) results from the failure of the fetal hyaloid vascular complex to regress, and is almost always unilateral. Clinically, a retrolental membrane of varying size and density is attached to the posterior lens surface. In contrast to retinoblastoma, which typically occurs in normal-sized eyes, these eyes are nearly always microphthalmic (small and disorganized globe) to some degree. Nanophthalmos refers to small eyes (axial length < 18 mm ) that have a high lens-to-anterior segment ratio but otherwise lack disorganization. Buphthalmos ("ox eye") refers to diffuse globe enlargement, usually in the setting of congenital glaucoma.

What is appropriate management for a persistent pupillary membrane?
Correct answer: C. observation
Rationale
Persistent pupillary membranes are rarely of visual significance. They can adhere to the anterior lens capsule and cause an anterior polar cataract, but these are usually small and do not need to be managed surgically.

Q1372
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the earliest sign of anterior segment ischemia following strabismus surgery?
Correct answer: C. anterior chamber cell and flare
Rationale
The blood supply to the anterior segment of the eye is partially supplied by the anterior ciliary arteries that travel within the 4 rectus muscles. Simultaneous rectus muscle surgery, especially on 3 or 4 muscles (but also 2 muscles in patients with poor circulation) can result in anterior segment ischemia. The earliest sign of this complication is cells and flare in the anterior chamber, with more severe cases causing corneal epithelial edema, Descemet membrane folds, and an irregular pupil. In the most extreme cases, anterior segment necrosis and phthisis bulbi can occur.

What is the most common cause of visual impairment in children with abusive head trauma?

Rationale
The most common cause of visual impairment in children with abusive head trauma is from cortical or cerebral visual injury due to neurologic damage. Optic atrophy and retinal injury can also cause decreased vision, but they are less-common causes.

Q1374
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
Most commonly, orbital cellulitis is caused by the spread of the infection from where?
Correct answer: A. the paranasal sinuses
Rationale
Orbital cellulitis is an infection of the orbit that involves the tissues posterior to the orbital septum. It is most commonly caused by the spread of infection from ethmoid or frontal sinusitis. Eyelid margin disease and insect bites can lead to lid swelling and can become secondarily infected. However, the infection is typically confined to the lid anterior to the orbital septum, leading to preseptal cellulitis rather than orbital cellulitis.

Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 16-year-old boy with a history of a congenital cranial nerve (CN) IV palsy is found to have marked overaction of the inferior oblique muscle, underaction of the superior oblique muscle, and excyclotorsion in the affected eye. What is the most appropriate surgical treatment option for this patient?
Correct answer: D. recession of the inferior oblique muscle in the affected eye
Rationale
In a unilateral CN IV palsy, weakness of the superior oblique muscle leads to underaction on depression and adduction. Thus, there is typically overaction of the antagonist muscle, the inferior oblique, leading to overelevation on adduction. Thus, the first approach to unilateral superior oblique paralysis is weakening of the antagonist inferior oblique muscle.

Q1376
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
An infant with epiphora and periocular crusting has a bluish mass inferior and nasal to the right medial canthus that has been present since birth. What diagnosis is most likely?
Correct answer: A. dacryocystocele
Rationale
Dacryocystocele (dacryocele) is a congenital condition present in approximately 3% of infants with nasolacrimal duct obstruction. It develops when a distal blockage causes distention of the lacrimal sac. Dacryocystocele presents at birth or within the first few days of life as a bluish swelling just below and nasal to the medial canthus. Symptoms of nasolacrimal duct obstruction, such as epiphora and periocular crusting, are often present. The differential diagnosis includes hemangioma, dermoid cyst, and encephalocele. Dermoid cysts and encephaloceles typically present above the medial canthal tendon. Hemangiomas have a vascular appearance and are not typically present at birth.

What genetic disorder is congenital iris ectropion most commonly seen in?

Rationale
Congenital iris ectropion can be an isolated finding or can be associated with neurofibromatosis 1, Prader-Willi syndrome, or facial hemihypertrophy. Retinal abnormalities can be seen in incontinentia pigmenti, dislocated lenses in Marfan syndrome, and corneal crystals in cystinosis.

What beneficial effect on the visual field can occur as a result of strabismus surgery?
Correct answer: D. expansion of the binocular visual field following surgery for esotropia
Rationale
Correction of esotropia can expand the binocular visual field. Surgery for exotropia constricts the binocular visual field. Monofixation is not eliminated in patients with infantile strabismus even if the eyes are aligned well.

Q1379
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 13-year-old boy presents with the fundus findings in the figures and cataracts in both eyes. What congenital infection did he most likely have?
Correct answer: B. rubella
Rationale
Congenital rubella syndrome is caused by the rubella virus, transmitted transplacentally (from pregnant woman to fetus). Eye findings include a variable pigmentary retinopathy from salt-and-pepper appearance to pseudoretinitis pigmentosa. In this case, the patient has macular pigmentary changes as well as peripheral pigmentary changes. Other eye findings in congenital rubella syndrome include cataract, glaucoma, and microphthalmos. Rubella has also been identified as a cause of Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis. Extraocular manifestations include hearing loss and cardiac abnormalities.
Congenital syphilis can present in the eye as a chorioretinitis with a salt-and-pepper retinopathy. However, cataracts are not seen with syphilis. Other eye findings include interstitial keratitis, uveitis, and glaucoma. Other early manifestations include persistent rhinitis, rash, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and pneumonia. Late findings include peg-shaped teeth and deafness.
Toxocariasis is infection caused by nematode larvae of a parasite common to dogs and cats; it is transmitted to humans through ingestion of soil contaminated by dog or cat feces. It presents in the eye as a typically unilateral posterior uveitis characterized by a large white granuloma in the retina that can cause retinal dragging. Cataracts are not typically seen in toxocariasis.
Congenital toxoplasmosis can present in the eye with retinitis or uveitis. The retina is usually thickened and white, with overlying vitritis. There may be a flat retinal scar at the edge of the lesion in the retina. Cataracts are not typical. Other findings include microcephaly, developmental delay, hepatosplenomegaly, and intracranial calcifications.

A 32-year-old woman undergoes strabismus surgery with adjustable sutures. What type of anesthesia is the most appropriate for postoperative suture adjustment?

Rationale
Topical anesthetic is most appropriate for adjustment of sutures postoperatively in adults. General anesthesia is necessary in children. Retrobulbar and sub-Tenon infusion are not indicated, because they can affect ocular motility.

Q1381
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the most likely type of strabismus expected to be seen in a child with fetal alcohol syndrome?
Correct answer: A. esotropia
Rationale
Fetal alcohol syndrome is a craniofacial condition caused by in-utero exposure to ethanol due to heavy alcohol use by women during pregnancy. Fetal alcohol syndrome is characterized by prenatal and postnatal growth retardation, central nervous system abnormalities, and a wide spectrum of malformations, the most typical of these being craniofacial. Pertinent facial features include short palpebral fissures, telecanthus, strabismus (especially esotropia), and ptosis. Ocular involvement can also include optic nerve hypoplasia (unilateral or bilateral) and increased tortuosity of the retinal vasculature. Nerve and muscle palsies and hypertropia are not components of fetal alcohol syndrome.

Q1382
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
An individual was involved in a car accident and has had vertical diplopia for 6 months. He has a right hypertropia that increases on left gaze and on right head tilt. The deviation is largest in gaze up and to the left. Surgery has been recommended. What procedure would be the most appropriate?
Correct answer: D. recession of the right inferior oblique
Rationale
These findings are consistent with a diagnosis of a right superior oblique weakness. The right eye is higher and the left eye is lower. The deviation is greater in left gaze. The muscle to be operated should be one whose greatest vertical action is in the direction of the greatest vertical deviation, which would be left gaze. Recessing the right inferior oblique (RIO) would lessen the hypertropia and would be the treatment of choice.
Resection of the left inferior rectus would increase the hypotropia of the left eye and increase the deviation. Resection of the right inferior rectus would lessen the left hypotropia, but since the deviation is worse in gaze up and left, it would not be the ideal choice. Intrasheath tenectomy of the right superior oblique would further weaken the right superior oblique and thereby increase the vertical deviation.

A patient is found to have A-pattern exotropia with a compensatory head posture. What head posture is the clinician most likely to observe?
Correct answer: B. chin down
Rationale
A and V patterns are variations of a primary position horizontal misalignment, so there is no reason for a compensatory head position unless it allows single binocular vision. For a patient with A-pattern exotropia, single binocular vision, if achievable, is attained only with the eyes directed upward, so a chin-down head position is most likely. Head tilting or viewing in lateral gaze does not achieve this result.

Q1386
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 3-year-old boy presents to the emergency room. The patient’s mother states that he accidentally fell from her lap and hit the floor. There is no reported loss of consciousness. After the ophthalmologist treats the abrasion and lid swelling, what is the appropriate next step?
Correct answer: C. Contact the designated governmental agency to report suspected child abuse.
Rationale
The patient presents with multiple head injuries in different locations, including lid ecchymosis and an occipital skull fracture. The patient’s mother states the patient fell from her lap and hit the floor. A fall to the floor is not consistent with the injuries examined. Therefore, the suspicion is raised for nonaccidental trauma. Any physician who suspects nonaccidental trauma is required by law in every US state and Canadian province to report the incident to the designated governmental agency. Indications of nonaccidental trauma include an account of events that does not correlate with the injuries observed (eg, multiple injuries in different locations from a fall) or with the child’s developmental stage (eg, a 1-month-old infant rolling off the edge of the bed).

In this picture, the broad epicanthal folds create the appearance of a left esotropia. The corneal light reflexes show that the eyes are in fact aligned.

Retinoblastoma is the most common malignant ocular tumor of childhood. In familial cases, it presents in the first year of life or between ages 1 and 3 in sporadic unilateral cases. The most common initial sign is leukocoria, followed by strabismus, vitreous hemorrhage, hyphema, hypopyon, ocular/periocular inflammation, glaucoma, and proptosis. Occasionally, the malignant cells enter the anterior chamber and present as pseudohypopyon. Hypopyon in childhood is retinoblastoma, until proven otherwise. Rationale
The figure depicts a molluscum contagiosum lesion. Molluscum contagiosum is a viral infection of the skin caused by a DNA poxvirus and generally occurs in children and immunocompromised patients. Parvovirus B19 causes a childhood rash called fifth disease, which is commonly called slapped cheek syndrome. Homocystinuria is an autosomal recessive condition associated with lens dislocation, with associated central nervous system and skeletal defects. The diagnosis is confirmed by detecting disulfides in the urine. Sulfite oxidase deficiency or molybdenum cofactor deficiency can also result in ectopia lentis. This enzyme deficiency interferes with conversion of sulfite to sulfate, resulting in increased urine excretion of sulfite. Increased sulfites and molybdenum cofactor deficiency are characteristic of sulfite oxidase deficiency. Epimerase deficiency is seen in a type of galactosemia.

Q1391
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What term describes a small and disorganized eye?
Correct answer: D. microphthalmia
Rationale
Congenital and developmental anomalies of the globe include:
  • Anophthalmia is absence of any ocular globe tissue. It is very rare; usually, when anophthalmia is clinically suspected, the child actually has severe microphthalmia.
  • Coloboma is the most common and least severe manifestation of the MAC spectrum. It is typically an inferonasal gap in the iris or retina.
  • Microphthalmia is a small, disorganized globe that can be associated with cystic outpouching of the posteroinferior sclera.
  • Nanophthalmos is a small eye, typically with an axial length of 18 mm or less and with associated high hyperopia.

What is the most likely ocular finding in a neonate with congenital rubella syndrome (CRS)?
Correct answer: A. bilateral pigmentary retinopathy
Rationale
A unilateral or bilateral pigmentary retinopathy is the most common ocular manifestation of CRS (25%–50%), followed by cataract (15%) and glaucoma (10%). The pigmentary disturbance, often described as “salt-and-pepper” fundus, shows considerable variation, ranging from finely stippled, bone spicule–like, small, black, irregular masses to gross pigmentary irregularities with coarse, blotchy mottling. It can be stationary or progressive. Despite loss of the foveal light reflex and prominent pigmentary changes, neither vision nor electroretinogram results are typically affected. Congenital (nuclear) cataracts and microphthalmia are the most frequent causes of poor visual acuity and, rarely, choroidal neovascularization (CNV). Unless otherwise compromised by glaucoma, the optic nerve and the retinal vessels are typically normal in appearance.

What rectus muscles form the spiral of Tillaux, inserting closest to the limbus to most posterior from the limbus?

The rectus muscles insert in a spiral, forming the spiral of Tillaux. The medial rectus inserts closest to the limbus, followed by the inferior rectus, then the lateral rectus, then the superior rectus, which inserts furthest (most posterior) from the limbus.

Neuroblastoma is a common childhood cancer that originates in the sympathetic ganglion chain or adrenal gland. It is the most common cause of orbital metastasis in children. Neuroblastomas undergo spontaneous regression in approximately 10% of cases.

A child with tilted optic discs and vision difficulties at night should be worked up for what possible hereditary condition?

A tilted disc appears as a disc with the superior portion elevated and the inferior portion displaced posteriorly. In addition, the disc may be horizontally rotated. Situs inversus (vessels initially go nasally before turning temporally off the disc) may be observed. Visual field may show a bitemporal hemianopia that does not respect the vertical midline, unlike a chiasmal lesion. Patients often have myopic astigmatism. Tilted disc syndrome is associated with X-linked congenital stationary night blindness. Congenital stationary night blindness is a group of hereditary conditions (X-linked most common form) causing rod dysfunction. Patients often present in infancy with nystagmus and a normal appearing fundus. However, some patients with the X-linked form present with myopic tilt and temporal pallor. Visual acuity varies from normal to poor. In CSNB, the most common ERG pattern shows a "negative" dark-adapted ERG: large a-wave with reduced (negative) b-wave.

Rationale
Juvenile xanthogranuloma is a self-limited, nonneoplastic histiocytic proliferation, occurring in infants younger than 2 years and typically regressing spontaneously by age 5 years. As in this patient, skin is involved as small, round, orange or tan papules. Iris lesions are unilateral and may occur either as small, localized, fleshy yellow-brown masses or be diffusely infiltrative, manifesting as heterochromia. The most characteristic clinical finding in patients with juvenile xanthogranuloma is spontaneous bleeding with hyphema. These patients may develop secondary glaucoma and significant vision loss and must be treated appropriately to avoid complications.
Child abuse must always remain in the differential in children; however, this patient has examination findings consistent with juvenile xanthogranuloma. Neurofibromatosis patients exhibit neurofibromas and café au lait spots different from the papules of juvenile xanthogranuloma. Furthermore, Lisch nodules in neurofibromatosis are not associated with spontaneous hyphemas.
