A child is being treated for orbital cellulitis and presents with worsening clinical symptoms. Orbital imaging should be performed to evaluate for what diagnosis?
Correct answer: A. subperiosteal abscess
Rationale
Orbital cellulitis, an infection of the orbit, involves the tissues posterior to the orbital septum. In children, worsening clinical symptoms are often associated with a subperiosteal abscess that requires surgical drainage; worsening symptoms are an indication for orbital imaging.
Preseptal cellulitis and eyelid abscess occur anterior to the orbital septum are less worrisome than orbital cellulitis and generally do not require imaging. Acute maxillary sinusitis is not usually associated with orbital cellulitis; ethmoid sinusitis is more commonly associated with it.

A pediatrician performs the red reflex exam (Brückner test) on a 3-month-old infant. What does this test assess?
Correct answer: A. ocular alignment
Rationale
The Brückner test evaluates the clarity and symmetry of the red reflex, identifies significant or asymmetric refractive errors, and determines the position of the corneal light reflex, which provides an estimate of ocular misalignment.

Q1399
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What type of childhood cataract is caused by thinning of the lens capsule?
Correct answer: B. posterior lenticonus
Rationale
Posterior lenticonus is caused by progressive thinning of the central part of the posterior capsule. This thinning may cause an oil droplet appearance in the red reflex. As the outpouching of the lens progresses, the surrounding cortical fibers gradually opacify. This process can take many years, but if the lens capsule develops a small tear, rapid, total opacification of the lens can occur.
PHPV may have a posterior plaque. Anterior polar and lamellar cataracts are not associated with thinning of the posterior capsule.

Q1400
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
In congenital nasolacrimal obstruction, what is the most common blockage location?
Correct answer: C. valve of Hasner
Rationale
Nasolacrimal duct obstruction typically occurs at the most distal portion of the lacrimal duct due to incomplete canalization near full-term gestation (40 weeks) of what was a solid structure in the fetus. This blockage occurs at the valve of Hasner. The canaliculi and puncta as well as the valve of Rosenmüller, which is in the region of the junction of the canaliculi, are more likely to have canalized normally.

Q1401
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What medication is the most appropriate treatment for an infant with ophthalmia neonatorum presenting at 1 week of age?
Correct answer: B. oral erythromycin
Rationale
Chlamydia trachomatis is the most likely etiology of ophthalmia neonatorum in this case. Systemic rather than simply topical treatment for Chlamydia is indicated because there is a risk of pneumonitis and otitis media. Doxycycline covers chlamydia; however, tetracyclines are contraindicated in children under 8 years old, since they can cause permanent discoloration of teeth. Topical ofloxacin (fluoroquinolone) and topical azithromycin (macrolide) would not provide systemic treatment.

Q1402
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
Why is active force generation tested in the evaluation of strabismus?
Correct answer: C. to differentiate paretic and restrictive strabismus
Rationale
Active force generation testing is indicated when there is a need to assess a muscle's contraction strength. An example involving extraocular muscles would be when differentiating a paretic from a restrictive strabismus. This test may also be revealing when deciding whether to recess or resect a muscle in a reoperative or a transposition procedure. Active force generation testing is relatively contraindicated in individuals with prior syncope or vasovagal reactions. It may also be contraindicated in individuals with filtering or inadvertent blebs if the globe must be grasped in the region of the elevated conjunctiva. Complications of the procedure include subconjunctival hemorrhage, which is expected, and corneal abrasion. The force generated by the levator palpebrae superioris or orbicularis oculi muscles is not usually assessed, because this information does not affect clinical management. Active force generation is not useful in differentiating an intermittent from a constant strabismus.

Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
Overaction of what muscle can result in an A-pattern strabismus?
Correct answer: B. superior oblique
Rationale
Superior oblique overaction results in an A-pattern strabismus and is commonly associated with exotropia. V-pattern and elevation of the involved eye in adduction are signs of inferior oblique overaction. Overaction of the rectus muscles does not cause A- or V-pattern strabismus.

Q1404
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the most likely benefit of strabismus surgery for congenital nystagmus with a null point?
Correct answer: A. reduced head turn
Rationale
Indications for strabismus surgery include improving functional vision by decreasing diplopia, relieving asthenopia, improving ocular alignment and establishing or restoring stereopsis, expanding binocular visual fields, or shifting best vision to a more central location (and by extension, reducing head turn). In congenital nystagmus with a null point, the null point may not be in primary gaze, and patients will adopt a compensatory head turn. A Kestenbaum-Anderson procedure shifts the null point to primary position. While some forms of congenital nystagmus are associated with strabismus, many may present in isolation. Strabismus surgery for nystagmus is not considered cosmetic, and strabismus surgery for nystagmus would not restore stereopsis.

When performing cataract surgery on children, why is the capsulorrhexis a technically challenging procedure?
Correct answer: D. The capsule is more elastic in children.
Rationale
A manual continuous curvilinear capsulorrhexis (CCC) can be difficult in pediatric cases due to the elasticity of the pediatric capsule. In children, the capsule is not more brittle and zonules are typically robust. Capsule thickness does not affect the surgical characteristics of the anterior capsule.

Q1406
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 5-month-old boy has nystagmus and poor visual attention. The anterior segment is normal, but the posterior pole shows bilateral double-ring signs. What finding may be expected on neuroimaging?
Correct answer: C. absent septum pellucidum
Rationale
The double-ring sign is diagnostic of optic nerve hypoplasia (ONH). When bilateral, ONH is associated with midline central nervous system (CNS) defects, with an absent septum pellucidum and agenesis of the corpus callosum; sensory nystagmus is also commonly present. Pineal gland tumors are not associated with ONH. ONH is associated with pituitary abnormalities, but not pituitary adenomas. The lateral ventricles are normal sized in ONH.

Q1407
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
For high accommodative convergence/accommodation (AC/A) esotropia, what is the most appropriate initial therapy?
Correct answer: A. bifocal spectacles
Rationale
Bifocals reduce the need for accommodation at near and thus allow the potential development of fusion and stereopsis. Overminused glasses increase accommodation. Alternate occlusion theoretically reduces suppression, but has no role in treating high AC/A esotropia. Base-in prism would increase the deviation in a patient with high AC/A esotropia.

Q1408
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A child presents for a second opinion for chronic follicular conjunctivitis recalcitrant to topical steroids and antibiotics. The ophthalmologist notes a 2-mm skin-colored, dome-shaped mass on the eyelid margin with a central small crater. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. molluscum contagiosum
Rationale
Molluscum contagiosum affects primarily children 1 to 10 years of age, but adults may be infected from exposure to lesions, especially through sexual activity or if immunodeficient. The virus spreads from close contact (children at play, wrestling, sexual contact) or from scratching the nodules or coming in contact with fomites directly or through towels, communal baths, or tattoo instruments. The lesions typically last 6 to 8 weeks. Any area of skin may be affected, usually torso or limbs but occasional eyelids. The lesions are single or multiple flesh-colored, opalescent, and domeshaped, measuring 1 to 5 mm in diameter. A central depressed crater develops with a waxy core. The eyelid margin location may be associated with unilateral, chronic follicular conjunctivitis.
Multiple molluscum lesions in an adult should prompt consideration of HIV/AIDS. In contrast to other pox viruses, necrosis at the site of the lesion usually does not occur. Molluscum "bodies" can be demonstrated by smearing a glass slide with the material expressed from the central crater and examination with Giemsa, Gram-Wright, or Papanicolaou stains. Minor trauma (expression of the core, curettage, cryotherapy) often leads to regression. Eyelid margin lesions (usually single) may be removed by excisional biopsy and submitted for standard histopathologic diagnosis. This is usually curative for molluscum-associated follicular conjunctivitis.
Molluscum contagiosum is caused by a DNA pox virus (molluscum contagiosum virus-MCV). The virus has 4 subtypes (MCV 1-4), with MCV-1 most prevalent, but with geographic variation. MCV infects all layers of the epithelium, multiplying in the cytoplasm of squamous cells, eventually creating a central crater filled with debris, which includes viable, contagious viral particles that are easily shed or abraded. Pathologic findings are marked thickening of the squamous layer of the epithelium, forming expanded, localized intraepidermal nodules. The squamous cells are filled with granular material (MCV particles), which replaces the cytoplasm and compresses the nucleus, forming molluscum inclusions. The central crater contains a plug of necrotic debris, molluscum bodies, and contagious viral particles. The figures show selected findings.

A child with bilateral optic nerve hypoplasia is found to have an absent septum pellucidum. What further workup is necessary?
Correct answer: A. endocrine workup
Rationale
The correct answer is an endocrine workup. De Morsier (septo-optic dysplasia) syndrome involves optic nerve hypoplasia, absent septum pellucidum, and pituitary dysfunction. The decreased pituitary function can be life-threatening, and any patient with concern for this syndrome should have rapid endocrine evaluation for the need of hormone replacement. Any child with optic nerve hypoplasia should have magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain as part of the evaluation.

Q1412

At what age is intraocular lens implantation in children widely accepted?
Correct answer: B. age 1-2 years
Rationale
The choice of optical device for correction of aphakia depends primarily on the age of the patient and the laterality of the cataract. Intraocular lens (IOL) implantation in children aged 1–2 years and older is widely accepted. The use of IOLs in younger infants, however, is associated with a higher rate of complications and larger shifts in refractive error with age.

Q1413
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What imaging tests should be obtained in a patient with a morning glory disc anomaly?
Correct answer: D. brain MRI and magnetic resonance angiography (MRA)
Rationale
Morning glory disc anomaly (MGDA) is the result of abnormal development of the distal optic stalk at its junction with the primitive optic vesicle. The anomaly is typically unilateral and is more common in girls. A morning glory disc anomaly appears clinically as a funnel-shaped excavation enveloping the optic disc. There is an increased number of blood vessels coming off the disc, and a white tuft of glial tissue may be observed in the center of the optic disc cup. Morning glory disc anomaly is typically unilateral and visual acuity can range from 20/20 to no light perception. Retinal detachment is a known complication. Morning glory disc anomaly is associated with basal encephalocele and midface anomalies. It is also associated with moyamoya disease. Moyamoya disease typically presents with constriction of the internal carotid arteries as they enter the skull base and join the circle of Willis. Blood vessel constriction often leads to recurrent strokes, and patients may be started on antiplatelet therapy. Therefore, all patients with morning glory disc anomaly should have both a brain MRI and brain MRA to rule out these 2 conditions.

Q1414
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
An 8-year-old patient presents with lethargy, bilateral vision loss, bilateral pain with eye movement, and swollen optic discs. Her neurologic examination is normal, and aside from optic nerve enhancement, the magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) result is normal as well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: C. optic neuritis
Rationale
Optic neuritis is a demyelinating disorder of the optic nerve, usually considered to be autoimmune. In children, it usually presents after a viral illness. Optic neuritis in children, in contrast with that in adults, is more frequently bilateral and associated with disc edema, as well as vision loss, systemic symptoms, and pain on eye movement. Although multiple sclerosis can present with optic neuritis, the diagnosis requires brain lesions on MRI. Increased intracranial pressure and compressive optic neuropathy can present with vision loss and swollen optic discs, but typically do not involve pain with eye movements.

Q1415

During probing of the lacrimal system, the sensation of a "hard" stop at the end of the horizontal passage of the probe is characteristic of what condition?
Correct answer: B. successful probing to the nasal bone of the lacrimal sac
Rationale
A hard stop at the end of the horizontal phase of lacrimal system probing is a helpful tactile sign, indicating that the probe is contacting the thin tissues overlying the bony lacrimal fossa and that then the probe may be redirected down into the nasolacrimal duct. Lacrimal tumor or canalicular obstruction would be associated with the sensation of a soft stop and would warrant further evaluation.

What is the best management of a white-eyed blowout fracture in a child?

White-eyed blowout fractures present with marked vertical motility restriction in both directions with minimal soft-tissue findings. Unless there is early surgical repair of the fracture, the inferior rectus muscle and its associated nerve can be permanently damaged.

Q1417
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
Corneal light reflex (reflection) tests should be used to evaluate binocular alignment for what patients?
Correct answer: A. patients with poor vision in one or both eyes
Rationale
Corneal light reflex tests are useful in assessing ocular alignment in patients who are unable to cooperate sufficiently to allow cover testing or who have poor vision in one or both eyes, and consequently have poor fixation. The main tests of this type are the Hirschberg, modified Krimsky, Brückner, and major amblyoscope methods. Children with good vision in both eyes will usually tolerate cover methods and do not display avoidance. The corneal light reflex method is less sensitive or quantitatively precise than cover-uncover or cross-cover methods, so it is less helpful in less severe amblyopia or strabismus.
The Hirschberg method is based on the premise that 1 mm of decentration of the corneal light reflection corresponds to approximately 7°, or 15 prism diopters, of ocular deviation of the visual axis.
The Krimsky method uses reflections produced on both corneas by a penlight and is ideally used at near fixation. The original method involved placing prisms in front of the deviating eye. More common modifications today involve holding prisms before the fixating eye or split between the 2 eyes. By adjusting the prisms to center the corneal reflection in the deviated eye, it is possible to approximate and quantitate the near deviation.
In order to perform the Brückner test, the examiner uses a direct ophthalmoscope to obtain a red reflex simultaneously in both eyes. Note that this test detects but does not measure the deviation. The major amblyoscope method uses separate target illumination, which can be moved to center the corneal light reflection. The amount of deviation is then read directly from the scale of the amblyoscope.

Q1418
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the most common ocular finding associated with morning glory disc anomaly?
Correct answer: D. retinal detachment
Rationale
Morning glory disc anomaly (MGDA) is the result of abnormal development of the distal optic stalk at its junction with the primitive optic vesicle. The anomaly is typically unilateral and is more common in girls. A morning glory disc anomaly appears clinically as a funnel-shaped excavation enveloping the optic disc. There is an increased number of blood vessels coming off the disc, and a white tuft of glial tissue may be observed in the center of the optic disc cup. Morning glory disc anomaly is typically unilateral and visual acuity can range from 20/20 to no light perception. Retinal detachment is seen in up to 30% of these patients. Morning glory disc anomaly is associated with basal encephalocele and midface anomalies. It is also associated with moyamoya disease. Moyamoya disease typically presents with constriction of the internal carotid arteries as they enter the skull base and join the circle of Willis. Blood vessel constriction often leads to recurrent strokes, and patients may be started on antiplatelet therapy. Therefore, all patients with morning glory disc anomaly should have both a brain MRI and a brain MRA to rule out these 2 conditions.
Peripheral retinal nonperfusion has been reported with morning glory disc anomaly but is not common. Disc drusen and combined hamartoma of the retina and retinal pigment epithelium are not associated with this condition.

Q1419

Anterior segment ischemia most commonly occurs following what type of ophthalmic surgery?
Correct answer: B. strabismus surgery
Rationale
Anterior segment ischemia is most frequently induced by disruption of the anterior ciliary arteries that travel within the 4 rectus muscles. Strabismus surgery (particularly that which involves more than 2 rectus muscles) is the most common cause of anterior segment ischemia. The other surgeries listed (pterygium excision with conjunctival graft, glaucoma tube shunt implantation, and limbal stem cell transplantation) are not typically associated with disruption of the anterior segment vasculature.

Q1420

A 71-year-old man presents with binocular diplopia on the morning following cataract surgery with retrobulbar anesthesia. What mechanism is most likely responsible for the diplopia?
Correct answer: A. inferior rectus injury
Rationale
Injected local anesthesia can have a direct toxic effect on muscle tissue. Hyaluronidase may be partially protective by allowing more rapid diffusion of the anesthetic agent. The inferior and superior recti are susceptible to direct injury with the needle in retrobulbar and peribulbar anesthesia, respectively. Inadvertent intravenous injection of local anesthetics can cause cardiac arrhythmia. Inadvertent intradural injection is associated with seizures, respiratory arrest, and brainstem anesthesia. Other complications of retrobulbar injection include retrobulbar hemorrhage and globe perforation.
Other causes of binocular diplopia after cataract surgery could include disruption of fusion in predisposed patients. Surgically induced astigmatism could be associated with monocular diplopia.

Q1421

A 4-day-old infant presents with chemosis, significant discharge, and corneal ulceration. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: A. Neisseria gonorrhoeae conjunctivitis
Rationale
Neisseria gonorrhoeae conjunctivitis

Ophthalmia neonatorum caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae typically presents in the first 3–4 days of life. In severe cases, it is associated with marked chemosis, significant discharge, and a risk of corneal perforation. Chemical conjunctivitis is a mild, self-limited inflammation occurring in the first 24 hours of life due to instillation of silver nitrate. Herpes simplex virus conjunctivitis usually presents later, often in the second week of life. Chlamydial conjunctivitis usually occurs around 1 week of age and is associated with minimal to moderate discharge and possible pseudomembrane formation.

Q1422
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the mechanism of action of botulinum toxin?
Correct answer: D. It prevents the release of acetylcholine from presynaptic motoneurons.
Rationale
Purified botulinum toxin type A is used for various ophthalmic applications for its effect at paralyzing muscles in a local area. The botulinum toxin binds to the presynaptic motoneuron of skeletal muscles and prevents the release of acetylcholine into the neuromuscular junction. Agents such as curare derivatives, as well as myasthenia gravis, block acetylcholine receptors in the postsynaptic motor end plate.
There are no known agents that increase cholinesterase activity in the neuromuscular junction, though many medications have been developed to inhibit cholinesterase activity. Succinylcholine causes systemic skeletal muscle weakness by persistently depolarizing the postsynaptic motor end plate.

Q1423

An ophthalmologist is in the operating room to repair a globe that is ruptured due to a piece of metal that struck the patient’s right eye. The ophthalmologist identifies the full thickness scleral laceration that starts at the inferior limbus and extends posteriorly. A generous peritomy allows the surgeon to identify all extents of the laceration, which starts at the limbus and extends to the anterior border of the inferior rectus, but does not extend beyond that. What is the best estimate of the length of the laceration?
Correct answer: A. 6.5 mm
Rationale
This question is testing knowledge regarding the spiral of Tillaux, which describes the distance posterior to the limbus where the rectus muscles insert. The muscle closest to the limbus is the medial rectus (5.5 mm). From here, heading inferiorly, the muscles "spiral" out with increasing distances from the limbus: inferior rectus (6.5 mm), lateral rectus (6.9 mm), and superior rectus (7.5 mm). There is some variation in the exact distances, but 6.5 mm is the best choice.

The 4-prism diopter base-out test is used to document a small macular scotoma in a patient with monofixation syndrome. When the prism is placed before one eye and then the other during binocular viewing, a patient with bifixation will show movement away from the eye covered by the prism. A patient with monofixation will not show any movement. The 4-prism diopter base-out test is not a test for amblyopia, peripheral scotomas, or sensory fusion.

This child presents with an esotropic deviation and is at an age typical of a patient with accommodative esotropia. The refraction of significant hyperopia suggests that this is indeed accommodative esotropia, and glasses for the hyperopic correction should be prescribed. Surgery or botulinum toxin injection should not be performed unless there is residual esotropia after all the hyperopia is corrected for with glasses. However, they are relatively orthotropic at distance.

In what cardinal position is the left superior oblique muscle the prime mover?

Cardinal positions are those positions in which the prime mover is 1 muscle of each eye, together called yoke muscles. The 6 cardinal positions of gaze are straight right, up to the right, up to the left, straight left, down to the left, and down to the right. Straight up and straight down are not cardinal positions. The left superior oblique is the primary mover in the left eye when the eyes are positioned down and to the right. The 9 diagnostic positions of gaze incorporate the 6 cardinal positions plus straight up and down and primary position.

The addition of parentheses around the T indicates an intermittent tropia. Constant deviation is denoted without any parentheses. Comitant deviation is determined by noting the same deviation in all directions of gaze. X denotes outward deviation (exo-), E denotes inward deviation (eso-), H denotes upward deviation (hyper-), and Ho denotes downward deviation (hypo-).

Congenital aphakia is rare and is typically associated with a severely abnormal eye. Lens colobomas involve flattening or notching of the lens, usually inferonasally, and may be associated with iris, optic nerve, or retinal colobomas, all of which relate to incomplete closure of the embryonic fissure. The eye may be otherwise normal. Spherophakic lenses are smaller, round, and usually occur bilaterally. They may prolapse into the anterior chamber or cause pupillary block. Q1432

A 6-year-old child presents with a 35Δ intermittent exotropia at distance and a 20Δ intermittent exotropia at near. After the patch test, measurements for this patient are 35Δ exotropia at distance and 30Δ exotropia at near. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Rationale
When the exodeviation at distance is larger than the deviation at near fixation by 10Δ or more but the distance and near measurements become similar after 30–60 minutes of binocular occlusion using a patch (the patch test), pseudodivergence excess intermittent exotropia is the likely diagnosis. An intermittent exotropia may become constant after disruption of binocular fusion with patch testing. In true divergence excess intermittent exotropia, the distance–near discrepancy would persist after patch testing. A patient with distance–near discrepancy may have a high accommodative convergence/accommodation (AC/A) ratio, which would be defined by persistence of the distance–near discrepancy after the patch test but resolution of this discrepancy with a +3.00 add. In a patient with basic intermittent exotropia, the measurement of the deviation at distance would be within 10Δ of the deviation measurement at near without patch testing or a +3.00 add.

Q1433
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What clinical finding can distinguish orbital cellulitis from preseptal cellulitis?
Correct answer: D. conjunctival chemosis
Rationale
The presence of conjunctival chemosis suggests orbital involvement. Eyelid swelling, sinusitis, and fever can be present with both preseptal cellulitis and orbital cellulitis.

Q1434
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A mother brings her 7-year-old son in for evaluation after observing his "excessive blinking." His ophthalmologic examination is unremarkable. What is the preferred management?
Correct answer: B. reassurance and observation
Rationale
Excessive blinking is a common complaint in children. Medical causes can include surface irritation, dry eye syndrome, allergic conjunctivitis, intermittent strabismus, uncorrected refractive error, and tics. However, most cases are benign and self-limited and require only observation and reassurance. Psychiatric consultation or neurologic consultation is not indicated without other findings; head imaging is not indicated.

Q1435
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What are the cardinal positions of gaze?
Correct answer: D. up and right, up and left, right, left, down and right, down and left
Rationale
The positions of gaze are:
  • Primary position is the position of the eyes when they are fixating straight ahead.
  • Secondary diagnostic positions are straight up, straight down, right gaze, and left gaze.
  • Tertiary diagnostic positions are the 4 oblique positions of gaze: up and right, up and left, down and right, down and left, as well as the right and left head-tilt positions.
  • Cardinal positions, which correspond to the primary fields of action of the extraocular muscles (EOMs), are up and right, up and left, right, left, down and right, down and left.

Q1436
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
An ophthalmologist evaluates a woman referred for the symptomatic A-pattern exotropia shown. What clinical finding might the examination disclose?
Correct answer: A. superior oblique overaction
Rationale
Superior oblique muscle overaction is associated with A patterns, and inferior oblique muscle overaction is associated with V patterns. An A pattern is considered clinically significant when the difference in measurement between upgaze and downgaze is at least 10 prism diopters. For a V pattern, the difference for clinical significance must be at least 15 prism diopters. The measurements in upgaze and downgaze are recorded approximately 25 degrees from primary position. These patients may experience diplopia in primary gaze.

Q1437
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 6-year-old child presents with persistent tearing and pain OD after playing outside. Slit-lamp examination reveals linear corneal defects. What is the appropriate next step?
Correct answer: C. Evert the upper eyelid.
Rationale
Retained corneal and conjunctival foreign bodies can be associated with failure of the patient to properly heal. Corneal foreign bodies can sometimes be removed in cooperative children at the slit lamp. If there is suspicion of a retained conjunctival/tarsal foreign body, the eyelids can be everted and a cotton swab can be used to sweep the fornices.

What is the most common type of strabismus associated with craniosynostosis?
Correct answer: D. V-pattern exotropia
Rationale
Patients with craniosynostoses can have various types of horizontal strabismus. V-pattern exotropia is the most common type.

Q1439
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
An adult presents with a right hypertropia worse in left gaze. What would suggest that the strabismus is longstanding?
Correct answer: A. old photos showing a left head tilt
Rationale
This adult has signs of a superior oblique palsy. Signs of chronicity would include gradual onset of symptoms, increased vertical fusional amplitudes, and a history of a head tilt (which can be assessed from old photos or a driver's license). When obtaining a history from a patient with strabismus, onset of symptoms should be assessed, as well as whether the condition is intermittent or constant, or associated with other events (trauma or illness), and whether the symptoms vary in different gazes. Comparing superior oblique size on MRI between the affected and unaffected sides does not reliably distinguish acquired from congenital palsies.

Q1440
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A child presents with a broad forehead and bilateral coronal suture synostosis. No abnormalities of the hands or feet are noted. Genetic testing shows a mutation in the fibroblast growth factor receptor FGFR2 gene. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. Crouzon syndrome
Rationale
Craniosynostosis syndromes have premature closure of the calvarial sutures and are often associated with syndactyly and brachydactyly. They are caused by defects in the FGFR or TWIST genes. Crouzon syndrome is the only craniosynostosis syndrome without digit abnormalities. Apert syndrome and Pfeiffer syndrome always have syndactyly or brachydactyly. Saethre-Chotzen syndrome is a milder craniosynostosis and is associated with brachydactyly and mild syndactyly.

Q1441
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the most common ocular finding associated with nonaccidental abusive head trauma?
Correct answer: D. retinal hemorrhage
Rationale
Violent shaking of infants is associated with ocular, intracranial, and other injuries. The historical terminology “shaken baby syndrome,” is still in use but being replaced by the preferred “abusive head trauma,” or “inflicted childhood neurotrauma.” Most often, patients affected are less than 1 year old, and often less than 6 months old, because a crying, inconsolable infant is believed to trigger a frustrated or angry caregiver. There may be a history of mental status changes with a reported history of minor trauma. In the United States and Canada, any physician suspicious of child abuse is required to report the case to the appropriate governmental agency.
The most common ocular finding in abusive head trauma is retinal hemorrhage, which is present in 80% of positive cases. Hemorrhages can be present in all layers, may be unilateral or bilateral, and often resolve quickly. Other ocular findings associated with abusive head trauma include circumferential full-thickness perimacular folds of the neurosensory retina, retinoschisis cavities (often partially filled with blood), and vitreous hemorrhage. Retinal breaks and detachments are notably rare in this clinical scenario. Adnexal and anterior segment injuries are also typically absent. AHT is associated with high morbidity and mortality. A mortality rate of 29% among a large cohort of AHT patients has been reported.
Long-term cognitive and motor dysfunction, as well as visual impairment are potential complications. The most common cause of vision loss in AHT is cortical injury, followed by optic atrophy, although dense vitreous hemorrhage can also be amblyogenic.

Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
The greatest risk of rebleeding in traumatic hyphema occurs how long after initial injury?
Correct answer: C. 3-7 days
Rationale
One of the risks of hyphema is rebleeding, with worsening symptoms. This is especially critical in children, who often are noncompliant with activity restrictions. The greatest risk for rebleeding occurs within 3 to 7 days. After 7 days, the risk progressively decreases.

Q1443
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What term describes the deviation measured when a paretic or restricted eye is fixating?
Correct answer: A. secondary
Rationale
A secondary deviation is the deviation measured when the paretic or restricted eye is fixating. It is larger than a primary deviation, which is the deviation measured when the nonparetic eye is fixating. A consecutive deviation is a strabismus that is in the direction opposite to one that the patient had originally. A comitant deviation is a strabismus that is the same size in all positions of gaze.

Q1444
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 10-year-old child is evaluated for a right hypertropia noted after closed head trauma. Upon covering the left eye, the uncovered right eye depresses, while the covered left eye elevates. What is the most likely cause of this child's strabismus?
Correct answer: D. infantile
Rationale
When evaluating a vertical deviation, cover testing helps assess the relationship between the elevators and depressors of the 2 eyes. In this case, the covered left eye violates Hering's law by elevating instead of depressing. This anomalous movement is consistent with dissociated vertical deviation, found in individuals with infantile strabismus. If the child had a paralytic strabismus (such as a right 4th nerve palsy) or a restrictive strabismus (such as one secondary to a posterior orbital floor fracture), the left eye would adopt a hypotropic position. Poor vision after trauma can cause a sensory strabismus, but is typically horizontal, and on cover testing the poor-seeing eye may not be able to reestablish fixation.

Q1445
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the ophthalmic clinical feature most commonly associated with Goldenhar syndrome?
Correct answer: D. limbal dermoid
Rationale
Goldenhar syndrome (oculoauricular dysplasia) is frequently associated with limbal dermoids, which can be bilateral in 25% of cases. They occasionally impinge on the visual axis, but most likely affect vision by inducing astigmatism. In addition, Goldenhar syndrome can be associated with eyelid colobomas, ptosis, narrow palpebral fissures and Duane retraction syndrome.
Exophthalmos is seen in Crouzon syndrome and Alpert syndrome, among other conditions; microphthalmos is seen in Goldenhar syndrome. Wedge-shaped cortical cataract is idiopathic or associated with occult posterior segment tumor, previous blunt trauma, or retinal coloboma. Eyelid ptosis is associated with various conditions, including fetal alcohol syndrome, third nerve palsy, and rhabdomyosarcoma.

Q1446
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 5-month-old boy with cerebral palsy is referred for poor visual responses. On examination, the infant is noted to have searching eye movements associated with an otherwise normal eye examination, including normal pupillary responses. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. cerebral visual impairment
Rationale
The loss of vision due to pathology posterior to the lateral geniculate nucleus is called cerebral visual impairment. It is characterized by normal ocular structures and normal pupillary responses, with searching eye movements and varying amounts of visual attentiveness. Nystagmus and optic nerve hypoplasia are not seen in cerebral visual impairment. Nonaccidental trauma can be a cause of cerebral visual impairment but is typically associated with posterior pole abnormalities as well.

Q1447
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 5-year-old patient has acute, progressive erythema and swelling of the right upper eyelid. The patient has normal globe movement without pain, and there is no afferent pupillary defect. Further history taking reveals that the patient had a recent upper respiratory infection. What is this patient's most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: D. preseptal cellulitis
Rationale
Preseptal cellulitis is an inflammatory process involving the tissues anterior to the orbital septum. This is in contrast to orbital cellulitis, which involves the tissues posterior to the orbital septum. In preseptal cellulitis the globe remains uninflamed, and there is full ocular motility, absence of pain on eye movement, and no optic neuropathy. Upper respiratory tract or sinus infections from Streptococcus pneumoniae other streptococcal species, or S. aureus are the most common causative organisms.
Orbital cellulitis, idiopathic orbital inflammation, and rhabdomyosarcoma all involve orbital structures, leading to a motility abnormality, possible pain on eye movement, and possible involvement of optic nerve function.

Q1448
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What would be the most likely finding in a 15-month-old patient diagnosed with congenital fibrosis syndrome?
Correct answer: B. bilateral ptosis and limitations of vertical eye movements
Rationale
Congenital fibrosis syndrome or congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles (CFEOM)  is a group of conditions within the general category of congenital cranial dysinnervation disorders caused by primary dysinnervation of the extraocular muscles. Congenital fibrosis syndrome leads to replacement of sparsely innervated muscle by fibrous tissue.
Congenital fibrosis syndrome must be differentiated from thyroid eye disease, myasthenia gravis, 3rd nerve palsy, and chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO). Thyroid eye disease would more likely present with proptosis and lid retraction with limitations of extraocular eye movements. Myasthenia gravis may present with ptosis and progressive decrease in extraocular movements, and this would be variable from day to day.
Superior rectus weakness or overaction are recognized associations and contribute to causing vertical deviations.
Progressive loss of extraocular movements over years would be consistent with CPEO. A third nerve palsy may present with unilateral or bilateral ptosis and limitation of adduction, along with limitation of supra- and infraduction while abduction is intact. Möbius syndrome will have facial nerve weakness, and vertical motility will be intact.

Q1449
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What are the primary synergistic (yoke) muscles that are used for gazing up and to the right?
Correct answer: A. left inferior oblique and right superior rectus
Rationale
The left inferior oblique and right superior rectus muscles are the prime agonists for gazing up and to the right, whereas the superior oblique muscle is an eye depressor, and the main elevation action of the right inferior oblique is in left gaze.

Q1450
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the most common location of a teardrop-shaped iris coloboma?
Correct answer: D. inferonasal
Rationale
Typical iris colobomas are in the inferonasal quadrant and are caused by the failure of the embryonic fissure to close in the 5th week of gestation. These can be associated with chorioretinal and/or optic nerve colobomas. Atypical iris colobomas that occur in areas other than the inferonasal quadrant are not associated with more posterior colobomas. These may result from fibrovascular remnants of the anterior hyaloid system and pupillary membrane.

Q1451
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
Leukemia has the highest likelihood to infiltrate what ocular tissues?
Correct answer: A. retina and choroid
Rationale
Leukemia is most likely to infiltrate the retina and choroid. Retinal hemorrhages in the nerve fiber layer are the most likely finding. Optic nerve infiltration may occur and requires emergent treatment, due to the risk of vision loss. All ocular structures may be affected. Leukemic infiltration of the orbit can occur, but it is uncommon.

Q1452
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the effect of a posterior fixation suture in strabismus surgery?
Correct answer: B. weakening of the muscle in its field of action
Rationale
A posterior fixation suture involves the attachment of a rectus muscle with a nonabsorbable suture 11-18 mm posterior to the insertion site and is used to weaken the muscle in its field of action without significantly affecting alignment in primary position. This procedure is particularly useful for treatment of incomitant strabismus.
Transposition procedures involve redirection of the paths of the extraocular muscles. Advancement of the anterior half of the superior oblique tendon reduces excyclotorsion in patients with superior oblique palsy.

Q1453
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 2-month-old, otherwise developmentally normal girl presents with the disc finding seen in the figure below. What further testing should be ordered?
Correct answer: D. magnetic resonance imaging/angiography
Rationale
Morning glory disc anomaly (MGDA) is the result of abnormal development of the distal optic stalk at its junction with the primitive optic vesicle. A morning glory disc anomaly appears clinically as a funnel-shaped excavation enveloping the optic disc. There are an increased number of blood vessels coming off the disc, and a white tuft of glial tissue may be observed in the center of the optic disc cup. Morning glory disc anomaly is typically unilateral, and visual acuity can range from 20/20 to no light perception. Retinal detachment is a known complication. Morning glory disc anomaly is associated with basal encephalocele and midface anomalies (cleft lip, cleft palate, flattened nasal bridge). It is also associated with moyamoya disease. Moyamoya disease typically presents with constriction of the internal carotid arteries as they enter the skull base and join the circle of Willis. Blood vessel constriction often leads to recurrent strokes, and patients may be started on antiplatelet therapy. Therefore, all patients with morning glory disc anomaly should have a brain MRI/MRA to rule out these 2 conditions.
Choanal atresia, lop ears, and tetralogy of Fallot are associated with ocular coloboma in CHARGE (coloboma, heart defects, choanal atresia, mental retardation, genitourinary abnormalities, and ear abnormalities) syndrome.

Q1454
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 7-year-old girl has an acute-onset esotropia with diplopia. The esotropia increases in left gaze and she has a left head turn. Her visual acuity is 20/20 in each eye and cycloplegic refraction is +1.00 OU. What is the next step in management?
Correct answer: C. neuroimaging
Rationale
A sixth nerve palsy in an older child often presents with diplopia, a compensatory head turn toward the side of the paralyzed lateral rectus muscle, and an esotropia that increases in gaze toward the size of the paralyzed lateral rectus muscle. Vision is usually equal in both eyes if the child presents soon after the onset of deviation.
Because sixth nerve palsy in older children is associated with intracranial lesions in one-third of cases, neuroimaging is recommended, even in the absence of other neurologic signs.
Correction of hyperopia with glasses is the treatment for refractive accommodative esotropia. Patients have an average of +4.00 D of hyperopia.

Eye muscle surgery may be used to treat an esotropia secondary to sixth nerve palsy if it does not resolve, but it would not be the initial management.
Orthoptic exercises are helpful in the treatment of exodeviation caused by convergence insufficiency.

Q1455
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A child has craniosynostosis with hydrocephalus, normal intelligence, and normal hands and feet. What craniosynostosis syndrome is most likely?
Correct answer: A. Crouzon syndrome
Rationale
Common features of the craniosynostosis syndromes include fusion of multiple calvarial sutures and skull base sutures. Syndactyly (partial fusion of the digits) and brachydachtyly (short digits) are hallmarks of the craniosynostosis syndromes, with the exception of Crouzon syndrome. Crouzon syndrome is the most common craniosystosis syndrome. Hydrocephalus is common but intelligence is usually normal. The absence of anomalies of the hands and feet can aid in the diagnosis of Crouzon syndrome.

Q1456
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
An 18-month-old child with congenital jerk-wave nystagmus has dampening of her nystagmus when she crosses her eyes. Examination reveals nystagmus with attempted abduction and a head turn with occlusion of either eye. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. nystagmus blockage syndrome
Rationale
Nystagmus blockage syndrome occurs because nystagmus is dampened by convergence. Classic findings are increased jerk nystagmus on lateral gaze, esotropia, and "eating up prism" on attempted measurement of misalignment. In some situations, it may be difficult to distinguish nystagmus blockage with resultant esotropia from overlying esotropia and nystagmus. It may also be difficult to distinguish from coexisting strabismus with latent nystagmus.
Möbius syndrome is not typically associated with nystagmus. Möbius syndrome results in incomitant strabismus (may be orthotropic in primary position [40%], esotropic [50%], or exotropic [10%]) from a cranial nerve (CN) VI palsy and masklike facies from a CN VII on the ipsilateral side. It is sometimes associated with limb, chest, or tongue defects. Poland syndrome with absent pectoralis muscle is a variant of Möbius syndrome.
Cyclic esotropia is not typically associated with nystagmus either. It has onset in preschool years, is comitant and intermittent, and usually occurs every other day (48-hour cycle).
Convergence-retraction nystagmus is not a true nystagmus, but a disjunctive saccadic oscillation. It is part of the dorsal midbrain syndrome, with other findings of paralysis of upgaze, eyelid retraction, and pupillary light-near dissociation.

Q1457
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the average corneal horizontal diameter in a full-term newborn?
Correct answer: C. 10 mm
Rationale
The average corneal horizontal diameter in a newborn is 9.5 to 10.5 mm. This diameter increases to 12 mm on average in an adult. The keratometry readings decrease significantly in the first 6 months of life as the cornea flattens with increasing diameter.

Q1458
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 5-year-old girl has cyclic esotropia, with esotropia occurring every other day. What would be the expected findings when her fusion and binocular vision are tested?
Correct answer: A. absent fusion and binocular vision on strabismic days, and improved fusion and binocular vision on orthotropic days
Rationale
Cyclic esotropia is rare and typically occurs in preschool-aged children. The esotropia is comitant and intermittent, usually occurring every other day (48-hour cycle). Fusion and binocular vision are absent or poor on strabismic days and greatly improved on days in which the eyes are well-aligned. Surgical treatment of cyclic esotropia is usually effective.

Q1459
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
In differentiating true papilledema from pseudopapilledema what is the most reliable sign?
Correct answer: C. obscuration of the vessels at the disc margin in papilledema
Rationale
Pseudopapilledema refers to any elevated anomaly of the optic disc that resembles papilledema. Conditions that are frequently confused with papilledema in children include optic disc drusen, hyperopic discs, and prominent optic glial tissue. Pseudopapilledema can be differentiated from true papilledema by the absence of disc hyperemia and retinal hemorrhages or exudates. With papilledema, there is obscuration of the disc margin. In cases of optic nerve drusen, trifurcated rather than bifurcated vessels can be seen emerging from the disc.
Other features associated with drusen rather than papilledema include refractile bodies on the disc surface, absence of hyperemia, absence of surface hemorrhages, presence of spontaneous venous pulsations in most, and normal thickness of the peripapillary nerve fiber layer. Blurring of the disc margin and elevation of the disc can occur in both pseudopapilledema and true papilledema. Identification of disc drusen on examination or with imaging studies confirms the diagnosis of pseudopapilledema.

Q1460
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A developmentally delayed 5-month-old child presents with a constant 30 prism-diopter (Δ) exotropia that is comitant in lateral gazes. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
Correct answer: D. strabismus surgery
Rationale
This patient has infantile exotropia. Infantile exotropia presents with a large-angle constant exotropia prior to 6 months of age. There is an increased risk of neurologic impairment and craniofacial disorders in these patients. The treatment of constant infantile exotropia is early surgery. Surgery can lead to monofixation with gross binocular vision, but restoration of normal binocular function is rare.
Correction of myopia and use of base-in prisms can be used to treat intermittent exotropia, but they are not helpful for infantile exotropia. Observation would not be appropriate, since infantile exotropia will not resolve on its own.

Q1461
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
Pathologic examination of an infant's eye demonstrates multiple ocular malformations including microphthalmos, iris and ciliary body colobomas, retinal dysplasia, and an area of cartilage within the ciliary body coloboma (figure). What diagnosis is most appropriate?
Correct answer: D. trisomy 13
Rationale
The photomicrograph shows an area of colobomatous malformation with cartilage in trisomy 13. Trisomy 13 (Patau) is a common embryonic malformation, affecting 1 in 250 embryos. It is usually incompatible with birth. It is seen in 1 in 10,000 newborns, with 80% failing to survive to one year of life. The trisomy is due to nondisjunction or, less commonly, translocation. The ciliary body colobomas in trisomy 13 may demonstrate a unique finding of intraocular cartilage. Intraocular cartilage may also be found in medulloepitheliomas and persistent fetal vasculature (persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous, PHPV). Abnormalities in trisomy 13 include microcephaly, holoprosencephaly (failure of the forebrain to divide into 2 hemispheres), a single orbit, nasal proboscis, and digital, urogenital, and cardiac defects. Ocular development is often markedly abnormal, with synophthalmia (some degree of fusion of the 2 optic vesicles and eventually globes), large iris and ciliary body colobomas, and retinal dysplasia.

Q1462
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
When examining an optic nerve, what clinical finding may support a suspicion for optic disc drusen rather than true papilledema?
Correct answer: B. anomalous branching of large vessels
Rationale
Pseudopapilledema refers to an elevated appearance of the optic disc mimicking papilledema. Unlike papilledema, pseudopapilledema typically does not have retinal hemorrhages, disc hyperemia, or vessel obscuration. The most common cause of pseudopapilledema in children is disc drusen. Other causes include hyperopia and prominent glial tissue.
Disc drusen is often inherited and becomes apparent in the first couple decades of life. Disc drusen may appear as refractile gray-yellow bodies if near the surface of the nerve. However, often they are buried and not clinically visible. One useful clinical finding often seen with disc drusen is anomalous branching of the large retinal vessels over the disc. Rare complications of disc drusen include subretinal neovascular membrane or hemorrhage. B scan ultrasonography and computed tomography are useful imaging tools to identify disc drusen. Patients with pseudoxanthoma elasticum have a higher incidence of disc drusen.

What type of urinalysis is the most appropriate for establishing the diagnosis of neuroblastoma?
Correct answer: D. urine catecholamines
Rationale
Neuroblastoma is one of the more common childhood tumors that frequently have orbital manifestations. The primary tumor is typically in the adrenal glands or sympathetic ganglion chain. Urine catecholamines are positive in 90% to 95% of patients. Urine glucose levels, red blood cell counts, and white blood cell counts are not helpful in making the diagnosis.

Q1464
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the name of the clinical test of binocular alignment that makes use of the corneal light reflex, prisms, and pupil/iris landmarks?
Correct answer: D. Krimsky test
Rationale
The Krimsky test uses the light reflections on both corneas and involves placing a prism on the deviating eye until the light reflex is centered. The amount of prism required to center the light reflex is equivalent to the amount of deviation. The Hirschberg test estimates the angle of deviation based on the millimeters of light decentration in the deviating eye but does not use a prism. The Brückner test detects but does not measure strabismus. This involves a comparison of the red reflexes. The Bielschowsky test is used to isolate a paresis of a cyclovertical muscle. This test does not involve the light reflex.

Ophthalmia neonatorum caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae has its onset typically how long after birth?
Correct answer: D. within 3-4 days

Ophthalmia neonatorum is a conjunctivitis that occurs in the first month of life and can be caused by numerous organisms, in addition to chemical agents. Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes the most serious form of the disease and typically has a delayed but abrupt onset. It usually presents in the first 3 to 4 days after birth.

Q1466
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
The International Classification for Retinopathy of Prematurity (ICROP) defines stage 1 disease as having what finding?
Correct answer: D. demarcation line
Rationale
The correct staging of ROP is necessary to determine treatment and screening protocols, as well as standardize research. Stage 1 ROP is defined as the presence of a demarcation line between the vascularized and avascular retina. In this stage, the shunt vessels are essentially flat. A ridge, where the shunt vessels at the border between vascular and avascular retina are thickened and elevated, is the definition of stage 2. Extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation defines stage 3. A subtotal retinal detachment occurs in stage 4.

Q1467

What is the prevalence of amblyopia in the North American population?
Correct answer: A. 2%-4%
Rationale
Amblyopia is the most common cause of monocular vision impairment in North American children, affecting 2%-4% of the population. Risk factors include prematurity, developmental delays, and a family history of amblyopia.

Q1468

A 5-year-old boy presents with an esotropia that occurs every third day. The ophthalmologist confirms this observation and has examined him on a day he is esotropic and on days that he is orthotropic. What is the best treatment for this child?
Correct answer: A. surgery for the maximum angle of esotropia
Rationale
This patient has cyclic esotropia. Surgery for the maximum angle of esotropia is indicated. Any accommodative component should be addressed, but +1.0 refractive error does not suggest an accommodative esotropia, and glasses are not likely to be of benefit. This is not likely to resolve spontaneously. Occlusion therapy may convert the cyclic deviation into a constant one. These patients are not typically amblyopic.

A 6-year-old boy with visual acuity of 20/400 OD and 20/20 OS has a cycloplegic refraction of +3.00 sphere OD and +0.25 sphere OS. He is prescribed full-time glasses. At the 3-month follow-up visit, his visual acuity is 20/200 OD and 20/20 OS. What is the preferred treatment for this condition?
Correct answer: B. patching
Rationale
Refractive amblyopia frequently occurs in the more hyperopic eye of anisometropic hyperopia. If the vision is worse than 20/100, the preferred initial therapy is patching. Atropine is typically used in moderate amblyopia with vision of 20/100 or better. Bifocal lenses treat high accommodative convergence/accommodation (AC/A) ratio esotropia, not amblyopia. Other neurologic findings are rare in refractive amblyopia, and neurologic consultation is not typically needed.

Rationale
Although epiblepharon can produce an in-turning of the eyelashes, there is often minimal or no irritation of the cornea. If no significant fluorescein staining of the cornea is detected, only observation is required. The epiblepharon often resolves spontaneously with time and seldom requires surgical treatment.

Correct answer: B. 25 mm
Rationale
The nerves to the rectus muscles and the superior oblique muscle enter the muscles approximately one-third of the distance from the origin to the insertion (or trochlea). An instrument thrust more than 26 mm posterior to a rectus muscle's insertion may cause injury to the nerve.

Intermittent exotropia is the most common exodeviation. Infantile exotropia and type 2 Duane retraction syndrome are uncommon entities. Pseudoexotropia is the result of certain facial features or a structural abnormality of the retina and is not a true strabismus disorder.

Q1473
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What are the clinical features of Brown syndrome?
Correct answer: C. deficient elevation in adduction, improved elevation in abduction, associated with a V pattern
Rationale
Pertinent clinical features of Brown syndrome include deficient elevation in adduction that improves in abduction but often not completely. Adduction is associated with widening of the palpebral fissure and a downshoot of the involved eye (figure). Individuals may also have a hypotropia of the involved eye in the primary position. Attempts to elevate the eye straight upward usually cause divergence due to resistence from the tight superior obliques, causing lateral diversion of the globe. This results in a V pattern, which contrasts with the A pattern exhibited in inferior oblique muscle paralysis. Positive forced duction testing confirms the diagnosis. Brown syndrome may be congenital or acquired, constant or intermittent. Acquired cases may result from local trauma to the region of the trochlea, systemic inflammatory conditions, or sinusitis. Computed tomography scan should be considered in acquired cases. Management can be medical and/or surgical. Spontaneous resolution has also been reported.

Paraneoplastic effects of neuroblastoma can cause opsoclonus. Arnold-Chiari malformations can cause vertical nystagmus.

Q1476
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 6-month-old patient with strabismus, fixating on an accommodative target at 14 inches, is examined with a penlight. The corneal light reflex in the right eye is displaced temporally relative to the center of the pupil, whereas the corneal light reflex in the left eye is in the center of the pupil. The patient has what type of strabismus?
Correct answer: A. esotropia
Rationale
Corneal light reflex tests are useful in assessing ocular alignment in patients who cannot cooperate sufficiently to allow cover testing or who have poor fixation. Two main types of this test are the Hirschberg and modified Krimsky. The Hirschberg method is based on the premise that 1 mm of decentration of the corneal light reflection corresponds to approximately 7 degrees or 15 diopters of ocular deviation, using the iris as an anatomical landmark. The modified Krimsky method uses the alignment of the light reflex by neutralizing with prisms. In either case, an eye deviated inward (esotropic) will produce a light reflex that is displaced temporally from the center of the pupil while the opposite eye is central.

Q1479

A 1-year-old child presents for evaluation of constant, large-angle exotropia that has been present since birth. Aside from a complete ophthalmic examination, what additional piece of information is crucial to obtain?
Correct answer: D. a developmental history
Rationale
Infantile exotropia (XT) presents before age 6 months with a large-angle, constant exodeviation. Patients who are otherwise healthy (no ocular or systemic disease) are classified as primary infantile XT. However, one must consider secondary causes, as patients with infantile XT are at increased risk of associated neurologic impairment or developmental delay. Referral for neurologic assessment may be necessary if there concerns about neurologic or developmental delay. As mentioned in the question stem, a complete ophthalmic exam, including a dilated fundus examination, is required in new patients with strabismus, as XT may also result from retinal or optic nerve abnormalities.
Monocular occlusion testing is helpful when evaluating patients with intermittent XT with more exodeviation at distance than near. Interpupillary distance, if large, can result in pseudoexotropia. Infantile XT is classically large angle (> 30 prism diopters) and difficult to mistake as pseudoexotropia.

Infants with Chlamydia trachomatis infection acquired at birth can present with papillary conjunctivitis during the first week of life. Although the eye disease is usually self-­limited, C trachomatis infection can cause pneumonia and otitis media in neonates. Therefore, systemic treatment with oral erythromycin is indicated.

Q1481

What characteristic best distinguishes acquired nystagmus from congenital motor nystagmus (infantile nystagmus syndrome)?
Correct answer: B. oscillopsia
Rationale
Oscillopsia is characteristic of nystagmus acquired in adulthood and is rare in CMN. Patients with congenital motor nystagmus (CMN; infantile nystagmus syndrome) often adopt an abnormal head position to take advantage of the better vision that is possible at a null point. An exponential decrease in velocity of the slow phase and a fast-phase direction that reverses with a change in fixation are characteristic of latent nystagmus (fusion maldevelopment nystagmus syndrome).

Q1482
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What surgical step is usually included in surgical treatment for esotropic Duane syndrome?
Correct answer: D. recession of the medial rectus on the affected side
Rationale
Duane retraction syndrome is a spectrum of ocular motility disorders characterized by anomalous co-contracture of the medial and lateral rectus muscles on actual or attempted adduction. It is caused by a hypoplastic or absent 6th cranial nerve with aberrant innervation to the lateral rectus muscle by the third cranial nerve. This leads to globe retraction on attempted adduction.
No surgery will fully normalize rotations in Duane syndrome due to innervational abnormalities. Therefore, surgery is reserved for primary position deviations, head turns, marked globe retraction, or large upshoots or downshoots.
Treatment of esotropic Duane syndrome is primarily recession of the medial rectus muscle on the affected side. The purpose of surgery in this situation is to expand the field of single binocular vision and reduce the head turn. Resection of the lateral rectus muscle in this case could induce further globe retraction, so resections are generally avoided in Duane syndrome.

Q1483
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
Where is the origin of the superior oblique?
Correct answer: B. orbital apex
Rationale
The superior oblique originates from the orbital apex above the annulus of Zinn. It passes through the trochlea, which is the functional origin of the muscle. The inferior oblique originates from the orbital rim, and the remaining extraocular muscles originate from the annulus of Zinn.

Rationale
Kawasaki disease, which typically affects children younger than 5 years, is marked by bilateral conjunctival injection, erythema of the palms, a reddened tongue, cervical lymphadenopathy, and fever lasting longer than 5 days. The most serious complication associated with Kawasaki disease is coronary artery aneurysm, which is minimized by treatment with aspirin and IgG. The most common ocular finding is conjunctivitis, followed by anterior uveitis (10%).
Subconjunctival hemorrhage is possible but less commonly associated with Kawasaki disease. Although Kawasaki disease is a systemic vasculitis, retinal vasculitis is not typically an associated ocular complication of this disorder.

Correct answer: D. persistent fetal vasculature
Rationale
Persistent fetal vasculature (PFV, previously referred to as persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous or PHPV) is a congenital condition caused by the failure of the fetal hyaloid vasculature to regress properly. Clinically, there is almost always associated microcornea. Congenital glaucoma is associated with buphthalmos, or enlarged corneal diameters. In Coats disease, the corneal diameter is normal. In posterior lenticonus, the corneal diameter is normal.

Correct answer: D. amblyoscope
Rationale
Determining the potential for postoperative single binocular vision is a vital component of the preoperative assessment for strabismus surgery. Although the cover-uncover test, the Hess screen, and the Lancaster red-green test are all helpful for measuring strabismic deviation, only the amblyoscope also tests for retinal correspondence. Another method of simulating the target postoperative alignment is by using prisms.

Q1487

A 5-month-old girl presents for evaluation of a large-angle exotropia and face turn that have been present since birth. What clinical feature can be seen in children with this type of strabismus?
Correct answer: C. neurologic impairment
Rationale
Infantile exotropia is characterized by a large-angle outward deviation that is often associated with neurologic impairment or craniofacial disorders. Although the child may appear healthy, a careful developmental history is important, and referral for neurologic evaluation should be considered if there are indications of developmental delay.
High hyperopia is associated with accommodative esotropia.
Cross-fixation occurs in a large-angle esotropia with the use of the adducted eye for fixation of objects in the contralateral temporal field.
Convergence-retraction nystagmus is part of the dorsal midbrain syndrome, associated with paralysis of upward gaze, defective convergence, eyelid retraction, and pupillary light-near dissociation. With attempted upgaze, co-contraction of all the horizontal muscles occurs, and the eyes are pulled into the orbit. During this movement, the medial rectus muscles overpower the lateral rectus muscles, causing the eyes to converge.

Q1488
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
Teller Acuity Cards II are likely to overestimate the vision in what eye condition?
Correct answer: A. strabismic amblyopia
Rationale
Strabismic amblyopia has features that differ from other types of amblyopia. Grating acuity, such as is tested with Teller Acuity Cards II and the LEA Grating Acuity Test, is reduced less than acuity measured with optotypes. Therefore, grating acuity can overestimate the vision. Linear LEA symbols, ETDRS (Early Treatment of Diabetic Retinopathy Study) charts, and crowded HOTV charts accurately measure visual acuity in strabismic amblyopia. In refractive and deprivational amblyopia, this effect is not seen. The presence of astigmatism does not affect the accuracy of grating acuity measurements.

Q1489
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What part of the visual system demonstrates abnormal neuronal development in amblyopia?
Correct answer: C. the lateral geniculate body
Rationale
Amblyopic visual deficits result primarily from visual cortical changes. With abnormal visual experience early in life, cells of the primary visual cortex can lose their ability to respond to stimulation of 1 or both eyes, and the cells that remain responsive show significant functional deficiencies, including abnormally large receptive fields. Visual cortex deficiencies may account for the crowding phenomenon, in which optotypes are easier to recognize when isolated than when surrounded by similar forms. Abnormalities are also found in neurons within the lateral geniculate body, but the retina in amblyopia is essentially normal. Amblyopia is primarily a defect of central vision; the peripheral visual field is usually normal.

Correct answer: D. between birth and 1 year
Rationale
In a human newborn, the average axial length of the eye is 14.5-15.5 mm. The majority of growth of the axial length occurs in the first year of life, increasing by approximately 4 mm in the first 6 months and 2 mm in the subsequent 6 months. The final axial length is reached when the individual is 13 to 16 years old. The average axial length in an adult is 23-24 mm.

Q1492

A parent brings a child to the clinic for evaluation of strabismus. What finding on examination would suggest the strabismus is longstanding?
Correct answer: B. anomalous retinal correspondence
Rationale
Anomalous retinal correspondence (ARC) occurs when the fovea of the fixating eye has acquired a visual direction in common with a peripheral retinal element in the deviated eye. This is an adaptive mechanism that takes time to develop; therefore, a short history of esotropia would not be associated with ARC. ARC would not develop with decreased vision in one eye in the absence of strabismus. An exophoria would not be associated with ARC, since the eyes are not deviated under binocular conditions.
Abnormal head position, "spread of comitance," and suppression, as opposed to diplopia, would be features suggesting a more longstanding deviation.

Correct answer: A. HOTV
Rationale
Various optotypes are available for recognition visual acuity testing in preliterate children. LEA symbols and the HOTV test are reliably calibrated and have high testability rates for preschool-aged children. For a shy child, testability may be improved by having the child point to match optotypes on a chart with those on a hand-held card rather than verbally identify them. Several symbol charts, such as Allen figures and the Lighthouse chart, are not recommended by the World Health Organization and the National Academy of Sciences because the optotypes are considered confusing, culturally biased, or nonstandardized. The Tumbling E Chart is accurate but conceptually difficult for many preschool children.

Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the fibrillin gene, which is a major constituent of extracellular microfibrils. Affected individuals are characteristically tall, with long limbs and fingers (arachnodactyly); loose, flexible joints; scoliosis; and chest deformities. Lens dislocation (ectopia lentis) can occur, but not the small, round lenses (microspherophakia) of patients with Weill-Marchesani syndrome. Polydactyly refers to having extra digits, whereas brachydactyly refers to having short digits. Hypodactyly refers to having fewer digits than normal.

The most common type of leukemia in children is acute lymphoblastic leukemia (75%-80%). Acute myelogenous leukemia (20%-25%) and chronic myelogenous leukemia (<5%) are much less common. In a patient with achromatopsia, what characteristic findings are expected on the electroretinogram (ERG)?

Rationale
Achromatopsia is a retinal disorder in which patients have no color vision, as well as poor central vision, nystagmus, and photophobia (rather than pain or discomfort, the photophobia represents a preference to avoid bright light); hemeralopia (inability to see clearly in bright light) also occurs in these patients. Achromatopsia is caused by deficient cone function with normal rod functioning. ERG test results show normal scotopic response, but severely abnormal photopic response. Achromatopsia was initially thought to be a stationary disorder; however, recent studies have shown deterioration of visual acuity, macular appearance, and cone function on ERG.
A poor scotopic and photopic response suggests a different diagnosis, as does a normal ERG result.

The figure shows a fibrovascular stalk arising from the optic nerve and coursing through the vitreous towards the lens. This is an example of persistent fetal vasculature (PFV), which results from failure of regression of the primary vitreous and hyaloid artery. This condition is typically sporadic and unilateral. Its presentation varies from Bergmeister papillae or Mittendorf dot in the milder cases to a microphthalmic eye with retrolental plaque in more severe cases. Incontinentia pigmenti (IP; Bloch-Sulzberger syndrome) is an X-linked dominant condition characterized by progressive skin findings, pigmentary retinopathy, and proliferative vascular retinopathy of the peripheral retina that can lead to tractional retinal detachment. In IP, erythema and bullae develop in the first few days of life.
X-linked retinitis pigmentosa is a retinal degeneration associated with vision loss and pigmentary retinopathy, but no dermatologic manifestations.
Goldmann-Favre disease is also a pigmentary retinopathy associated with characteristic electroretinogram (ERG) abnormalities and nyctalopia, but no skin findings.
Gyrate atrophy is an autosomally recessive congenital deficiency in ornithine aminotransferase that leads to peripheral progressive paving stone-like degeneration of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and choroid. It has no association with dermatologic changes.

Retinoblastoma occurs when both copies of RB1, a tumor suppressor gene, have mutations. In the other 40% of cases, a germline mutation in 1 of the 2 alleles of RB1 either is inherited from an affected parent (10% of all retinoblastoma cases) or occurs spontaneously in 1 of the gametes.

Q1504

A child has asthma, eczema, chronic tearing and red eyes. Examination shows papillae of the palpebral conjunctiva and punctate corneal erosions. Correct answer: C. corticosteroids
Rationale
Atopic keratoconjunctivitis is a chronic ocular surface allergy-related inflammatory disorder. It is characterized by a history of asthma and eczema in association with ocular findings of papillae and chronic tearing. More severe findings include punctate corneal erosions, epithelial defects, and neovascularization. Topical medications include mast-cell stabilizers, H1-receptor antagonists, antihistamines, vasoconstrictors, corticosteroids, or combinations of these drugs. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drops should be used with caution: Cases of corneal perforation, though rare, have been reported. Topical corticosteroid drops, used in pulsed doses, can effectively reduce severe allergic ocular symptoms. Patients must be closely monitored for adverse effects, including glaucoma and cataracts.

The lack of obscuration of vessels at the disc margin and absence of hyperemia is suggestive of pseudopapilledema rather than true papilledema. Pseudopapilledema is elevation of the optic nerve head not associated with increased intracranial pressure. The most common etiologies in children are drusen of the optic disc, hyperopia, and prominent glial tissue. Optic disc drusen are frequently inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion, and examination of parents is helpful when drusen are suspected in children. Chiari malformation and Dandy-Walker syndrome are causes of hydrocephalus that can cause true disc edema. IIH is also a cause of true disc edema, not pseudopapilledema.

Q1507
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
An otherwise-healthy 5-year-old child presents for evaluation of a conjunctival lesion. On examination, the child is found to have a dermolipoma located near the temporal fornix in his left eye. The child is playful and appears asymptomatic. Other than the dermolipoma, the remainder of the examination is unremarkable. What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient's condition?
Correct answer: C. observation
Rationale
Lipodermoid tumors are complex choristomas composed of fatty tissue and dense connective tissue. Little if any postnatal growth occurs. Thus there is no urgency for their removal unless irritation symptoms develop.

Q1508
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 12-year-old girl presents with 1 day of severe headache, nausea, vomiting, and diplopia. On examination, she is found to have bilateral optic nerve head swelling. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) shows no mass lesions and no abnormal enhancement. What is the likely finding to explain the diplopia?
Correct answer: A. incomitant esotropia
Rationale
Visual acuity, color vision, and pupillary reactions often initially are normal in the setting of increased intracranial pressure. A sixth nerve palsy can result from increased intracranial pressure and is referred to as a false localizing sign in this setting. This would appear clinically as an incomitant esotropia. Comitant alignment would be suggestive of a phoria (with or without decompensation), which would not be expected to explain diplopia in the setting of increased intracranial pressure. Incomitant exotropia could occur due to a third nerve palsy or an internuclear ophthalmoplegia, neither of which would be expected in the setting of increased intracranial pressure with no masses or enhancement on MRI.

Q1509
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
An ophthalmologist examines a 3-month-old child born at full term to a mother who was diagnosed with rubella during the first trimester of pregnancy. What would the most likely finding be?
Correct answer: C. nuclear cataract
Rationale
Congenital rubella (German measles) syndrome occurs when the rubella virus is transmitted to the fetus transplacentally. The syndrome includes a peculiar nuclear cataract that is sometimes floating in liquified cortex, as well as glaucoma, microphthalmos, and retinopathy (salt-and-pepper fundus). Retinopathy is the most common finding. Sensorineural hearing loss, microcephaly, and developmental delay are other systemic manifestations.
Choroiditis and uveitis are typically seen in toxoplasmosis or cytomegalovirus infections. Bilateral interstitial keratitis is found in approximately 10% of older children and adults with congenital syphilis. Bitot spots are seen in vitamin A deficiency.
