Q1510
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is appropriate treatment for a partially accommodative esotropia?
Correct answer: A. strabismus surgery to correct the amount of esotropia measured with glasses, followed by full hyperopic correction with glasses
Rationale
Accommodative esotropia is a convergent ocular deviation associated with activation of the accommodative reflex. Patients with partially accommodative esotropia show a reduction in the amplitude of esotropia when wearing a full hyperopic correction but still have some residual esotropia. Treatment of a partially accommodative esotropia consists of strabismus surgery to correct the esotropia that persists while the patient is wearing the full hyperopic correction, with the goal of producing straight eyes with glasses postoperatively.

Q1511
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A patient had the fundus appearance shown below on the previous examination. The patient presents at the current examination with a mild decrease in vision. What would be an indication for a course of systemic therapy with antimicrobials and corticosteroids?
Correct answer: A. retinitis near the macula
Rationale
Toxoplasma gondii chorioretinitis is typically due to a reactivation of latent disease. The disease can be acquired transplacentally (as one of the congenital "TORCH" infections) or after birth, upon exposure to cysts in soil, food, or cat feces. Many episodes are self-limited and do not require therapy. Indications for treatment include an immunocompromised patient, dense vitreous opacity, large lesions greater than 1 disc diameter in size, multiple lesions, decreased visual acuity, frequent recurrences, or retinitis threatening the optic nerve or macula. Milder vitritis and peripheral retinitis do not necessarily require treatment; however, some experts suggest prophylactic therapy for patients with frequently recurrent disease. Findings can include anterior chamber reaction and intraocular pressure elevation, but these do not necessitate antimicrobial and steroid treatment.
The classic regimen for the treatment of ocular toxoplasmosis consists of triple therapy: pyrimethamine (loading dose, 50–100 mg; treatment dose, 25–50 mg/day), sulfadiazine (treatment dose, 1 g, 4 times/day), and prednisone (treatment dose, 0.5–1 mg/kg/day, depending on the severity of the inflammation). Because sulfonamides and pyrimethamine inhibit folic acid metabolism, folinic acid (15 mg every day) is added to prevent myelosuppression (leukopenia and/or thrombocytopenia), which may result from pyrimethamine therapy.
Systemic corticosteroids are generally begun either at the time of antimicrobial therapy or within 48 hours in immunocompetent patients. The use of systemic corticosteroids without appropriate antimicrobial coverage or the use of long- acting periocular and intraocular corticosteroid formulations such as triamcinolone acetonide is contraindicated because of the potential for severe, uncontrollable intraocular inflammation and loss of the eye.

Q1512
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What maternal disorder has been associated with segmental fetal optic nerve hypoplasia (ONH)?
Correct answer: D. diabetes mellitus
Rationale
Segmental optic nerve hypoplasia (ONH) may be associated with maternal diabetes mellitus. ONH is characterized by a decrease in the number of optic nerve axons. The disc is small, pale or grey, and is classically associated with a yellow-to-white ring around the disc (double ring sign). It may be unilateral or bilateral and is often asymmetric.
Patients with ONH are at risk for midline central nervous system anomalies, including absence of the septum pellucidum and agenesis of the corpus callosum, as well as other cerebral hemisphere and pituitary gland abnormalities. Thus, an associated seizure disorder and hypothyroidism may be present. ONH has been associated with fetal alcohol syndrome and maternal ingestion of phenytoin, quinine, and LSD.

Q1513
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What are the demographic and epidemiologic characteristics of pediatric uveitis?
Correct answer: B. slight female preponderance, mostly bilateral, age 8–9 at diagnosis, no family history
Rationale
Pediatric uveitis accounts for 2%–14% of all uveitis cases. The distribution between females and males is similar to that found in adults; there is a slight female preponderance. The mean age at diagnosis is 8–9 years. Most types of uveitis are not inherited, although some are associated with various HLA types.

Q1514
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A child has uncontrolled glaucoma secondary to the condition shown in the picture. If glaucoma surgery is needed, what is a particular intraoperative risk?
Correct answer: B. choroidal hemorrhage
Rationale
Sturge-Weber syndrome (SWS), or encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis, is a capillary malformation of the leptomeninges with or without ocular or facial involvement. This patient has the classic manifestations of a port-wine stain and associated glaucoma manifesting as an enlarged cornea. SWS glaucoma is difficult to treat. Surgery is indicated in early-onset cases and when medical treatment is inadequate. Multiple operations are typically necessary. A particular risk of glaucoma surgery in SWS is intraoperative or postoperative exudation or hemorrhage from anomalous choroidal vessels; this complication is caused by rapid ocular decompression. The other complications (hyphema, exposure of tube under conjunctiva, leakage from trabeculectomy flap) are not particularly higher in SWS glaucoma.

Q1515
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What type of nystagmus reverses direction with change in fixation?
Correct answer: B. fusion maldevelopment
Rationale
Fusion maldevelopment nystagmus syndrome (or latent nystagmus) is a form of infantile-onset nystagmus. It is a conjugate, horizontal jerk nystagmus that reverses direction with change in fixation. A left jerk nystagmus occurs with when the right eye is covered, and a right jerk occurs when the left is covered.
Spasmus nutans presents as a triad of small-amplitude, high-frequency, dysconjugate nystagmus; head nodding; and torticollis.
Convergence-retraction nystagmus occurs with co-contraction of all the horizontal extraocular muscles, resulting in globe retraction and convergence in attempted upgaze.
Central vestibular instability nystagmus (periodic alternating nystagmus) is a jerk nystagmus that periodically changes direction (often every 4 minutes), with potentially alternating head turn, but the direction is not related to fixation.

Q1516
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
In congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction, when is silicone intubation used?
Correct answer: A. when 1 or more simple probing or balloon dilations have failed
Rationale
Intubation of the nasolacrimal system is usually recommended when one or more initial probings have failed. Surgical intervention is not recommended in infants without complications who are younger than 12 months, since the nasolacrimal duct obstruction may resolve spontaneously. Older children and adults have a different etiology for epiphora, which must be addressed based on the findings. If a Jones tube is placed, silicone intubation is unnecessary. Probing should be done for dacryocystoceles to prevent complications related to infection.

Q1517
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 4-year-old boy presents with an orbital mass. A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan is performed, and orbital lymphatic malformation (previously known as lymphangioma) is diagnosed. What other information may be obtained to support the diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. exacerbation of symptoms with upper respiratory infection
Rationale
Orbital lymphatic malformations (previously known as lymphangiomas) often contain venous and lymphatic components, and may enlarge during upper respiratory tract infections because of the response of the lymphoid tissues within the lesion. Sudden hemorrhage from interstitial capillaries may present with abrupt proptosis; thus, normal exophthalmometer measurement does not confirm or negate the diagnosis. These malformations are best managed conservatively, but partial resection and drainage may be necessary if vision is threatened. Complete removal is usually impossible due to the infiltrative nature of the lesion.

Q1518
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What clinical finding suggests a bilateral rather than a unilateral superior oblique muscle palsy?
Correct answer: B. large V pattern
Rationale
Unilateral cases of superior oblique paresis usually show little if any V pattern and less than 10° of extorsion in downgaze. In contrast bilateral cases of superior oblique paresis usually show a V pattern. Extorsion is 10° or more in downgaze; more than 15° of extorsion in primary position is highly suggestive of bilateral involvement. Subjective incyclodiplopia is common in acquired bilateral cases. The Bielschowsky head-tilt test yields positive results on tilt to each side--that is, right head tilt produces a right hypertropia and left head tilt, a left hypertropia. There is bilateral oblique muscle dysfunction. Patients may exhibit a chin-down head position. Symmetric palsies may show little or no hypertropia in primary position.

Q1519
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
The Prism Adaptation Study showed improved rates of undercorrection of what strabismus type, when the surgery was based on the prism-adapted angle?
Correct answer: A. basic acquired nonaccommodative esotropia
Rationale
In the prism adaptation test, a patient is fitted with prisms to align the visual axes. This can help predict whether fusion can be restored following strabismus surgery. It also can help predict diplopia following strabismus surgery and might help determine if anomalous retinal correspondence is present. The Prism Adaptation Study showed improved rates of undercorrection (about 10% less) of basic acquired nonaccommodative esotropia, when the surgery was based on the prism-adapted angle.

Q1520
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 2-year-old boy presents with 3 days of pain, redness, and photophobia. Slit-lamp examination shows a small hyphema and a tan-colored iris lesion. The intraocular pressure is 30 mm Hg. What is the best initial treatment?
Correct answer: B. topical steroids and aqueous suppressants
Rationale
This presentation is characteristic of juvenile xanthogranuloma, a nonneoplastic, histiocytic proliferation seen in the first 2 years of life. It typically presents with cutaneous orange or tan papules that show Touton giant cells on histopathology. Iris involvement is relatively rare and may present as discrete, tan-colored nodules or a diffuse infiltration causing heterochromia.
Spontaneous bleeding from iris lesions results in hyphema and secondary glaucoma, which may cause acute pain and photophobia. Conservative management with topical steroids and aqueous suppressants is usually sufficient, since this condition is self-limited and spontaneously regresses by 5 years of age. If intractable glaucoma is present, surgical excision or radiation may be considered.
Topical antibiotics are not indicated, since the etiology of this condition is not infection. Glaucoma surgery is not indicated in the initial management.

Q1521
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 3-year-old girl has had recurrent episodes of redness and discharge in both eyes. The external examination of her right eye is abnormal, as shown. Deficiency of what protein can lead to this condition?
Correct answer: D. plasminogen deficiency
Rationale
The figure demonstrates firm, yellow, woody-like pseudomembranous lesions on the tarsal conjunctivae. This appearance is of ligneous conjunctivitis, a rare disorder associated with a systemic plasminogen deficiency. Fibrinogen (factor I) is needed for platelet aggregation, and therefore patients with fibrinogen deficiency present with a bleeding disorder. Hexosaminidase A deficiency is found in patients with Tay-Sachs disease; α-galactosidase A deficiency is found in patients with Fabry disease.

Q1522
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the inheritance pattern of ectopia lentis et pupillae?
Correct answer: D. autosomal recessive
Rationale
Ectopia lentis et pupillae is a rare autosomal recessive condition consisting of bilateral displacement of the pupil, usually inferotemporally, with lens dislocation in the opposite direction. This condition is also associated with microspherophakia. Lens dislocation can lead to anisometropia or visual deprivation and subsequent amblyopia.

Q1523
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the most likely threat to long-term visual acuity in a 6-month-old infant with a unilateral cataract?
Correct answer: D. deprivation amblyopia
Rationale
Deprivation amblyopia occurs when the visual axis is obstructed; it is a common cause of visual loss in unilateral cataracts. Quick removal of visually significant unilateral cataracts is recommended to prevent deprivation amblyopia, which can degrade acuity to 20/200 or worse. Although aphakic glaucoma, chronic iritis, and corneal decompensation are all complications of cataract surgery, they are less frequent than deprivation amblyopia in this setting.

Q1524
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the most appropriate surgical management for a patient with unilateral superior oblique palsy where excyclotorsion is the primary problem?
Correct answer: C. Harada-Ito procedure
Rationale
Treatment of superior oblique palsy typically involves strengthening the muscle with a tuck, weakening the antagonist inferior oblique muscle, or recessing the other elevator of the eye, the superior rectus muscle. However, all of these procedures are intended to correct the vertical misalignment. When the primary problem is excyclotorsion, the Harada-Ito procedure is preferred. This operation involves displacement of the anterior portions of the superior oblique tendons to a location adjacent to the upper edge of the lateral rectus muscle, about 8.0 mm posterior to that muscle's insertion.
Superior rectus recession and a Faden procedure may be part of surgical correction for a larger vertical deviation. Superior oblique tenotomy would be a treatment for superior oblique overaction.

Q1525
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is a common cause of a third cranial nerve palsy in children?
Correct answer: D. dysinnervation
Rationale
In children, third nerve palsies can be congenital (dysinnervation), or can be caused by trauma, inflammation, or viral infection. Other causes include ophthalmoplegic migraine, vaccination, or, infrequently, neoplasm. Head trauma is more commonly associated with a sixth or fourth nerve palsy. In adults, the usual causes of third nerve palsies are intracranial aneurysm and microvascular disease.

Q1526
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
In a 3-month-old child, what is an advantage of in-office probing and irrigation of the nasolacrimal duct?
Correct answer: D. avoidance of general anesthesia
Rationale
Nasolacrimal duct probing is a common surgical procedure. Some ophthalmologists recommend early probing of the infant in the office. Advantages of early probing include avoidance of general anesthesia and hospitalization, as well as earlier resolution of symptoms. A disadvantage of early surgery is that the condition may subsequently resolve spontaneously, thus treating more infants who may have not required surgery. A procedure is more painful in an awake infant and less controlled than under general anesthesia in an operating room.

Q1527
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
During a cover/uncover test of the right eye, the patient's right eye drifts out when covered. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: C. exophoria
Rationale
A phoria is a latent deviation that is controlled under binocular conditions. With cover testing, fusion is disrupted and the eye will deviate. Exo- prefix represents a divergent strabismus. Eso- prefix represents a convergent strabismus. A tropia represents a deviation that manifests under binocular conditions.
Intermittent exotropia, on the other hand, is an exodeviation intermittently controlled by fusional mechanisms. Unlike a pure phoria, intermittent exotropia spontaneously breaks down into a manifest exotropia.

Q1528
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 36-year-old man presents for evaluation of a chin down head position. On further testing, he exhibits a right hypertropia on right head tilt and a left hypertropia on left head tilt. On downgaze, the ophthalmologist measures 10 degrees of excyclotorsion. A palsy of what extraocular muscle(s) would produce the findings in this patient?
Correct answer: B. bilateral superior oblique
Rationale
A bilateral superior oblique palsy usually exhibits a V pattern. Additionally, on 3-step testing it would be expected to have a right hyperdeviation on right head tilt and left gaze, and a left hyperdeviation on left head tilt and right gaze. Any esodeviation would be expected to be less in upgaze, due to overaction of the inferior oblique muscles. Excyclotorsion would be expected to be greater than 10 degrees in downgaze.
Inferior oblique palsy, unilateral superior oblique palsy, and superior rectus palsy would not be expected to exhibit the clinical findings in this patient.

Q1529
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the most common ocular manifestation of abusive head trauma?
Correct answer: D. retinal hemorrhage
Rationale
The most common ocular manifestation of abusive head trauma (AHT), present in approximately 85% of cases, is retinal hemorrhage. These hemorrhages can be seen in all layers of the retina and may be unilateral or bilateral. They are found most commonly in the posterior pole but can also be present peripherally. The anterior segment and ocular adnexa are often normal. Hyphema, corneal abrasion, and subconjunctival hemorrhages are less commonly seen in AHT.

Q1530
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
On exam of a patient with congenital glaucoma, what finding can dynamically change and indicate progressive glaucoma even though IOP appears to be controlled?
Correct answer: D. axial length
Rationale
In children younger than 3 years, the sclera is elastic and will stretch if IOP is not well controlled. This can result in increased axial length despite a normal range IOP during exam under anesthesia. Corneal thickness decreases as corneal edema resolves and, once stable, is often less than the average central corneal thickness. The angle can further develop as a child ages, but this does not indicate poor pressure control. Myopia in congenital glaucoma is not necessarily an axial myopia.

Q1531
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
Seven days following strabismus surgery, a patient presents with mild corneal thinning anterior to the limbus. Fluorescein reveals pooling in the area of depression. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
Correct answer: B. frequent lubrication
Rationale
Dellen refers to shallow depressions and corneal thinning just anterior to the limbus. These occur when raised abnormal bulbar conjunctiva prevents the eyelid from adequately resurfacing the cornea with tear fluid during blinking. Artificial tears and lubricants are used until the chemosis subsides and healing occurs. Conjunctiva resection can be required, along with the use of corticosteroids, if the dellen and conjunctival inflammation persist despite aggressive initial lubrication.

Q1532
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
In a patient with infantile nystagmus, what symptom does the Kestenbaum-Anderson procedure primarily ameliorate?
Correct answer: D. anomalous head position
Rationale
A compensatory head-turn into the null point occurs frequently in patients with infantile nystagmus syndrome. The Kestenbaum-Anderson procedure, via recession-resection, corrects this anomalous head position by shifting the null point closer to the primary position.
Patients with infantile nystagmus syndrome do not experience oscillopsia. The Kestenbaum-Anderson procedure does not correct deviations in primary gaze. Although surgeries involving the 4 horizontal muscles have been shown to improve visual acuity in some patients with infantile nystagmus syndrome, this is not the primary goal of a Kestenbaum-Anderson procedure.

Q1533
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 1-year-old girl presents with severe ptosis and no levator function on the right side. She shows signs of amblyopia in the right eye. What is the most appropriate method of ptosis repair?
Correct answer: D. frontalis suspension
Rationale
This patient presents with congenital ptosis and absent levator function. Because of her young age, conservative follow-up until she is older would be appropriate as long as there was no evidence of amblyopia. In this case, the presence of amblyopia (usually either occlusive or secondary to anisometropic amblyopia) necessitates surgical intervention.
Levator advancement is an appropriate option for congenital ptosis treatment as long as there is adequate levator function; in this case, levator advancement would fail. Neither blepharoplasty nor brow lift would be successful—congenital ptosis is not typically associated with dermatochalasis or brow ptosis.
In this case, a frontalis sling is the appropriate procedure. Harvesting autologous fascia lata may be difficult in a 1-year-old child. Many surgeons would utilize either suture (prolene, nylon) or a silicone rod to temporarily elevate the lid, and proceed with a fascial sling once the child is older. Some surgeons would opt for banked fascia lata.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q1534
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What optic nerve finding may be seen in periventricular leukomalacia?
Correct answer: D. optic nerve cupping
Rationale
Periventricular leukomalacia is a prominent cause of cerebral (retrogeniculate) visual impairment (CVI), which is the most common cause of childhood visual impairment in developed countries. Periventricular leukomalacia is associated with premature birth and is the most common cause of glaucoma-like optic nerve cupping in preterm infants. The optic nerve cupping is a result of transsynaptic degeneration from bilateral lesions in the optic radiations. It presents as a large cup within a normal-sized optic disc, described as an unusual form of optic nerve hypoplasia.
Morning glory disc anomaly is a funnel-shaped excavation of the posterior fundus involving the optic disc. It is associated with basal encephalocele in patients with midline anomalies, PHACE syndrome (posterior fossa malformations, hemangiomas, arterial lesions, cardiac and eye anomalies, and abnormalities of the carotid circulation (moyamoya disease).
Optic atrophy may occur in pregeniculate causes of visual impairment and are seen in conditions such as hydrocephalus, brain tumors, trauma, hypoxic-ischemic injury, metabolic storage diseases, and inherited optic neuropathies such as Behr optic atrophy.
Optic nerve colobomas may form in isolation or in association with retinal or uveal colobomas, and may be associated with systemic diseases such as CHARGE syndrome (coloboma, heart defects, choanal atresia, mental retardation, genitourinary abnormalities, and ear abnormalities), or the papillorenal syndrome (renal anomalies and optic nerve defects).

Q1535
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 4-year-old child presents with conjunctival injection and fever. He also notably has a swollen tongue, swollen hands, and enlarged cervical lymph nodes. What extraocular evaluation is most urgently indicated?
Correct answer: A. echocardiogram
Rationale
The most significant complication of Kawasaki disease is coronary artery aneurysm. Coronary artery evaluation by 2-dimensional echocardiography is, therefore, warranted upon diagnosing Kawasaki disease. Kawasaki disease is a febrile illness primarily affecting children younger than 5 years. The cause is unknown. Abnormalities include unexplainable fever lasting 5 or more days; bilateral conjunctival injection; mucous membrane changes of injected or fissured lips, injected pharynx, or "strawberry tongue" extremity changes involving erythema of the palms or soles, edema of the hands or feet, or generalized or periungual desquamation; rash; and cervical lymphadenopathy. Beside conjunctivitis, the next most common ocular finding is anterior uveitis that is generally self-limited. Rare ocular findings can include keratitis, papilledema, optic neuritis, and subconjunctival hemorrhage.

Q1536
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
When operating on the inferior oblique muscle, damage to the associated nerve can cause what unwanted side effect?
Correct answer: C. pupillary enlargement
Rationale
The nerve to the inferior oblique carries the pupillary parasympathetic fibers; damage to this structure can cause an enlarged pupil. Anterior segment ischemia occurs when more than 2 rectus muscles are operated on at once, as they carry much of the blood supply to the anterior segment; the oblique muscles do not carry any blood to the anterior segment. Strabismus surgery on the inferior rectus muscle frequently causes widening or narrowing of the palpebral fissure because of that muscle's fascial attachments to the lower lid; the inferior oblique does not have similar attachments. The nerves to the lacrimal gland are not typically encountered during strabismus surgery.

Q1537
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
Patients with pseudoxanthoma elasticum have a higher incidence of what ocular finding?
Correct answer: B. disc drusen
Rationale
Pseudoxanthoma elasticum (PXE) is an autosomal recessive disease characterized by fragmentation of elastic fibers commonly affecting skin, blood vessels, and eyes. Patients may present with small papular lesions of the axilla, neck, and groin. These skin regions may also have laxity ("chicken neck"). Other complications include gastrointestinal bleeding, premature atherosclerosis, and myocardial infarction. Ocular manifestations include angioid streaks and a dimpling of Bruch membrane causing a peau d’orange (orange peel) fundus appearance.
Patients with pseudoxanthoma elasticum have a higher incidence of disc drusen. Disc drusen are often inherited from the patient’s parents and appear in the first couple of decades of life. Disc drusen may appear as refractile gray-yellow bodies if near the surface of the nerve. However, often they are buried and not clinically visible. One useful clinical finding often seen with disc drusen is anomalous branching of the large retinal vessels over the disc. Rare complications of disc drusen include subretinal neovascular membrane or hemorrhage. B scan ultrasonography and computed tomography are useful imaging tools to identify disc drusen.

Q1538
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
Constant tearing with copious mucus discharge in the infant shown suggests what condition?
Correct answer: C. nasolacrimal duct obstruction
Rationale
Constant tearing with copious mucus discharge suggests nasolacrimal duct obstruction. Constant tearing with minimal mucopurulence suggests punctal or canalicular agenesis. Intermittent tearing with mucus discharge suggests intermittent obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct, most likely due to swollen inferior turbinate mucosa associated with upper respiratory tract infection or allergy. Congenital glaucoma is not associated with mucus discharge.

Q1539
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the most appropriate method of visual acuity testing in a typical 3- to 4-year-old child?
Correct answer: B. HOTV testing, and if unable, follow with LEA symbol testing
Rationale
Visual acuity testing is dependent upon age and whether the child knows the letters of the alphabet. The Snellen acuity test is the gold standard, but in children ages 2 to 5, matching tests such as the HOTV and LEA symbols might be cognitively easier. Teller acuity testing is typically reserved for preverbal infants, or children with cognitive and verbal delays.

Q1540
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
For a 7-year-old child with orbital cellulitis, what would be the most likely characteristic of the causative source?
Correct answer: D. single organism
Rationale
Most young children with orbital cellulitis have infections caused by a single aerobic pathogen. In the neonate, S aureus and gram-negative bacilli are most common. In older children and adults, S aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, and S pneumoniae are common etiologic agents. Concurrent infections with multiple pathogens, including gram-negative and anaerobic organisms, can occur in older or immunosuppressed patients.

Q1541
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the most likely diagnosis in an infant with decreased vision and paradoxical pupillary responses?
Correct answer: D. retinal dystrophy
Rationale
Paradoxical pupils, a pupillary constriction in response to darkness, are most commonly associated with retinal dystrophies, although they can occur with optic neuropathies.
Amblyopia is a unilateral, or less commonly, a bilateral reduction of best-corrected visual acuity that cannot be attributed directly to the effect of any structural abnormality of the eye or visual pathways. Subtle afferent pupillary defects occur rarely and only in severe cases of amblyopia, not a paradoxical pupillary response.
Delayed visual maturation (DVM) is the condition wherein normal visual fixation and tracking do not develop in an infant within the first 3 months of life.
Cortical or cerebral visual impairment (CVI) is a condition in which visual deficits result from pathology posterior to the lateral geniculate nucleus. They usually have normal pupillary responses.

Q1542
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What nerve typically provides aberrant innervation to the levator in Marcus Gunn jaw-winking syndrome?
Correct answer: B. trigeminal nerve
Rationale
Marcus Gunn jaw-winking syndrome is the result of a congenital trigemino-oculomotor synkinesis of the jaw and levator muscles. The motor division of the trigeminal nerve aberrantly provides innervation in this scenario. The ptotic eyelid elevates with opening of the mouth or movement of the jaw to the contralateral side.

Q1543
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 4-year-old boy presents with recent onset intermittent exotropia and is found to have a cycloplegic refraction of +5.50 D sphere OD and OS. What is the most appropriate initial management?
Correct answer: B. correction of full cycloplegic refractive error
Rationale
Intermittent exotropia is characterized by a variable outward drifting of an eye when fusional factors become disrupted. Most often this condition becomes manifest during times of inattention, fatigue, or stress. Because equal and appropriate visual acuity helps maintain fusion, with a decrease in the ability to accommodate and compensate for an underlying latent hyperopia, some patients with more than 4.0 D of uncorrected hyperopia may gain better control of the exodeviation after optical correction. Mild-to-moderate hyperopia would not routinely be corrected.
As the visual acuity of this patient is currently unknown, the first management step would be to correct the refractive error. Vision therapy with active orthoptic exercises could be instituted but might not be necessary. For some cases, overcorrection of myopia by 2.00 D to 4.00 D can stimulate accommodative convergence to help control the exodeviation. However, the patient in this case is hyperopic.
Base-in prisms might also be used if there is any residual angle despite glasses, but typically only in those patients who might not be surgical candidates for correction of any residual deviation.

Q1544
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 13-year-old patient presents with bilateral vision loss, pain with eye movement, and bilateral optic disc swelling. What finding is most predictive of future risk for multiple sclerosis (MS)?
Correct answer: C. abnormal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain
Rationale
Pediatric patients are more likely than adults to present with papillitis rather than retrobulbar optic neuritis, and bilateral disease also is more common. Younger children are especially likely to have bilateral disease, although it can occur in teens as well. While older age at presentation confers greater risk for future MS, it is the presence of white matter lesions on brain MRI, as in adults, that is the most important risk factor. Laterality is not an independent risk factor, nor is a viral illness preceding the optic neuritis.

Q1545
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
An 8-year-old boy is diagnosed with a condition as demonstrated in the figure. What is the most likely etiology of this patient's disorder?
Correct answer: D. anomalous innervation of the lateral rectus by aberrant branches of oculomotor nuclei
Rationale
The figure depicts type II Duane syndrome. In the top row, there is full abduction and marked limitation of adduction. In the bottom row, there is variable up- or downshoot of the left eye with extreme right gaze effort. The typical primary position exotropia is not present in this patient.
Exotropic Duane syndrome results from the abnormal development of the abducens nerve/nucleus. The result is anomalous innervation of the lateral rectus muscle by aberrant branches of oculomotor nuclei. Globe retraction and palpebral fissure narrowing are caused by simultaneous activation of the horizontal recti. Exotropic (Type II) Duane syndrome is much less common than esotropic (Type I) Duane syndrome. Treatment for exotropic Duane syndrome may be attempted using prisms to correct for deviations in primary gaze. Surgical treatment options include lateral rectus muscle recession in one or both eyes. However, medial rectus muscle resection should be avoided because this procedure often worsens globe retraction.

Q1546
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 2-month-old infant has an enlarging hemangioma of an upper eyelid and orbit, with anisometropic astigmatism and secondary blepharoptosis. What is the preferred primary treatment for this patient?
Correct answer: B. oral propranolol
Rationale
Although all the listed treatments can be effective for some hemangiomas, oral propranolol is now preferred for the treatment of vision-threatening periocular hemangiomas. Topical timolol can be an effective treatment for superficial hemangiomas, but not for orbital lesions.

Q1547
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A premature infant born at 34 weeks and weighing 1100 grams has microcephaly, intraventricular calcifications, and bilateral retinitis. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
Correct answer: D. intravenous ganciclovir
Rationale
Congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection is an acquired congenital infection, most commonly causing disease in immunocompromised and ill infants. Congenital CMV disease is characterized by intraventricular calcifications, microcephaly, fever, jaundice, hearing loss, retinitis, optic nerve abnormalities, microphthalmos, cataract, and uveitis. The retinal inflammation is characterized by retinal whitening, edema, perivascular sheathing, and intraretinal hemorrhages. The mainstay treatment for sight-threatening congenital CMV is antiviral therapy such as ganciclovir. Intravenous (IV) penicillin G is treatment for syphilis, IV prednisolone would be treatment for noninfectious disease, and IV vancomycin is an antibiotic for bacterial disease.

Q1548
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 2-month-old boy presents with the finding shown in the photograph. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
Correct answer: A. magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
Rationale
The photograph demonstrates optic nerve hypoplasia, a developmental optic disc anomaly characterized by a reduced number of optic nerve axons. Children with optic nerve hypoplasia also are at risk for other central nervous system and pituitary abnormalities, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is recommended in these cases. The finding of an ectopic pituitary bright spot is associated with hypopituitarism, which can be life-threatening if left untreated.

Q1549
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What congenital iris abnormality represents a sequestration of epithelium during embryologic development?
Correct answer: C. cyst of the iris stroma
Rationale
Iris stromal cysts are enlarging congenital lesions that are caused by sequestration of epithelial tissues during embryogenesis. Due to enlargement, they may cause visual obstruction, glaucoma, and corneal decompensation.
Cysts of the iris pigment epithelium are caused by separation of the 2 layers of the iris pigment epithelium, not by sequestration of tissue. They typically are stable and do not usually cause clinical complications. Pigment epithelial cysts at the pupil border, also referred to as central cysts, can be hereditary. Although they sometimes enlarge slowly, they rarely cause complications. Lisch nodules are hamartomas of the iris that are present in patients with neurofibromatosis type 1.

Q1550
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 26-year-old woman has had 3 years of diplopia. She had an eye injury 5 years ago. Her best corrected visual acuity is 20/20 OD, 20/400 OS. Examination reveals a 40 prism-diopter left exotropia with a slight adduction deficit. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: A. sensory exotropia
Rationale
Sensory exotropia develops in the setting of significant visual loss in one eye. The exotropia can develop years after the vision loss, and if it occurs in older children or adults it can be associated with diplopia. A small adduction deficit can be present.
Medial rectus entrapment is relatively uncommon, and it would typically present with strabismus soon after the injury, not years later. Myasthenia gravis and thyroid eye disease can both present with a large-angle exotropia, but they would not be expected to be associated with visual decrease.

Q1551
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
Epiblepharon is a congenital anomaly of the eyelid characterized by what anatomical findings?
Correct answer: A. horizontal fold of skin adjacent to the lower eyelid, causing inward rotation of the lashes against the cornea
Rationale
Epiblepharon is a congenital anomaly in which a horizontal fold of skin adjacent to either the upper or lower eyelid—most commonly, the lower eyelid—may rotate the lashes inward against the cornea, as shown. The eyelid margin is in normal height with respect to the globe. The eyelashes are noted to be rubbing against the conjunctiva and cornea; however, the cornea tends to tolerate this condition well, and it is often minimally symptomatic. The condition tends to occur more frequently in chubby-cheeked and Asian infants. Unlike congenital entropion, epiblepharon often resolves spontaneously in the first 2 years of life. Cases that do not resolve or that cause chronic corneal irritation require surgical repair. The crescent-shaped fold of skin running vertically between the eyelids and overlying the inner canthus is the epicanthus. The eversion of the eyelid margin secondary to a vertical deficiency of the skin is congenital ectropion. Euryblepharon is enlargement of the lateral aspect of the palpebral fissure, with downward displacement of a temporal half of the lower eyelid.

Q1552
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 6-month-old child presents with poor vision and searching nystagmus. The child has at least light perception vision but is unable to fixate or follow lighted objects. If the visual acuity could be measured, what vision level would the child most likely have?
Correct answer: C. worse than 20/200
Rationale
Searching nystagmus suggests that the child has poor vision, worse than 20/200. Pendular nystagmus typically occurs in patients with visual acuity better than 20/200 in at least 1 eye. Jerk nystagmus often is associated with visual acuity between 20/60 and 20/100.

Q1553
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What condition is associated with an abnormally high number of crossed fibers in the optic chiasm?
Correct answer: D. ocular albinism
Rationale
Ocular albinism is associated with iris transillumination, foveal aplasia or hypoplasia, and decreased retinal pigmentation. Both human and animal studies have shown an abnormally high number of crossed fibers in the optic chiasm, which precludes stereopsis and is associated with strabismus. Optic nerve hypoplasia and morning glory disc are not associated with abnormalities in the crossed fibers of the optic chiasm. Achromatopsia is not typically associated with optic nerve abnormalities.

Q1554
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the most common antimetabolite used to treat uveitis in children?
Correct answer: B. methotrexate
Rationale
Azathioprine, methotrexate, and mycophenolate mofetil are all antimetabolites that can be used to treat uveitis in children. Methotrexate is most commonly used, and numerous studies have shown its efficacy in treating both arthritis and uveitis in children. Etanercept is not an antimetabolite. It is a TNF-alpha inhibitor that should be avoided in the treatment of uveitis because it may cause inflammatory ocular disease.

Q1555
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
An 18-month-old boy who underwent bilateral nasolacrimal duct probing 6 months ago presents with recurrent epiphora and mucopurulent discharge from each eye. What is the most appropriate management?
Correct answer: C. balloon dacryoplasty
Rationale
Nasolacrimal duct (NLD) probing is indicated for congenital NLD obstruction that fails to resolve with age and conservative treatment, for a dacryocystocele in the newborn that is unresponsive to massage, and for previously failed NLD probing procedures. NLD probing is performed by passing Bowman probes of appropriate sizes through the canaliculus into the nasolacrimal sac, and then down the nasolacrimal duct into the nose. The patency of the NLD system is confirmed by metal-on-metal contact in the nose, as illustrated, and/or by successful irrigation of fluorescein solution into the nasopharynx. Infracture of the inferior turbinate is often performed in addition to the probing. Some surgeons employ balloon catheter dilation, intubation, or nasal endoscopy during the first surgery for NLD obstruction, but most reserve their use for patients who require a second procedure, as does the patient in this case.
Lacrimal massage is not typically useful for NLD obstruction that has already failed an initial probing. Dacryocystorhinostomy is a final option when NLD obstruction persists or recurs following the previously described procedures, and therefore is not yet indicated for this patient. Imaging studies such as dacryocystography are impractical in most instances and consequently are not required for diagnosing NLD obstruction.

Q1556
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What additional eye motility abnormality do patients with infantile esotropia commonly have?
Correct answer: A. dissociated vertical deviation (DVD)
Rationale
DVD is associated with infantile esotropia. Vertical nystagmus and ocular flutter are not. Patients with infantile esotropia have asymmetric smooth pursuit, which is better in the temporal-to-nasal direction.

Q1557
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
An infant presents with a hyperacute unilateral conjunctivitis, as shown in the image. What treatment is recommended?
Correct answer: C. systemic antibiotics
Rationale
The image shows ophthalmia neonatorum with purulent discharge caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Ophthalmia neonatorum from Neisseria gonorrhoeae typically presents in the first 3-4 days of life. Cultures should be obtained and systemic antibiotics should be administered. Neisseria gonorrhoeae may be associated with meningitis and sepsis and Chlamydia may be associated with pneumonia. Topical antibiotics will not treat systemic disease, but they can be used as an adjunct in cases with corneal involvement. Silver nitrate is prophylaxis, not treatment.

Q1558
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 6-month-old child presents with the lesion shown in the photograph. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: C. dermoid cyst
Rationale
Dermoid cysts are the most common space-occupying orbital lesions of childhood. They are choristomas that arise from primitive dermal and epidermal elements sequestered in fetal suture lines at the time of closure. The tissue forms a cyst lined with keratinized epithelium and dermal appendages, including hair follicles, sweat glands, and sebaceous glands. Clinically, they present as painless, mobile, smooth masses. Management is surgical, and cyst rupture during surgery should be avoided to prevent inflammation and scarring.

Teratomas are choristomas containing tissue from all 3 germinal layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm). Clinical presentation of orbital teratomas may be dramatic, with massive proptosis at birth. 

Meningoceles and encephaloceles may result from congenital bony defects that allow herniation of intracranial contents into the orbit, or they may occur as a result of trauma. Clinically, lesions with an orbital location present with proptosis or hypoglobus of the involved eye, whereas more anterior lesions present as a subcutaneous mass located above the medial canthal tendon.

Q1559
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What systemic condition is associated with microspherophakia?
Correct answer: D. Weill-Marchesani syndrome
Rationale
Weill-Marchesani syndrome is associated with short status, stocky body habitus, brachydactyly (short fingers and toes), and microspherophakia.
Homocystinuria, hyperlysinemia, and sulfite oxidase deficiency are all associated with mental retardation. Patients with these conditions can develop ectopia lentis.

Q1560
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What additional factors should be taken into account when selecting an intraocular lens for a small child undergoing cataract surgery?
Correct answer: A. The target refraction must account for the typical myopic shift that occurs with growth.
Rationale
Because the child's eye continues to elongate throughout the first decade and beyond, the selection of an appropriate IOL power is complicated. Most surgeons implant IOLs with powers that children are anticipated to require in adulthood. These children can be expected to become progressively more myopic with time.
Studies have shown that in aphakic pediatric eyes, a variable myopic shift in refractive error of approximately 7.00–8.00 D occurs from 1 year to 10 years of age, with a wide standard deviation. This suggests that if a child is made emmetropic with an IOL at 1 year of age, refractive error at 10 years of age can be –8.00 D or greater. Target refraction also takes into consideration the fellow eye, and the risk of amblyopia.

Q1561
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 32-year-old man has bilateral vestibular schwannomas found during evaluation for hearing loss. He has decreased vision OS with a left relative afferent pupillary defect and swollen left optic nerve. A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan is likely to show what additional abnormality?
Correct answer: C. enhancement and thickening of the left optic nerve sheath
Rationale
This patient most likely has an underlying diagnosis of neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2), suggested by bilateral vestibular schwannomas. In this disease, optic nerve sheath meningioma is a common reason for adult-onset optic neuropathy, described best on MRI as enhancement and thickening of the optic nerve sheath.
Extraocular muscle enlargement and orbital apex crowding is more characteristic of thyroid eye disease with compressive optic neuropathy, which can present with optic nerve edema but is not as likely to be the responsible etiology of optic disc edema in a patient with NF2.
Bulbous enlargement of the intracranial left optic nerve describes optic pathway glioma, found in 20% of patients with neurofibromatosis type 1. It usually presents in childhood, not young adulthood.
Due to the posterior location of the optic radiations and chiasm, their calcification would not produce optic disc edema, unless they exert a significant mass effect, which would more typically produce papilledema (bilateral disc edema from increased intracranial pressure). There is a wide differential diagnosis of calcifications; one example is calcified intracranial astrocytic hamartoma from tuberous sclerosis.

Q1562
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the typical range of visual acuity for a person with Leber congenital amaurosis?
Correct answer: B. 20/200 to light perception
Rationale
Leber congenital amaurosis is a retinal disease associated with severe vision loss in infancy, nystagmus, poor pupillary responses, and high hyperopia. Visual acuity is 20/200 or worse. A visual acuity of 20/100 or better would be atypical and suggest a different diagnosis.

Q1563
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A child has experienced a stable, large-angle left exotropia and hypotropia with left ptosis since birth. The lid fissure widens in right gaze. What is the most likely etiology?
Correct answer: A. congenital third cranial nerve palsy
Rationale
A third cranial nerve palsy is characterized by paralysis of the medial rectus, inferior oblique, superior rectus, inferior rectus, and levator muscles. This results in limitation to adduction, elevation, and depression, as well as in ptosis and fixed, dilated pupil. Because sixth and fourth cranial nerve function is maintained, the eye with third cranial nerve palsy is typically found exotropic and depressed. Signs of aberrant regeneration, which suggest a congenital abnormality, include widening of the lid fissure on attempted adduction.
Typically, a brainstem lesion presents as a more acute process, thus not demonstrating signs of aberrant regeneration. Congenital ptosis would not have the motility abnormality. In type 2 Duane syndrome the main limitation is adduction, but there is also some limitation to abduction. However, the lid-fissure narrowing on adduction is secondary to globe retraction, rather than aberrant innervation into the levator.

Q1564
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What would be the preferred surgical treatment to treat the exodeviation from a sensory exotropia caused by a macular scar in the right eye?
Correct answer: C. lateral rectus recession and medial rectus resection in the right eye
Rationale
Surgical treatment of a sensory exotropia would include a recession and resection procedure of the nonpreferred or nondominant eye. This reduces the risk to the dominant eye from the complications of strabismus surgery, which include globe perforation or ocular ischemia. In this case, the right eye is the nondominant eye because of the macular scar.

Q1565
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
An infant recently diagnosed with juvenile xanthogranuloma based on skin biopsy and presence of iris nodules is found not to have neurofibromatosis. What can you tell the parents about the progression and prognosis of this condition?
Correct answer: B. Juvenile xanthogranuloma is a self-limited condition that usually resolves spontaneously by the age of 5 years.
Rationale
Juvenile xanthogranuloma (JXG) is a nonneoplastic histiocytic proliferation.
It develops in children younger than 2 years and is characterized by Touton giant cells. Skin involvement is usually present and consists of small, round orange-tan papules. Iris lesions are relatively rare and almost always unilateral. The iris lesions are fleshy yellow-brown masses and may be small and localized or diffusely infiltrate the iris, resulting in heterochromia. Hyphema secondary to spontaneous bleeding is a characteristic clinical presentation. Children at greatest risk for ocular involvement are those with multiple skin lesions, and they are at risk of developing secondary glaucoma, presenting with pain, acute vision loss, and photophobia.
JXG is a self-limited condition that usually resolves spontaneously by age 5 years.

Q1566
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is a characteristic of trichotillomania on slit lamp examination?
Correct answer: B. hairs of varying length
Rationale
Trichotillomania is characterized by the pulling out of one’s hair, frequently including the eyebrows and eyelashes. The characteristic appearance includes madarosis, broken hairs, and regrowth of hairs of varying lengths. Distichiasis is the presence of an accessory row of eyelashes growing out of or slightly posterior to the meibomian gland orifices. Epiblepharon is a congenital horizontal fold of skin, typically of the lower lid, that turns the lashes inward against the cornea.

Q1567
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 30-year-old man presents for evaluation of “one eye turning out” when he is tired. He has experienced this for several years. Initial evaluation demonstrates orthophoria. Upon cover testing, an exodeviation becomes present, although he is able to resume fusion with blinking. How is his exodeviation most accurately described?
Correct answer: C. intermittent exotropia with fair control
Rationale
This is a case of intermittent exotropia. The grading of control of an intermittent exotropia is usually classified as poor, fair, or good. The patient is initially orthophoric, and by history also has periods of orthophoric alignment. The exotropia becomes manifest after disruption of fusion with cover testing, and fusion can be resumed with blinking, which indicates fair control. Poor control of an intermittent exotropia is indicated by periods of prolonged manifest exotropia occurring spontaneously, while good control is indicated by an exodeviation that is manifested only by cover testing and in which fusion can rapidly be regained without blinking or refixating. An exophoria would be suggested by an exodeviation that is present only with complete disruption of binocular vision (eg, alternate cover test).

Q1568
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
The results of a cycloplegic retinoscopy in an otherwise healthy, asymptomatic 3-year-old child are likely to reveal what approximate refractive error?
Correct answer: D. 2 - 3 diopters hyperopia
Rationale
A 3-year-old child is expected to have some hyperopia, approximately between 2 and 3 diopters. Infants are hyperopic and can become slightly more hyperopic until about 7 years of age. Then the refraction shifts toward plano until about age 16, during a process called emmetropization. If myopia presents before age 10, increased myopia (6.0 D or more) has a greater likelihood of developing. Low amounts of astigmatism are common in infants and can resolve, but it is most likely with-the-rule astigmatism in children. Anisometropia is amblyogenic.

Q1569
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
At what age should an infant be able to maintain fixation and react with facial expressions?
Correct answer: B. 6–8 weeks
Rationale
Although there is some variability, the nervous system is typically mature enough at age 6–8 weeks for an infant to maintain visual fixation and react with facial expressions. Infants aged 2–3 months should be interested in bright objects. By age 3–4 months, the nasal bias for smooth pursuit should have resolved, the eyes should be orthotropic, and fix-and-follow responses to a small (2–4 inches in diameter) toy should be present.

Q1570
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 4-year-old child is referred for failed vision screening. The acuity is 20/60 right eye and 20/20 left eye. Retinoscopy demonstrates a -4.00 refractive error of the right eye. On slit-lamp examination there is a central nuclear oil droplet cataract of the right eye. Fundoscopy easily demonstrates a normal-appearing optic nerve and retina. The ophthalmologist prescribes glasses, and the child returns in 3 months. Visual acuity in the right eye is now 20/50. What is the next step in the management of this child?
Correct answer: D. part-time patching of the left eye
Rationale
Amblyopia is diagnosed when a patient has a condition known to cause amblyopia and has decreased vision that cannot be fully explained by physical abnormities of the eye. Amblyopia sometimes coexists with vision loss associated with a structural defect. In this case, the central nuclear oil droplet cataract has caused anisometropic myopia. Thus, in order to determine the extent of visual impairment from anisometropic amblyopia rather than the cataract, a trial of amblyopia treatment with patching is the next appropriate step.

Q1571
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
Short palpebral fissures, telecanthus, epicanthus, ptosis, microphthalmia, and esotropia are classic for what syndrome?
Correct answer: A. fetal alcohol syndrome
Rationale
The classic ocular features of fetal alcohol syndrome are short palpebral fissures, telecanthus, epicanthus, ptosis, microphthalmia, and esotropia.
Goldenhar patients have hemifacial microsomia. Ocular abnormalities include epibulbar dermoids, dermolipomas, eyelid colobomas, microphthalmia, cataract, and iris abnormalities. Also, Duane retraction syndrome is more common in patients with Goldenhar syndrome.
Treacher Collins syndrome is caused by the underdevelopment and sometimes agenesis of the zygoma and malar eminences. The lateral orbital rims are depressed, and the palpebral fissures slant downward because of lateral canthal dystopia.
Saethre-Chotzen syndrome is a mild craniosynostosis syndrome that may present with facial asymmetry. Ptosis is a common feature.

Q1572
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
In a patient who has an amblyopic eye with 20/400 vision and eccentric fixation, what is the best method to measure the amount of ocular misalignment?
Correct answer: C. Krimsky test
Rationale
The Krimsky test does not rely on a sensory or motor response from the patient. Motor test results will not be accurate if there is eccentric fixation. The Lancaster test depends on the patient's subjective localization of the targets, which might not be accurate in the presence of poor vision or anomalous retinal correspondence.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q1573
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
For acquired esotropia, the maximal angle of strabismus and fusional potential can be assessed by what test?
Correct answer: C. prism adaptation
Rationale
In prism adaptation, the patient with acquired esotropia is fitted with prisms to induce orthophoria. The patient is reexamined every 1 to 2 weeks, and the prism correction is increased until a stable amount of prism to achieve orthophoria is found. More prism correction is often needed at each visit. The double Maddox rod test is dissociative and cannot be used to determine fusional potential. Likewise, a 30-minute patch test is a dissociative test, so it cannot determine fusional potential. The Lancaster red-green test does not determine the maximal angle of strabismus.

Dissociated horizontal deviation (DHD) is a dissociated strabismus with a predominantly horizontal aspect. The dissociated abduction movement is an exodeviation but not a true exotropia. It can coexist with vertical and torsional aspects, but if the vertical aspect is greater, it is typically referred to as dissociated vertical deviation (DVD).

A 45-year-old woman presents to the eye clinic for an annual examination. Best-corrected visual acuity is 20/25 in her right eye and 20/20 in her left eye. Correct answer: B. forceps delivery
Rationale
The figure demonstrates vertical-oblique breaks in Descemet membrane. This presentation is most consistent with forceps delivery. Congenital glaucoma is more often associated with horizontal breaks in the cornea (Haab striae) and with ocular findings of congenital glaucoma. Posterior polymorphous dystrophy presents with polygonal patterns in the endothelium but not full-thickness Descemet breaks. Patients with keratoconus may have vertical striae in Descemet membrane (Vogt striae), but these lines are finer (thinner) than the abnormal lines depicted in this photograph. Patients with keratoconus may rarely get focal breaks in Descemet membrane, with resultant acute corneal edema (hydrops).

Rationale
The correct answer is optic nerve hypoplasia. Babies born to mothers with insulin dependent diabetes (not gestational diabetes) have a higher risk of superior optic nerve hypoplasia with a corresponding inferior field defect. Congenital glaucoma, iris coloboma, and retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) are not known defects stemming from insulin-dependent diabetes. Inherited retinal dystrophies are the most common cause of paradoxical pupils. Patients with aniridia and anterior segment dysgenesis have abnormal irises, but not paradoxical pupils. Pupillary reactions are normal in cerebral visual impairment.

Q1578

What is the average axial length of the human eye in a newborn?

Rationale
The average axial length of the human eye in a newborn is 14.5-15.5 mm. The majority of growth of the axial length occurs in the first year of life; it increases by approximately 4 mm in the first 6 months of life and an additional 2 mm during the subsequent 6 months. The axial length reaches its final axial length when the individual is between the ages of 13 and 16 years. The average axial length in an adult is 23-24 mm.

What ocular motor dysfunction will result in a V pattern strabismus?
Correct answer: C. bilateral superior oblique palsy
Rationale
A V pattern is when a strabismus deviation measures 15 PD more in upgaze than in downgaze. Inferior oblique overaction would be present in superior oblique palsy, resulting in a V pattern strabismus. Congenital exotropia can have a pattern, but it is not necessarily a V pattern. A 6th nerve palsy would be expected to have an incomitant esotropia without a pattern. Duane syndrome type 1 would result in an incomitant esotropia due to limited abduction. There may be an upshoot or downshoot of the affected eye, but this would be evident on side gazes and would not result in a V pattern.

A comitant misalignment is one where the deviation does not vary in different gazes, and it does not matter which eye is fixating. With Duane syndrome or third nerve palsies, the misalignment differs dependent upon the fixating eye and the direction of gaze. Hypotropia secondary to Graves disease is a restrictive strabismus and again will differ with different head position.

Q1582
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A child with uncorrected infantile esotropia and manifest latent nystagmus has a face turn to the left. This head posture is most likely related to what?
Correct answer: B. null point
Rationale
Latent nystagmus occurs in children who have decreased fusion from early onset strabismus. When one eye is occluded, a jerk nystagmus develops in both eyes with the fast phase directed toward the uncovered eye. The null point is with the fixating eye in adduction. Latent nystagmus becomes manifest when both eyes are open but only 1 eye is being used for vision. Thus, in a child with manifest latent nystagmus, on fixation with the left eye, the null zone would be on adduction leading to a face turn to the left.

Eyelid colobomas are commonly associated with Goldenhar syndrome. They usually involve the upper eyelid and can range from a small notch to the absence of the entire length of the eyelid, which can sometimes be fused to the globe. Eyelid colobomas have also been associated with amniotic band syndrome.
Waardenburg syndrome type 1 is associated with dystopia canthorum, in which there is lateral displacement of both the lateral canthi and lacrimal puncta. In this condition an imaginary line connecting upper and lower puncta crosses the cornea.
Apert syndrome causes eyelid malposition secondary to forehead and superior retrusion and other craniofacial abnormalities.
Stickler syndrome is associated with midface flattening.

Q1586
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What procedure is effective at simultaneously treating dissociated vertical deviation and inferior oblique overaction?
Correct answer: B. inferior oblique anteriorization
Rationale
Dissociated vertical deviation (DVD) is an innervational disorder in which either eye slowly drifts upward and outward with extortion when the eye is occluded or there is visual inattention. It typically develops by age 2 years and is commonly associated with infantile strabismus, typically esotropia or exotropia (50%). Treatment of DVD is indicated when the deviation is noticeable (more than 6–8 prism diopters) or is present frequently during the day. Treatments include optical penalization for unilateral or highly asymmetric bilateral DVD or vertical muscle surgery.
Large superior rectus muscle recessions can be effective at treating DVD, titrated based on the amount of the hypertropia and the symmetry of the DVD. Inferior rectus muscle resection or plication can help treat residual DVD. In cases of DVD and inferior oblique overaction, inferior oblique muscle anterior transposition has been shown to be effective. Inferior oblique myectomy is effective at treating inferior oblique overaction without DVD.

Q1587

In what situation is a posterior capsulorrhexis at the time of pediatric cataract surgery indicated?
Correct answer: A. in patients younger than 5 years
Rationale
A significant problem following pediatric cataract surgery is the frequent development of visually significant posterior capsular opacification (PCO). The younger the child, the higher the risk of PCO. A posterior capsulorrhexis at the time of cataract surgery is not indicated in older children or in those who can undergo a YAG capsulotomy when indicated. An anterior capsulorrhexis is an important step in pediatric surgery but does not determine whether posterior capsulorrhexis is needed. An anterior vitrectomy is generally performed with posterior capsulorrhexis in young patients to decrease the incidence of visually significant fibrous membrane development.

What is the most common outcome when a needle perforates the sclera during strabismus surgery?
Correct answer: C. chorioretinal scar
Rationale
In most cases, scleral perforation results in a chorioretinal scar. Most perforations go unrecognized unless specifically investigated by indirect ophthalmoscopy. If vitreous escapes through the perforation, many surgeons will apply immediate cryotherapy or laser to the area. Topical antibiotics are usually given postoperatively when a perforation is recognized. Referral to a retina specialist is appropriate.
Perforation can result in vitreous hemorrhage, endophthalmitis, and retinal detachment, but these complications are less frequent.

Q1591
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A patient undergoes surgery to repair an orbital floor fracture and free an entrapped inferior rectus muscle. Postoperatively, a hypotropia is present and persists for 6 months following the surgery. What surgery is most likely to provide benefit at this time?
Correct answer: A. inferior rectus recession
Rationale
Despite the repair of the orbital floor and release of the entrapped muscle, restriction can persist. Re-exploration of the fracture will then not be of benefit. In these cases, recession of the restricted muscle is the next step. An inferior rectus recession is indicated in this case. A superior rectus resection may be done if the inferior rectus recession results in undercorrection. A transposition could be considered for a muscle palsy, but an inferior rectus muscle palsy would result in a hypertropia, not a hypotropia.

Q1592
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
The finding in the figure is most frequently inherited in what manner?
Correct answer: C. autosomal dominant
Rationale
Congenital/infantile cataracts include lamellar, polar, sutural, coronary, cerulean, nuclear, capsular, and complete. The figure in the question stem shows a sutural cataract, which is an opacity of the Y-suture from the fetal nucleus that is most commonly inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. The condition is bilateral, symmetric, and vision is usually not affected.
Of the congenital/infantile cataracts, a lamellar cataract is the most common. Lamellar cataracts (Figure 1) may be inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern and are horseshoe-shaped opacities in the cortex. Their effect on visual acuity varies with the size and density of the opacity. Polar cataracts are another type of congenital cataract that are sporadic or inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. Anterior polar cataracts (Figures 2A, 2B) generally do not impair vision; however, posterior polar cataracts generally produce more visual impairment because they tend to be larger and are located closer to the nodal point of the eye. Coronary cataracts are club-shaped opacities near the lens equator that do not typically affect vision. They are often inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. Cerulean, or "blue-dot," cataracts are small, bluish opacities in the lens cortex that typically do not decrease vision. Congenital nuclear cataracts may involve the embryonic nucleus alone or the fetal nucleus as well. They tend to be bilateral with a wide spectrum of severity and are often seen in microphthalmic eyes. Capsular cataracts involve the anterior lens capsule and do not decrease vision. A complete cataract is total opacification of the lens. They can be unilateral or bilateral and produce profound visual impairment.

Möbius syndrome is an association of sixth and seventh nerve palsies. Ptosis would be associated with a third nerve palsy. Cataract is not associated with Möbius syndrome.

Q1596
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the inheritance pattern for ectopia lentis et pupillae?
Correct answer: B. autosomal recessive pattern
Rationale
Ectopia lentis et pupillae is a rare, autosomal recessive condition. Pertinent clinical features include bilaterally displaced pupils, usually inferotemporally, with lens dislocation in the opposite direction of the displaced pupil. Ectopia lentis et pupillae may be the result of membranes extending from a posterior origin to attach to the proximal pupil margin. The figures show these findings. The membranes are believed to cause traction of the iris toward the membranes (resulting in the iris abnormality) and disruption of the zonules (resulting in lens subluxation in the opposite direction). Affected patients have microspherophakia, miosis, and poor pupillary dilation with mydriatics. Lens dislocation causes decreased visual acuity, making spectacle correction essential. High myopia secondary to axial globe elongation has been reported. Aphakic correction is often needed, depending on the degree of lens dislocation. Amblyopia is the main complication and is managed by refractive correction and occlusion therapy. Lensectomy may result in retinal detachment or vitreous hemorrhage. High-frequency ultrasound preoperatively may allow assessment of risk or retinal detachment or vitreous hemorrhage. Ectopia lentis et pupillae is nonprogressive.

Q1597
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
An ophthalmologist is measuring the misalignment of the eyes of a patient with strabismus. As the patient changes the fixating eye, the amount of misalignment measured differs significantly. What type of strabismus is this?
Correct answer: D. restrictive strabismus
Rationale
Hering's law states that yoke muscles receive equal and simultaneous innervation during gaze. In the case of restrictive and paralytic muscles, the abnormal response of one of the yoke muscles causes the angle of deviation to vary, depending on the fixating eye. The extra innervation required to move the restricted or paralytic eye is shared by the unaffected eye, causing excessive action of the yoke muscle and a greater angle of deviation. When the unaffected eye is fixating, the amount of misalignment is known as the primary deviation. When the restricted or paralytic eye is fixating, the amount of misalignment is known as the secondary deviation.
In infantile strabismus, comitant strabismus, and A-pattern strabismus, the yoke muscles contract normally, and the angle of deviation is not dependent on the fixating eye.

Q1598
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What congenital retinal dystrophy is associated with the disease depicted in the following photo?
Correct answer: B. Leber congenital amaurosis
Rationale
The answer is Leber congenital amaurosis. The photo shows a classic keratoconic bowing of the cornea. Keratoconus is a common progressive, noninflammatory disorder without a predictable hereditary pattern. The disease process is likely a combination of genetic and environmental factors. There are many associated diseases, including atopy (eye rubbing), aniridia, Leber congenital amaurosis, ectopia lentis, floppy eyelid syndrome, Down syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Marfan syndrome, and osteogenesis imperfecta.
Best disease is a macular dystrophy that initially presents as an orange cyst-like structure in the macula, "the egg yolk" stage. The cystic material progressively becomes granular, with possible choroidal neovascular membranes and retinal pigmentary detachments that result in reduced vision. Stargardt disease is a macular dystrophy associated with an accumulation of lipofuscin in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), RPE dystrophy, and photoreceptor loss. Congenital stationary night blindness refers to a group of nonprogressive retinal disorders characterized by abnormal function of the rod system. Autosomal recessive and X-linked forms of congenital stationary night blindness may be associated with high myopia and decreased visual acuity in the 20/200 range. Stargardt disease, Best disease, and congenital stationary night blindness are not associated with keratoconus.

Q1599
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What features might be found when evaluating the brain scan and cerebrospinal fluid of a child with idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri)?
Correct answer: C. normal-sized or small ventricles and normal cerebrospinal fluid composition
Rationale
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH), or pseudotumor cerebri, is characterized by an increase in intracranial pressure, normal-sized or small ventricles on neuroimaging and normal cerebrospinal fluid composition. IIH can occur in children of any age and has been associated with viral infections, drug use (tetracycline, corticosteroids, vitamin A, nalidixic acid, thyroid medications, growth hormone), and cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. Prepubescent children with IIH have a lower incidence of obesity compared with adult patients, and the male-to-female ratio is approximately equal. Postpubescent children with IIH have a clinical profile similar to that of adults, with a higher incidence of obesity compared with younger patients and female gender preponderance. Because IIH is a diagnosis of exclusion, findings that suggest another disorder, such as abnormal cerebrospinal fluid composition or enlarged ventricles, exclude the diagnosis.

A 4-year-old child is discovered to have a visual acuity of 20/25 OD and 20/200 OS. What is the recommended initial management?
Correct answer: C. cycloplegic retinoscopy
Rationale
Cycloplegic refraction is an important part of the evaluation of pediatric patients. Cycloplegia is necessary to paralyze accommodation and accurately determine refractive error. The recognition of significant refractive error is important in the diagnosis and treatment of amblyopia. Occlusion therapy, optical penalization, and prescription of prism lenses would not be appropriate until a workup including cycloplegic refraction was completed and the correct cause of amblyopia was determined.

Q1601
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
An infant born at 25 weeks' gestation is diagnosed with 3 clock hours of neovascularization in zone II with plus disease. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
Correct answer: A. laser photocoagulation
Rationale
Treatment of retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) has progressed from the original use of cryotherapy to laser in the attempt to prevent neovascularization and retinal detachment. Treatment with laser now is recommended for prethreshold disease, based on the results of the Early Treatment of Retinopathy of Prematurity (ETROP) trial.
Originally, the Cryotherapy for Retinopathy of Prematurity (CRYO-ROP) trial defined threshold disease as 5 contiguous or 8 total clock hours of stage 3 ROP in zone I or II with plus disease.
The ETROP went further to define which infants with prethreshold disease would benefit from treatment, including those with zone I any stage ROP with plus disease, zone I stage 3 ROP without plus disease, and zone II stage 2 or 3 ROP with plus disease.
In this case, the baby met treatment criteria by having zone II stage 3 with plus disease.

While most cases of aniridia are inherited through autosomal dominant transmission, one-third of cases are isolated sporadic mutations, of which 20% are associated with an increased risk for Wilms tumor of the kidney. Wilms tumor results from a large chromosomal deletion, including the Wilms tumor 1 gene (WT1), a tumor suppressor gene. Colon cancer, brain tumors, and adrenal malignancies have not been linked to aniridia.

A frontalis suspension is most strongly indicated for what type of blepharoptosis?

Frontalis suspension surgery is performed when levator function is poor or absent, to allow the frontalis muscle to lift the brow and elevate the eyelid. Congenital ptosis is characterized by decreased levator function, lid lag, and often absent or poorly formed upper eyelid crease due to dysgenesis of the levator muscle. Mechanical ptosis, involutional ptosis, and Horner syndrome involve normal levator function and would be suitable for levator advancement surgery.

Galactosemia leads to the development of cataracts, typically with an "oil droplet" appearance. The cataracts may resolve with dietary restriction before a child is 4 months old. Because a lack of treatment leads to cataracts and intellectual deficiency, the ophthalmologist can play an important role in preventing these complications by helping to make the correct diagnosis.

Q1605

An individual with no prior history of strabismus was involved in a car accident and has had stable vertical diplopia for over 6 months. He has a right hypertropia that increases on left gaze and on right head tilt. Surgery has been recommended. What procedure would be the most appropriate?
Correct answer: A. recession of the right inferior oblique
Rationale
These findings are consistent with a diagnosis of a right superior oblique weakness, a right hypertropia, greater in left gaze and right head tilt. Surgery needs to address the primary deviation and also the muscle most involved in the field of action where the deviation is largest. In the absence of specific measurements, surgery needs to address the primary deviation. Only a right inferior oblique recession would lessen a right hypertropia. Resection of the left inferior rectus, resection of the right superior rectus, and a tenectomy of the right superior oblique would all worsen the right hypertropia.

Telecanthus is greater-than-normal distance between the medial canthi. This can be secondary to and present with hypertelorism, or it can be only a soft-tissue abnormality.
Hypertelorism is the excessive distance between the medial orbital walls and is detected radiographically.
Exorbitism is prominent eyes due to shallow orbits or an increased angle of divergence of the orbital walls.
In scaphocephaly, the skull is long in anterior-posterior axis and narrow bitemporally, usually from premature closure of the sagittal suture.
