Q1607
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 4-year-old patient with +2.25 D of hyperopia in both eyes recently developed a small esotropia at distance and a large esotropia at near. What is the cause of her esotropia?
Correct answer: B. high AC/A ratio esotropia
Rationale
Patients with a high (AC/A) ratio esotropia have an excessive convergence response for the amount of accommodation required to focus while wearing their full cycloplegic correction. In this form of esotropia, the deviation is present only at near or is much larger at near. The refractive error in high AC/A ratio accommodative esotropia averages +2.25 D.
Refractive accommodative esotropia involves 3 factors: uncorrected hyperopia, accommodative convergence, and insufficient fusional divergence. Because of uncorrected hyperopia, the patient must accommodate to focus the retinal image. Accommodation is accompanied by the other components of the near reflex, namely convergence and miosis. If the patient's fusional divergence mechanism is insufficient to compensate for the increased convergence tonus, esotropia results. The angle of esotropia is approximately the same at distance and near fixation and is generally between 20 and 30 prism diopters. Patients with refractive accommodative esotropia have an average of +4.00 D of hyperopia.
Patients with divergence insufficiency esotropia show reduction in the angle of esotropia when wearing glasses but have a residual esotropia despite provision of the full hyperopic correction.
Congenital esotropia is another term for infantile esotropia, which is present by 6 months of age.

The axial length of the eye of a human being at birth is about 14.5-15.5 mm, or approximately 60% of the axial length of the average adult eye (23-24 mm).

Q1609

What is the function of fusional convergence?
Correct answer: B. to eliminate bitemporal retinal disparity
Rationale
Vergences are movements of the eyes in opposite directions. Fusional vergence is a motor response that serves to eliminate image disparity. Fusional convergence eliminates bitemporal retinal disparity and controls an exophoria. Fusional divergence eliminates binasal retinal disparity and controls an esophoria. Vertical fusional vergences are used to correct a hyperphoria.

Q1610

What is the preferred treatment to correct a compensatory head turn from nystagmus?
Correct answer: A. surgery to move the null point
Rationale
A compensatory head turn is adapted to move the eyes to the null point. If a patient has a null point in right gaze, then they will turn their head to the left so that as they are walking or doing their activities, their eyes are in the null point and relatively stable, and their visual acuity is improved. Surgery or prisms can be used to decrease or eliminate the head turn by shifting the eyes so that the null point will be in primary position rather than in an eccentric gaze position.
Surgery is done to move the eyes in the direction of the head turn (another way of saying this is away from the direction of the gaze preference). Therefore, if the patient has a left head turn, the eyes are both surgically moved towards the left. In the Anderson procedure, this is done with medial rectus recession in one eye and lateral rectus recession in the other eye (in a left head turn, the surgeon would recess the medial rectus of the left eye and recess the lateral rectus of the right eye). In the Kestenbaum procedure (a recess-resect procedure), moving all 4 rectus muscles can be done to move the null point into primary position to correct the head turn (in a left head turn, for the left eye the surgeon would recess the medial rectus and resect the lateral rectus, while for the right eye the surgeon would resect the medial rectus and recess the lateral rectus).
Base-in prism will decrease the patient's drive for convergence, making nystagmus worse, may induce strabismus, and will not correct the head turn. Although base-in prism over both eyes is incorrect, prisms can be used in nystagmus to decrease head turn.  Prisms could be used to shift the perceived object location toward the null point, but this would require base-in prism over one eye and base-out prism over the other eye (eg, if left head turn and right-gaze null point, a base-out prism would be used over the left eye and a base-in prism over the right eye). Alternatively, if the patient has binocular fusion, bilateral base-out prisms can be used to induce convergence and dampen nystagmus. Prisms are sometimes used as a trial to predict surgical success.
Alternate patching therapy can make the nystagmus worse while patching because it can disrupt fusion and will not correct the head turn.
Pharmacologic therapy may be tried to decrease the nystagmus but will not affect the head turn.

Q1611
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What orbital coherence tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings are most suggestive of orbital myositis?
Correct answer: D. thickening of the extraocular muscle belly with tendon involvement
Rationale
Orbital myositis describes a nonspecific orbital inflammation that is confined to 1 or more extraocular muscles. Imaging studies show diffusely enlarged muscles with tendon involvement; the enlargement extends all the way to the insertion. This is in contrast to thyroid myopathy, where the tendon is spared.
A vascular orbital mass would suggest a hemangioma. Orbital fat stranding would be suggestive of orbital cellulitis.

Extraocular motility defects suggest orbital involvement of cellulitis, which requires imaging. Tenderness to palpation, lid edema extending to the forehead, and even contralateral eyelid edema are seen with preseptal cellulitis but do not indicate orbital involvement.

Q1613

What is the most common presentation of retinoblastoma?
Correct answer: C. leukocoria
Rationale
The most common initial sign of retinoblastoma is leukocoria (white pupillary reflex), which is usually first noticed by the child's family and described as a glow, glint, or cat’s­ eye appearance. Approximately 25% of cases present with strabismus (esotropia or exotropia). Less common presentations include vitreous hemorrhage, hyphema, ocular or periocular inflammation, glaucoma, proptosis, and pseudohypopyon.

Q1614
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
The patient in the photograph has normal-appearing optic nerves. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: C. megalocornea
Rationale
The normal corneal diameter in a healthy 2-year-old child is 12.0 mm, the adult size. A cornea over 13.0 mm in diameter, as in this photo, without signs of congenital glaucoma, suggests a diagnosis of megalocornea. Congenital glaucoma is associated with corneal haze and optic nerve cupping. Keratoglobus is associated with a normal corneal diameter. Cornea plana is a phenotype of flat cornea, indistinct limbus, shallow anterior chamber hyperopia, and associated accommodative esotropia.

Q1615
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 16-year-old girl complains of eye fatigue, diplopia, and blurry vision with extended near work. Examination reveals no refractive error and no manifest strabismus. Convergence amplitudes are decreased and near point of convergence is remote. What intervention is recommended?
Correct answer: C. orthoptic eye exercises
Rationale
The question stem describes convergence insufficiency (CI). It is characterized by poor fusional convergence amplitudes and a remote near point of convergence. This sometimes results in symptoms of asthenopia, blurred near vision, and diplopia during near work, usually in older children or adults.
Treatment of symptomatic CI typically involves orthoptic exercises. Base-out prisms can be used to stimulate and strengthen fusional convergence amplitudes. Stereograms, pencil push ups, and computer-based or office-based convergence training programs are all viable options. If these exercises fail, base-in prism reading glasses may alleviate symptoms. Surgical treatment, usually medial rectus muscle resection, may be indicated in patients whose problems persist despite medical therapy.

Pseudopapilledema is most frequently seen in patients with what type of refractive error?
Correct answer: B. hyperopia
Rationale
Pseudopapilledema refers to any elevated anomaly of the optic disc that resembles papilledema. Disc anomalies that are frequently confused with papilledema in children include drusen, hyperopic discs, and prominent glial tissue.

Q1617

An infant presents with a rapidly enlarging infantile (capillary) hemangioma. The ophthalmologist is concerned for Kasabach-Merritt syndrome. What laboratory test or tests should be ordered to confirm that diagnosis?
Correct answer: D. platelet count
Rationale
Kasabach-Merritt syndrome is the sequestration of platelets within a large vascular lesion, such as a hemangioma, leading to thrombocytopenia. Therefore, a low platelet count would support the diagnosis. Hemangiomas would not affect thyroid hormone levels or red blood cell counts. Factor V Leiden is a genetic disorder causing hypercoagulability.

Q1618

What family of disorder includes Bardet-Biedl syndrome, Senior-Løken syndrome, and Alström syndrome?
Correct answer: A. ciliopathy
Rationale
A ciliopathy is a disorder of cilia structure or function. Bardet-Biedl syndrome encompasses mutations on the proteins that mediate and regulate the microtubule-based intracellular transport process. Ciliopathies manifest as a constellation of features that include retinal degeneration, renal disease, and cerebral anomalies. The number of genes being identified with cilia dysfunction is increasing.
Metabolic disorders include abnormalities in enzyme function. Phakomatoses are neurocutaneous syndromes. Connective tissue disorders are represented by defects affecting connective tissue, such as collagen and fibrillin.

Q1619

A 6-year-old boy with recent-onset esotropia is undergoing preoperative prism adaptation. After wearing prisms, his angle of esotropia increases. What measure should be used for surgical planning?
Correct answer: C. the full, prism-adapted angle of deviation
Rationale
In prism adaptation, the patient is fitted with prisms to restore alignment of the eyes and possibly binocularity. In some patients, the placement of prisms increases the deviation. A larger amount of prism is then placed until the deviation no longer increases. Surgery is then done for the largest angle the patient acquires. The Prism Adaptation Study showed a smaller undercorrection rate (approximately 10% less) when the amount of surgery was based on the prism-adapted angle.

What type of uveitis is most common in children?

Rationale
Anterior uveitis is the most common uveitis seen in children. It is most often idiopathic, related to trauma, or associated with juvenile idiopathic arthritis.

Q1621
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What duction deficit and ocular misalignment best characterizes type 2 Duane retraction syndrome?
Correct answer: B. poor adduction and exotropia
Rationale
Duane retraction syndrome is a spectrum of ocular motility disorders characterized by anomalous co-contraction of the medial and lateral rectus muscles on actual or attempted adduction of the involved eye or eyes; this co-contraction causes the globe to retract. Horizontal eye movement can be limited to various degrees in both abduction and adduction.

Type 1, the most common form of Duane retraction syndrome, is defined as poor abduction and esotropia. A patient may adopt a head turn to establish binocular fusion, and the esotropia may be seen only in primary gaze or with a head turn to the opposite direction. Type 2 is defined by limited adduction and exotropia. Type 3 is defined as poor abduction and adduction; either esotropia or exotropia may result. Poor abduction should not result in an exotropia.

Q1622
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 5-year-old girl presents with a 1-month history of intermittent nasal discharge, tearing, itchy eyes, and conjunctival injection. What is the most appropriate therapy?
Correct answer: D. oral antihistamines
Rationale
This patient presents with classic symptoms of seasonal allergies, including allergic conjunctivitis. The duration of these symptoms for 1 month, along with their intermittent nature makes viral conjunctivitis associated with a viral upper respiratory tract infection much less likely. Seasonal allergic conjunctivitis tends to occur in the spring and fall and is triggered by environmental contact with specific airborne allergens such as pollens from grasses, flowers, weeds, and trees. Patients typically present with reddened, watery eyes, boggy-appearing conjunctiva, and complaints of itchy eyes. Allergic shiners due to lower eyelid ecchymosis may also be present. Management of allergic conjunctivitis involves removal of the offending allergens from the patient's environment and systemic and/or topical medications. Oral antihistamines are the recommended systemic therapy. They tend to be less effective at relieving ocular symptoms, but are useful in cases where other symptoms, such as nasal congestion, are present. In addition, they are often better tolerated in children, because many children have an aversion to eyedrops. Cool compresses to the eyes can further increase patient comfort. Topical medications include mast-cell stabilizers, H1-receptor blockers, vasoconstrictors, anti-inflammatory agents, or combinations thereof.
Topical corticosteroid drops used in pulsed doses can effectively reduce allergic ocular symptoms, but should be reserved for severe cases, and patients need to be monitored closely for steroid adverse effects, such as cataracts or glaucoma. If scrapings of the conjunctiva are obtained in patients with allergic conjunctivitis, eosinophils are present which is almost diagnostic of an allergic response. Topical antibiotics are not an appropriate treatment choice for patients with seasonal allergic conjunctivitis.

Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
An adult with Parkinson disease has symptoms of asthenopia, blurred near vision, and problems reading. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: D. convergence insufficiency
Rationale
Convergence insufficiency is a convergence weakness exotropia that presents with no or minimal deviation at distance but an exotropia at near, with poor fusional convergence amplitudes and a remote near point of convergence. Treatment can include orthoptic exercises, prisms, or in some cases surgery, consisting of medial rectus resections.

Q1624
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
When testing visual acuity, what is meant by the crowding phenomenon?
Correct answer: A. increase in performance when reading a single optotype compared to a full line
Rationale
The crowding phenomenon is a characteristic feature of amblyopia in which letters or symbols of a given size are more difficult to recognize if they are closely surrounded by similar forms. As a result, the measured “linear” acuity of an amblyopic eye can be worse than visual acuity measured with isolated optotypes. For this reason, for the detection of amblyopia, it is best that isolated letters or pictures not be used to test visual acuity.

Q1625
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
For a pediatric patient diagnosed with Coats disease, what might the ophthalmologist expect to discover in the evaluation?
Correct answer: C. yellow subretinal and intraretinal exudates
Rationale
The classic findings in Coats disease are unilateral yellow subretinal and intraretinal exudates associated with retinal vascular abnormalities--most often telangiectasia, tortuosity, aneurysmal dilatations, and avascularity--with a variable clinical presentation, ranging from mild changes to total retinal detachment (figure). Once the fovea is detached and the subretinal exudate becomes organized, the prognosis for restoration of central vision is poor. Coats disease may mimic retinoblastoma. However, there is no white- to cream-colored mass. Intraocular calcification is extraordinarily rare in Coats disease. The etiology of Coats disease is unknown, but associations with various gene deletions have been reported. Treatment is directed at obliterating the abnormal vessels and includes cryotherapy or laser photocoagulation. The disease is stopped when the leaking vessels are destroyed. Recently, there have been reports of promising results with intravitreal bevacizumab and triamcinolone used as adjuncts to laser treatment.

Q1626
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
An 11-month-old girl presents with sudden-onset, unexplained somnolence for which an ophthalmologist is emergently consulted to evaluate her red eye. The external examination shows a total hyphema in the patient's right eye, as shown. What is the most likely explanation for this girl's condition?
Correct answer: B. nonaccidental trauma
Rationale
The most likely explanation for this girl's appearance is a recurrent traumatic hyphema with associated somnolence secondary to nonaccidental trauma. The cause of drowsiness is not well understood but is a well-known feature. In a patient for whom no mention is made of antecedent trauma, consideration must be given to the potential of nonaccidental trauma or child abuse. The degree of periorbital ecchymosis, subconjunctival hemorrhage, and course, and other potential extraocular trauma should be consistent with the history given. Children suspected of nonaccidental trauma must be reported and evaluated, preferably by an experienced multidisciplinary pediatric team. Sickle cell disease may be associated with increased risk of rebleeding and visual loss in cases of hyphema, but does not cause hyphema. Sickle cell crisis causes severe deep pain, usually of the abdomen or bones, but does not cause somnolence. Rarer nontraumatic causes of hyphema in children include retinoblastoma, juvenile xanthogranuloma of the iris, and rarely leukemia or other blood dyscrasia, but unlike traumatic hyphema, are not associated with impaired consciousness.

Q1627
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 12-year-old boy is diagnosed with well-controlled, intermittent exotropia. What is stereopsis testing most likely to reveal?
Correct answer: D. excellent stereopsis
Rationale
Intermittent exotropia is an outward deviation that becomes manifest during times of visual inattention, fatigue, or stress. In the early stages of the disorder, the deviation is usually larger for distance viewing than for near. Thus, sensory testing at near is typically excellent, including stereopsis and fusion on Worth 4 Dot testing. When the eye deviates, suppression of the image typically occurs, rather than the recognition of diplopia.

Q1628
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What feature is characteristic of congenital ptosis?
Correct answer: C. decreased levator function
Rationale
The most common form of congenital ptosis is thought to result from dystrophic development of the levator muscle without associated innervational abnormalities. Patients with congenital ptosis have decreased levator function and a poorly formed eyelid crease. The lid tissues and levator are not longer than normal. Congenital ptosis may be familial and may be unilateral or bilateral. Children with unilateral congenital ptosis will commonly elevate the affected eyelid by lifting the ipsilateral brow. Anisometropic astigmatism may be associated with ptosis and is the most common cause of amblyopia in these patients. Surgical correction serves as definitive treatment for congenital ptosis, and repeat procedures are common. Prompt surgery is recommended for the presence of amblyopia, occlusion of the visual axis, or a severe compensatory head posture (chin-up position).

Q1629
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
Orbital cellulitis in a 7-year-old patient most commonly arises from where?
Correct answer: A. ethmoidal sinus
Rationale
Infectious orbital cellulitis is an infection posterior to the orbital septum. The vast majority of cases are caused by bacterial sinusitis. In a 7-year-old patient, the maxillary and frontal sinuses are underdeveloped. Therefore, orbital cellulitis is most likely to arise from the ethmoidal sinus. Other causative factors include the thinness of the lamina papyracea and venous drainage from the ethmoid sinus to the orbit. In adults, infections are usually polymicrobial, including gram-positive cocci, Moraxella, and H. influenzae. However in children, the causative agent is usually a single organism that is typically a gram-positive organism. Adults often require early surgical intervention, while children typically improve with intravenous antibiotics alone.

A 30-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with pseudotumor cerebri, or idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH). Her current medications include lisinopril, tetracycline, vitamin E, and verapamil. What medication should be discontinued?
Correct answer: D. tetracycline
Rationale
Pseudotumor cerebri (or IIH) consists of increased intracranial pressure with normal or small-sized ventricles on neuroimaging and normal cerebrospinal fluid contents. Drugs that have been associated with IIH include tetracycline, corticosteroids, vitamin A, nalidixic acid, thyroid medications, and growth hormones. Medications for the increased intracranial pressure include diuretics, such as acetazolamide and hydrochlorothiazide.

A 7-year-old boy is referred for evaluation of a dermolipoma that has been visible in the temporal subconjunctival area since he was an infant. It is becoming larger and cosmetically objectionable, and his parents are requesting its removal. What is the most appropriate course of treatment?
Correct answer: C. surgical debulking
Rationale
Dermolipomas are benign lesions that may have deep extensions to the levator and extraocular muscles. These tumors typically require no treatment. If they become large and cosmetically objectionable, only the anterior, visible portion should be excised. Complete excision of the mass is not appropriate, because it may cause damage to delicate orbital structures. Chemotherapy and radiation would not be expected to have an effect on this slow-growing, benign tumor.

What approach is most effective in ensuring that a patient's parents or caregivers adhere to an amblyopia treatment plan?
Correct answer: A. counseling regarding treatment and side effects
Rationale
Counseling regarding treatment and side effects is an important part of amblyopia treatment because the outcome often depends on patient compliance. Parents and caregivers are more likely to adhere to treatment recommendations if they understand the diagnosis and rationale for treatment. In older children, it is important to obtain their commitment to the treatment program. In compliant patients, improvement is frequent but cannot be guaranteed. Future work opportunities also cannot be determined. Occlusion therapy is performed by covering the patient's better-seeing eye, not the amblyopic eye.

However, signs of poor visual development can include searching eye movements, lack of response to familiar faces or objects, nystagmus, and forceful rubbing or poking of the eyes.

Q1634

A 2-year-old with congenital rubella has developed bilateral white cataracts. Five days following uncomplicated right cataract surgery, the child has increased photophobia, redness, and eye pain. What aspect of congenital rubella syndrome most likely explains this development?
Correct answer: B. release of live virus particles
Rationale
Live virus particles can be recovered in the eye for up to 3 years after birth in a child with congenital rubella and can cause significant inflammation postsurgically. The vigorous postoperative inflammatory response should be managed aggressively with steroids and mydriatics in these patients because they are prone to secondary membrane development. 
Elevated episcleral venous pressure can result in abnormally high intraocular pressure because episcleral venous pressure accounts for a component of intraocular pressure. Presence of hemoglobin-laden macrophages can cause a secondary glaucoma due to outflow obstruction of the trabecular meshwork in hemolytic glaucoma. Sensitization to native lens proteins refers to phacoantigenic glaucoma in which there is granulomatous inflammation against native lens proteins. None of these are typically associated with congenital rubella syndrome.

A newborn is found to have a cloudy central cornea associated with central corneal thinning, adherent lens, and anterior polar cataract. Additionally, the newborn has short stature, cleft lip, and brachydactyly. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Peters syndrome is a corneal defect with an overlying stromal opacity, often associated with iris strands and lens adherence. If associated with short stature, brachydactyly (short fingers and toes), cleft lip, and intellectual disability, it is Peters-plus syndrome. Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome does not typically have central corneal thinning or adherent lens. Aniridia and Bardet-Biedl syndrome do not have primary corneal abnormalities.

Q1637
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
Three weeks ago, a 12-year-old boy developed diplopia and some pain with eye movement, worse on up and left gaze. His visual acuity was 20/20 OU and his pupils reacted briskly, without a relative afferent pupillary defect. He correctly identified 10 of 10 color plates OU. His Hertel measurements were symmetric and unremarkable OU. Given his ocular motility shown, what additional finding is expected?
Correct answer: C. tenderness of the right superonasal orbit
Rationale
The external photographs show a supraduction deficit on the right side consistent with an acquired Brown syndrome. Using the corneal reflex to estimate the amount of misalignment (Hirschberg test), the amount of misalignment is greatest in upgaze, not left gaze, in these photographs. If the cause of the supraduction deficit were from extraocular muscle restriction, the greatest increase in IOP would be in upgaze, not downgaze. There is no suggestion of an orbitopathy that is typical of gaze-evoked visual loss. Tenderness over the area of the trochlea in the superonasal orbit may be seen in patients with acquired Brown syndrome, and symptoms are often worst when the globe is elevated and adducted on the affected side.

Q1638
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What topical glaucoma medication is contraindicated in a 2-month-old baby due to risk of central nervous system (CNS) depression associated with bradycardia and apnea?
Correct answer: D. brimonidine
Rationale
Alpha-2 adrenergic agonists (eg, brimonidine) may have central nervous system (CNS)-mediated effects, and therefore their use is contraindicated in infants under the age of 2. There may be increased CNS penetration in young children, which can result in CNS depression, bradycardia, apnea, and hypotension in this age group. Beta blockers may also cause respiratory distress with apnea in small infants, but the mechanism is via bronchospasm.

Q1639
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 14-year-old girl presents for routine eye examination. She has an abduction deficit of the right eye. She is orthophoric in primary gaze. She denies diplopia. What is the most important next step in the examination?
Correct answer: D. Observe the lid fissure in left gaze.
Rationale
This girl demonstrates findings of type 1 Duane syndrome, whereby an abduction deficit is present, and the lid fissure narrows on attempted adduction. In anatomical and imaging studies, the nucleus of the sixth cranial nerve is absent, and an aberrant branch of the third cranial nerve innervates the lateral rectus muscle. This aberrancy results in firing of both the lateral and medial recti upon attempted adduction, causing globe retraction and narrowing of the interpalpebral fissure. Results of electromyographic studies support this finding. The patient is orthophoric in primary gaze and thus not diplopic, although many patients with type 1 Duane syndrome will have an esotropia at baseline. This condition is considered one entity in a class termed congenital cranial dysinnervation disorders, and it may be associated with systemic defects such as Goldenhar syndrome (hemifacial microsomia, ocular dermoids, ear anomalies, preauricular skin tags, and eyelid colobomas).
Lid position in abduction and downgaze would not be affected in a type 1 Duane syndrome. Lid elevation in downgaze could be seen in aberrant regeneration after a third nerve palsy. Lid position in sustained upgaze would change with myasthenia gravis, causing ptosis with muscle fatigue, but not in Duane syndrome. This patient is not diplopic, indicating a congenital, not acquired etiology such as myasthenia gravis.

Q1640
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the cause of lid-fissure narrowing on attempted adduction in type 1 Duane syndrome?
Correct answer: A. co-contracture of the lateral and medial rectus
Rationale
Duane syndrome is an innervational anomaly of the horizontal rectus muscles wherein an aberrant branch of the third cranial nerve innervates the lateral rectus muscle. Co-contracture of the medial and lateral rectus muscles on adduction causes globe retraction and secondary lid fissure narrowing (to be clear, it is not that the muscles of the eyelids are contracting and pulling the fissure closed, but rather that the globe's being pulled further back in the orbit is allowing the fissure to get smaller, just as would be true in enophthalmos or an undersized orbital implant after evisceration). Misinnervation of the levator muscle is associated with Marcus Gunn jaw-winking syndrome. Orbicularis oculi spasm is not typically reported in Duane syndrome. Diplopia is rare in Duane syndrome, as suppression develops early in life.

Q1641
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
An infant is diagnosed with type 1, prethreshold retinopathy of prematurity. What is the best step in management, according to the Early Treatment for Retinopathy of Prematurity (ETROP) study?
Correct answer: D. panretinal laser photocoagulation to ablate the peripheral retina
Rationale
Prethreshold ROP is classified into 2 types. Type 1 includes:
  • zone I, any stage ROP with plus disease
  • zone I, stage 3 ROP, without plus disease
  • zone II, stage 2 or 3 ROP, with plus disease
Type 2 includes:
  • zone 1, stage 1 or 2 ROP, without plus disease
  • zone II, stage 3 ROP, without plus disease.
The ETROP trial found that earlier treatment at prethreshold resulted in better structural and visual outcomes when compared with conventional treatment at threshold. Based on ETROP, laser treatment is recommended for any eye with type 1 ROP. Eyes with type 2 ROP should be closely observed and, if there is progression to type 1 or threshold disease, treated.
Prior to the ETROP trial, the Cryotherapy for Retinopathy of Prematurity (CRYO-ROP) study defined threshold disease as 5 contiguous or 8 total clock hours of stage 3 ROP in zone I or II with plus disease. Laser has largely replaced cryotherapy as treatment for ROP since that time.
The most recent treatment option for type 1 ROP is intravitreal injection of anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti­-VEGF) agents bevacizumab and ranibizumab. The initial study of anti­-VEGF agents for treatment of ROP, and the most influential, was Bevacizumab Eliminates the Angiogenic Threat of Retinopathy of Prematurity (BEAT­-ROP), which found a significant benefit to structural outcome for zone I eyes that received intravitreal bevacizumab monotherapy compared with those that received laser treatment. Subsequent publications have docu­mented that ROP may recur months after treatment with anti­-VEGF agents; thus, prolonged surveillance and re­treatment may be necessary after intravitreal anti­-VEGF injections. Anti­-VEGF treatment should not be administered to infants who are unlikely to return for frequent follow-­up examinations after they are discharged from the hospital.

Q1642
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
To test for a horizontal deviation using the Maddox rod, what direction should the cylinders be oriented in front of the right eye?
Correct answer: B. 180°
Rationale
In the Maddox rod test, a series of parallel cylinders convert a single point source of light into a line image perpendicular to the cylinders. To test for horizontal deviations, the Maddox rod cylinders are placed horizontally in front of the right eye (180°). The patient, fixating on a point source of light, sees a vertical line with the right eye and the point source of light with the left. If the line is superimposed on the point, there is no horizontal deviation (orthophoria). If the point is to the left of the line (the line is to the right of the point), esodeviation is present. If the point is to the right of the line (the line is to the left of the point), exodeviation is present.

A 5-month-old child presents with leukocoria, and B-scan ultrasonography shows an intraocular mass with internal calcification. A diagnosis of intraocular retinoblastoma is made. What adjunctive test should be performed?
Correct answer: D. magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain
Rationale
MRI of the brain is indicated in the evaluation of an infant with a clinical diagnosis of retinoblastoma to assess for extraocular or intracranial involvement of the disease. Invasive diagnostic testing such as transvitreal needle biopsy of the intraocular mass and aqueous humor aspiration are not indicated, as they may promote extraocular extension of the tumor. Fluorescein angiography is not needed for diagnosis and is technically challenging in an infant.

What term best describes the right medial rectus muscle as the right eye adducts in left gaze?
Correct answer: D. agonist
Rationale
There are 3 important terms relating to the muscles used in monocular eye movements: agonist, the primary muscle moving the eye in a given direction; synergist, the muscle in the same eye as the agonist that acts with the agonist to produce a given movement; and antagonist, the muscle in the same eye as the agonist that acts in the direction opposite to that of the agonist.

Correct answer: A. sensory deprivation esotropia
Rationale
Sensory deprivation esotropia (also termed sensory esotropia) develops in the setting of monocular vision loss, such as cataract, corneal opacity, or blurred retinal images from high anisometropia or other causes. Pseudoesotropia has no true ocular misalignment. Accommodative esotropia is associated with bilateral hyperopia. In infantile esotropia, misalignment is present by 6 months of age.

Rationale
Congenital ptosis may be associated with amblyopia due to occlusion of the visual axis or anisometropic astigmatism. If the amblyopia cannot be managed with glasses or patching, surgery is indicated. A specific amount of lid asymmetry is not an indication for surgery. Lagophthalmos may be a contraindication because surgery will make this worse. Exophoria is not an indication for surgery.

Q1647
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 6-month-old child presents with the findings shown for 4 weeks. Approximately what percentage of such cases will require surgical intervention?
Correct answer: A. 10%
Rationale
Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction (CNLD) occurs in about 5% of full-term newborns. Simple NLDO is usually secondary to a thin mucosal membrane at the lower end of the nasolacrimal duct (valve of Hasner). Signs of obstruction may be manifest as early as age 1 month in 80% to 90% of cases. Typical clinical features include excess tearing and retrograde discharge of mucopurulent material when digital pressure is applied on the lacrimal sac. The vast majority of cases spontaneously resolve (90%) within the first 9-12 months of life. Cases that do not resolve with conservative measures (lacrimal massage) within this time frame may require nasolacrimal probing.

Q1648
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A child has a visual acuity of 20/30 right eye and 20/20 left eye. Cover testing demonstrates a 4 diopter right esotropia. On Worth 4-dot testing, the child sees 3 lights at distance and 4 lights at near. What is this child demonstrating?
Correct answer: B. anomalous retinal correspondence (ARC)
Rationale
ARC is a condition wherein the fovea of the fixating eye has acquired an anomalous common visual direction with a peripheral retinal element in the deviating eye. ARC is an adaptation that restores some degree of binocular cooperation despite manifest strabismus. Seeing 4 dots indicates that if there is a suppression scotoma, it must subtend a smaller visual angle than the test target. In this case, the right eye is suppressing the Worth 4-dot at distance, since the lights are being projected into the suppression scotoma. At near, the lights are outside the suppression scotoma and a fused response is noted. This is consistent with ARC.
The child has ARC and monofixation syndrome. The clinician must demonstrate the absence of bimacular fusion by documenting a macular scotoma in the nonfixating eye under binocular conditions, as well as the presence of peripheral binocular vision (peripheral fusion).
A diplopic response or 5 lights would be given at near in normal retinal correspondence in this patient with a right esotropia. If a large suppression scotoma were present, only 3 lights would be seen at near. Paradoxical diplopia occurs when ARC persists following ocular realignment surgery and a previously misaligned eye is now straight.

Q1649
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
For 3 days, an 8-year-old boy has had generalized discomfort, fever, lethargy, and headache, and in his right eye, he has pain and eyelid edema. In the past, he has been told that he has sinusitis. At this examination, he has a visual acuity of 20/60 OD and 20/20 OS, full ocular motility of his left eye, and proptosis, limited ocular motility, and pain on movement of his right eye. What is the recommended initial management for this patient (shown)?
Correct answer: B. hospitalization and treatment with intravenous antibiotics
Rationale
The patient has a right orbital cellulitis with proptosis secondary to sinusitis. Orbital cellulitis in children is a potentially life-threatening disease requiring hospitalization and treatment with intravenous antibiotics. Orbital cellulitis is commonly associated with ethmoid or frontal sinusitis, as in this case. Early signs and symptoms of orbital cellulitis include fever, lethargy, eyelid edema, rhinorrhea, headache, orbital pain, and tenderness on palpation. Unlike preseptal cellulitis, patients with orbital cellulitis also have proptosis and limited ocular motility on exam. Orbital CT should be performed promptly to determine if a subperiosteal abscess is present, but it is not the most urgent intervention and should not delay hospitalization or initiation of antibiotic therapy. Likewise, consultation with an otolaryngologist is reasonable but may be delayed until antibiotics are begun. Treatment of a child with orbital cellulitis in an outpatient setting is not appropriate, due to the grave ramifications of antibiotic noncompliance and the potential need to emergently decompress a subperiosteal abscess.

Q1650
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 3-year-old child is referred to an ophthalmologist for bilateral central corneal opacities and iridocorneal adhesions.  He is noted to have a craniofacial abnormality, intellectual disability, and short stature. What is his most likely condition?
Correct answer: B. Peters-plus syndrome
Rationale
Based on this child's presentation, Peters-plus syndrome is the most likely cause. Peters anomaly is characterized by a posterior corneal defect with an overlying stromal opacity, often with adherent iris strands. When unilateral, it is likely isolated, but bilateral cases warrant genetic evaluation. Peters-plus syndrome is caused by biallelic B3GLCT mutations and is associated with short stature, craniofacial abnormalities, shortened fingers and toes, and intellectual disability.
Congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy (CHED) does have bilateral corneal haze but is not generally associated with any systemic anomalies. Epibulbar dermoid presents unilaterally in general, and the opacity may vary in size and location on the cornea, limbus, or adjacent sclera; Goldenhar syndrome can be associated with this finding, but its abnormalities include ear deformities, vertebral deformities, eyelid coloboma, or Duane retraction syndrome. Congenital glaucoma can result in bilateral corneal clouding due to high intraocular pressure and may also cause Haab striae and buphthalmos. Primary congenital glaucoma does not have any associated systemic findings.

Anterior segment ischemic syndrome (ASI) can occur after retinal surgery and presents with shallowing of the anterior chamber, marked flare, elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), and excessive eye congestion. In contrast to ASI after strabismus surgery, ASI after scleral buckling may present with high pressure and shallowing of the anterior chamber. ASI is more likely simply because the all of the other conditions listed (aqueous misdirection, acute angle closure, phacomorphic glaucoma) are much less likely after a scleral buckle and vitrectomy.

Congenital anomalies may be categorized as:
  • Agenesis is a developmental failure (anophthalmos)
  • Hypoplasia is a developmental arrest (optic nerve hypoplasia).
  • Hyperplasia is developmental excess (distichiasis)
  • Dysraphia is a failure to fuse (choroidal coloboma)
  • Failure to divide or canalize (congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction).
  • Persistence of vestigial structures (persistent fetal vasculature).

Correct answer: C. diabetes insipidus
Rationale
The findings suggest a diagnosis of eosinophilic granuloma. In this disease, the orbital lesion is usually located in the superotemporal quadrant of the orbit and most commonly results in lytic bony lesions of the orbital roof. Patients might be mistakenly treated for allergy or infection until the proper diagnosis is made by biopsy. Diabetes insipidus is a possible systemic manifestation.

Q1655
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the most common and serious ocular complication in the child pictured below?
Correct answer: B. glaucoma
Rationale
Port-wine stain on the eyelid, choroidal hemangioma, retinal vascular tortuosity, and glaucoma are all found in Sturge-Weber syndrome (SWS). However, glaucoma is the most serious ocular complication and can be quite difficult to control. Note the buphthalmos in the figure above on the side of the port-wine stain, because glaucoma can be present at birth. However, it can occur later in childhood as well. It has been reported to occur in up to approximately 70% of SWS patients. Causes of elevated IOP include elevated episcleral venous pressure, hyperemia of the ciliary body with hypersecretion of aqueous, and developmental anomaly of the anterior chamber angle.
SWS consists of a facial cutaneous angioma (port-wine stain), which is composed of well-formed capillaries in the dermis and usually involves the forehead and upper eyelid. The lesion can extend to the lower eyelid and maxillary and mandibular regions and does not always conform to the distribution of the trigeminal divisions. The eye ipsilateral to the port-wine stain may have tortuous vessels and arteriovenous communications in the retina and choroidal angiomatosis (ketchup fundus).
Choroidal hemangiomas are asymptomatic in childhood; however, in adolescence or adulthood, the choroid sometimes becomes markedly thickened. Degeneration or detachment of the overlying retina with severe vision loss may occur; however, this is less common than glaucoma. The likelihood of glaucoma is increased if there is involvement of the upper eyelid skin, choroidal hemangioma, iris heterochromia, and episcleral hemangioma. Other serious non-ocular complications include cerebral calcifications and seizures, and leptomeningeal vascular malformations ipsilateral to the skin lesion.

Q1656
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
For bilateral amblyopia due to high refractive error, what treatment is recommended?
Correct answer: C. full spectacle correction
Rationale
Ametropic amblyopia is a bilateral reduction in acuity resulting from large, approximately equal, uncorrected refractive errors in both eyes. Therefore, primary treatment is to optically correct the refractive error with spectacles or contact lenses. Since the amblyopia is bilateral, treatment with patching or atropine is inappropriate and may worsen the vision in the penalized eye.

Q1657
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
In a child with nystagmus blockage syndrome, what type of strabismic deviation is most commonly present?
Correct answer: B. esotropia
Rationale
Nystagmus blockage syndrome occurs when a child with congenital motor nystagmus overconverges to damp the nystagmus, resulting in esotropia. Patients with nystagmus blockage syndrome characteristically present with an esotropia that "eats up prism" as the strabismic deviation increases upon attempted measurement. The nystagmus is least apparent when the deviation is largest. Dissociated vertical deviation, exotropia, and V-pattern strabismus are not associated with nystagmus blockage syndrome.

Q1658
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A healthy 4-year-old boy with normal visual acuity in both eyes has a chin-up posture. What is the most likely cause of this boy's anomalous head position?
Correct answer: C. V-pattern exotropia
Rationale
The most likely cause of this boy's abnormal chin-up position is V-pattern exotropia (figure). A-pattern or V-pattern strabismus occurs in up to one-fourth of all horizontal strabismus cases. Patients with V-pattern forms of strabismus have a horizontal deviation that is more convergent or less divergent in downgaze compared with upgaze. Patients with pattern strabismus and sensory fusion may adopt an anomalous head posture in an effort to maintain a single image, for example, chin-up posture with V-pattern exotropia or chin-down posture with A-pattern exotropia. The etiology of pattern strabismus is unknown except in cases of extraocular muscle palsies. Despite this, multiple theories suggest primary or secondary muscle dysfunction involving the oblique muscles, horizontal rectus muscles, or vertical rectus muscles.
In A-pattern exotropia, a chin-up position would place the eyes in a position of increased exodeviation. Convergence insufficiency and dissociated vertical deviation do not lead to abnormal head positions.

Q1659
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A patient presents with orthophoria at distance and 30 prism diopters (30Δ) of esotropia at near. The cycloplegic refraction is -0.25 sphere OU. What is the most common treatment used to decrease the near deviation?
Correct answer: D. bifocals with -0.25 for distance and +3.00 add
Rationale
In cases of high accommodative convergence/accommodation (AC/A) ratio, excessive convergence tone results from accommodation, leading to esotropia at near.
The most common treatment for high AC/A ratio includes bifocals with a +3.00 add to decrease the accommodative drive. Cholinesterase inhibitors, such as echothiophate iodide, and surgery are other treatment modalities. Over-minused myopic glasses and cycloplegics increase accommodative drive and worsen the esotropia.

Correct answer: D. examination under anesthesia
Rationale
Penetrating injuries in children can often have subtle signs. In the setting of an injury, an eccentric or peaked pupil is suggestive of penetrating injury, which requires an examination under anesthesia (EUA) for exploration and repair. Topical antibiotics are not preferred initial treatments. Placing a bandage contact lens or any other device on the eye is contraindicated if there is risk for globe penetration. Observation alone is relatively contraindicated due to the risk of vision-threatening complications of a penetrating injury.

Correct answer: C. V pattern

This photo demonstrates a child with Crouzon syndrome, a craniosynostosis. Most craniosynostoses are associated with a V pattern exotropia. There is apparent inferior oblique overaction, but this could be due to orbital or globe extorsion, anomalous muscle insertions, or pulley abnormalities.
The A pattern typically occurs in exotropic patients and is associated with spina bifida. The X pattern is associated with a large-angle exotropia that increases in upgaze and downgaze. The Y pattern is also known as pseudo-overaction of the inferior obliques, and features orthotropia in primary position. The divergence in upgaze is thought to be due to anomalous lateral rectus innervation during upgaze.

Q1662
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
An 18-year-old man is referred to an ophthalmologist after a motor vehicle accident. He has had difficulty abducting the left eye and complained of left eye pain with abduction. He also reports 3 episodes of emesis with nausea since the accident. Coronal imaging is shown in the figure. The ophthalmologist performs an extensive examination. What are his extraocular muscle forced ductions and force generation expected to demonstrate?
Correct answer: A. abduction restriction with forced duction; normal force generation on abduction
Rationale
The figure shows entrapment of the left medial rectus muscle in a left medial orbital wall fracture. Clinically, the patient has pain and restriction on abduction in conjunction with nausea and emesis. In this setting, urgent surgical intervention is indicated. Sometimes, a trial of steroids with close observation for 24 hours may be indicated prior to surgical intervention. However, ongoing ischemia to an entrapped rectus muscle may lead to loss of function if release of the muscle is not performed in a timely manner.
Forced duction testing determines whether an ocular motility dysfunction is a restrictive or paretic process. The test is performed by first applying topical anesthesia to the eye. Then forceps are used to grasp the Tenon capsule and conjunctiva near the limbus and passively move the eye. With an acute entrapment of the medial rectus muscle, a restriction in abduction of the eye would be anticipated. There may also be restriction with adduction of the eye. Forced generation testing determines the active force produced by the extraocular muscles. After topical anesthesia is applied, the examiner grasps the Tenon capsule and conjunctiva near the limbus. The examiner then asks the patient to attempt an eye movement, and the force generated by the extraocular muscle is observed.
Patients with paretic muscles have reduced forced generations. In a patient with an entrapped medial rectus muscle, reduced forced generation may be observed with adduction if the medial rectus is injured. However, forced generation with abduction should be normal, since the lateral rectus appears uninjured.

Correct answer: D. genetic counseling and low-vision assessment
Rationale
Hereditary optic atrophy does not respond to prednisone, since it is not inflammatory, or to optic nerve sheath decompression, since it is not a result of high pressure. High-dose vitamin A has been tried in retinitis pigmentosa. Genetic counseling is indicated, because there is a risk that future siblings can be affected. Vision assessment and aids for the expected vision potential are also indicated.

What is the most likely cause for painless blurry vision and 2+ anterior chamber cell in an 8-year-old girl?
Correct answer: D. juvenile idiopathic arthritis
Rationale
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is the most common identifiable cause of anterior uveitis in children. JIA-associated uveitis is usually bilateral and nongranulomatous with fine keratic precipitates (KPs), usually with a white eye without obvious inflammation. Chronic inflammation can cause band keratopathy, posterior synechiae, glaucoma, cataract, and hypotony. Traumatic iritis almost always is painful. Sarcoidosis is typically a granulomatous iritis and commonly is associated with pain. Iritis associated with reactive arthritis typically presents with photophobia and is less likely in an 8-year-old child.

Correct answer: B. facial angiofibromas
Rationale
Tuberous sclerosis (Bourneville disease) is a phakomatosis associated with defects in the tuberin gene or hamartin gene. The most common retinal finding is retinal phakoma. Associated findings include cognitive disabilities, seizures, facial angiofibromas, ungual or periungual fibromas, ash leaf spots, and shagreen patches. Lisch nodules and plexiform neurofibromas are associated with neurofibromatosis type 1. Acoustic neuromas are associated with neurofibromatosis type 2.

Q1666

A 4-year-old child who has unilateral, chronic uveitis is being treated with cycloplegics. What additional treatment can be done to best prevent amblyopia?
Correct answer: B. full glasses correction with bifocal
Rationale
Cycloplegia is used in uveitis to prevent synechiae formation and decrease pain. However, cycloplegic drugs also blur vision, which can induce amblyopia. Indeed, amblyopia can be treated pharmacologically by using cycloplegics (atropine) on the fellow eye, rather than occlusion therapy, for this reason. Dispensing the full hyperopic prescription with a bifocal gives a clear image at near and distance, to decrease the risk of amblyopia. Orthoptics will not treat amblyopia in this situation. Patching is not the best treatment, as the affected eye will be defocused for near work. Pilocarpine is contraindicated, because it will reverse the beneficial effects of the cycloplegics and may exacerbate inflammation.

Q1673
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What finding is an indication for urgent surgical intervention in a pediatric orbital floor fracture?
Correct answer: C. restriction with forced-duction testing
Rationale
Upon fracture of the orbital floor, orbital contents may prolapse into the maxillary sinus and become entrapped. Restriction occurs with entrapment of the inferior rectus beneath either a trapdoor fracture or a linear opening caused by flexion deformity of the floor. Injury to the inferior rectus muscle or to its nerve, with resulting weakness, may be caused by hemorrhage or ischemia, in addition to restriction. If muscle entrapment is present, a forced duction test shows restriction of passive movement of the eye. Eye movement may stimulate the oculocardiac reflex, causing pain, nausea, and bradycardia. Urgent repair should be undertaken in these cases, as release of the entrapped muscle may improve the final ocular motility by limiting fibrosis.
Diplopia, orbital ecchymosis, eyelid edema, enophthalmos, hypoesthesia in the cutaneous distribution of the infraorbital nerve, and involvement of the lacrimal drainage system are commonly present with acute orbital fracture but are not indications for urgent repair.

The lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) can cause severe congenital infections. By what route or vector is the virus transmitted to the pregnant woman?

Rationale
Rodents are the natural host and reservoir for LCMV. It is a single-stranded RNA virus of the Arenaviridae family; transmission to humans is often through exposure to rodents and thought to be airborne, possibly through food contamination or the rodent's bite. Ocular findings include macular and chorioretinal peripheral scarring, similar in morphology and distribution to that of congenital toxoplasmosis. Vertical transmission to a fetus occurs during episodes of maternal viremia. The earlier in gestation the transmission occurs, the more serious the sequelae.

Correct answer: C. meridional amblyopia
Rationale
Meridional amblyopia occurs in the setting of uncorrected high astigmatism, causing loss of resolving ability specific to the chronically blurred meridians. This is a type of isoametropic amblyopia, which is bilateral decreased visual acuity from chronically defocused retinal images. It usually occurs with hyperopia exceeding 4.00 to 5.00 D or myopia exceeding 5.00 to 6.00 D. These types of amblyopia are treated with refractive correction.
Strabismic amblyopia is not typically seen in bilateral astigmatism.
Anisometropic amblyopia occurs in the setting of asymmetric high astigmatism or asymmetric high hyperopia.
Deprivational amblyopia occurs when the visual axis is obstructed, such as in congenital cataracts, severe ptosis, or corneal opacity.

Peripheral suppression is the sensory adaptation that can develop in strabismic patients to eliminate diplopia. Visual confusion and diplopia are the normal consequences of strabismus when there are no sensory adaptations to prevent them. Although some degree of stereopsis can be present in small-angle strabismus with monofixation syndrome, good stereopsis indicates that there is no manifest strabismus and no suppression.

How does postoperative steroid treatment in pediatric cataract surgery patients with intraocular lens (IOL) placement compare to such treatment in those without IOL placement?
Correct answer: A. Patients with an IOL require more aggressive steroid treatment postoperatively compared to patients without an IOL.
Rationale
Topical steroids should be used more aggressively in children who have undergone IOL implantation than those without a lens implant. Some surgeons administer intracameral steroids postoperatively, and others use oral steroids, especially in very young children and children with heavily pigmented irides. If all cortical material is adequately removed, postoperative inflammation in children without a lens implant is usually mild, and postoperative topical antibiotics, corticosteroids, and cycloplegics are commonly applied for a few weeks.

Q1679
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A child alternates between esotropia and orthotropia on a 48-hour cycle. Fusion and binocular vision are absent on the esotropic days, and markedly improved on orthotropic days. What treatment is most appropriate?
Correct answer: B. strabismus surgery
Rationale
Cyclic esotropia is a rare strabismus syndrome where esotropia is present every other day. Fusion and binocular vision are absent or poor on strabismic days and improved or normal on orthotropic days. Its etiology is poorly understood. Surgical treatment, based on the maximum angle of deviation when the eyes are esotropic, is usually effective. Hyperopic correction is used to treat refractive accommodative esotropia, and bifocals can be used to treat high AC/A ratio accommodative esotropia. These are not useful for cyclic esotropia.

Q1680

Following several missed follow-up appointments, a 2-year-old child presents for further evaluation of amblyopia in the left eye. Since his last kept appointment, the child has received cycloplegic penalization in the right eye. What problem might the ophthalmologist expect to find?
Correct answer: B. amblyopia in the right eye
Rationale
Patient and parent counseling regarding treatment and side effects are a fundamental part of amblyopia management because patient and parent compliance and cooperation are crucial to a successful functional or visual outcome. Pharmacologic penalization is the placement of a cycloplegic agent (usually atropine 1% drops or homatropine 5% drops) into the better-seeing eye so that it is unable to accommodate. As a result, the better eye experiences blur with near viewing and, with uncorrected hyperopia, with distance viewing as well. Regular follow-up of amblyopic patients on treatment with cycloplegia is necessary to avoid reverse amblyopia to the contralateral eye. Pharmacologic penalization has been used to successfully treat moderate levels of amblyopia. The child described is not likely to have experienced decreased vision in the originally amblyopic (left) eye. Increased myopia in the right eye or increased hyperopia in the left eye are not risks associated with the use of pharmacologic penalization.

The actions of the inferior oblique vary in different gazes because the muscle axis is not parallel with the visual axis. Therefore, in primary position the primary action is extorsion. Corneal blood staining is a definite indication for surgical intervention in the amblyopic age group and a relative indication in older patients. Anterior chamber washout can be done without admission to a hospital; the surgery is performed in an operating room but can be done on an outpatient basis. Whether the surgery is done on an outpatient or inpatient basis, the patient must be examined on the day after the surgery. Infantile esotropia is characterized by a large-angle (usually greater than 30 prism diopters) esotropia that develops in the first 6 months of life. What is the most likely mechanism of glaucoma in Sturge-Weber syndrome?

Glaucoma is the most serious complication of Sturge-Weber syndrome, and it develops in 70% of patients. Q1691
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the earliest sign of malignant hyperthermia?
Correct answer: A. unexplained elevation of end-tidal carbon dioxide concentration
Rationale
Malignant hyperthermia is a sporadic or autosomal dominantly inherited disorder characterized by a defect of calcium binding by the sarcoplasmic reticulum of skeletal muscle. Intracellular calcium levels can rise dramatically causing muscle contraction with acidosis, heat production, hyperkalemia, and muscle breakdown. Clinically the patient may have muscle rigidity, tachypnea, tachycardia, sweating, cyanosis, skin discoloration, or dark urine. The disorder is triggered by certain inhalational anesthetics or succinylcholine, and the earliest sign is unexplained elevation of end-tidal carbon dioxide concentration. If untreated, malignant hyperthermia can be fatal. Treatment involves dantrolene and should be managed by the anesthesia team.

Both peribulbar and retrobulbar anesthesia make most EOM procedures pain-­free and should be considered in adults for whom general anesthesia may pose an undue hazard. The administration of a short-­acting hypnotic by an anesthesiologist just before retrobulbar injection greatly improves patient comfort. ­Because injected anesthetics may influence alignment during the first few hours ­after surgery, suture adjustment is best delayed for at least half a day.
General anesthesia is necessary for ­children and is often used for adults as well, particularly ­those requiring bilateral surgery. Neuromuscular blocking agents such as succinylcholine, which are administered to facilitate intubation for general anesthesia, can temporarily affect the results of a traction test. Nondepolarizing agents, which do not have this effect, can be used instead.
Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting
Eye muscle surgery is a risk ­factor for postoperative nausea and vomiting. This risk can be reduced by prophylaxis with dexamethasone and serotonin type 3 (5-­HT3) antagonists (eg, ondansetron), propofol use, adequate hydration, and reduced use of inhalation anesthetics and opioid analgesia.
Oculocardiac Reflex
The oculocardiac reflex is a slowing of the heart rate caused by traction on the EOMs, particularly the medial rectus muscle. In its most severe form, the reflex can produce asystole. The surgeon should be aware of the possibility of inducing the oculocardiac reflex when manipulating a muscle and should be prepared to release tension if the heart rate drops excessively. Intravenous atropine and other agents can protect against this reflex.
Malignant Hyperthermia
Malignant hyperthermia (MH) is an impor­tant disorder for pediatric ophthalmologists ­because of its association with strabismus, myopathies, ptosis, and musculoskeletal abnormalities. MH is a defect of calcium binding by the sarcoplasmic reticulum of skeletal muscle that can occur sporadically or be dominantly inherited with incomplete penetrance. When MH is triggered by inhalational anesthetics or the muscle relaxant succinylcholine, unbound intracellular calcium concentration increases. This stimulates muscle contracture, causing massive acidosis. In its fully developed form, MH is characterized by extreme heat production, resulting from the hypermetabolic state.
MH can be fatal if diagnosis and treatment are delayed. The earliest sign is unexplained elevation of end-­tidal carbon dioxide concentration. As soon as the diagnosis is made, surgery should be terminated, even if incomplete.

What extraocular muscle disorder can pseudoptosis be associated with?
Correct answer: A. hypotropia
Rationale
The upper eyelid follows the eye in upgaze and downgaze; that is, the eyelid moves in the same direction as the eye. Therefore, the upper eyelid of a hypotropic eye will be lower than that of the fellow eye, producing the false appearance of ptosis. Conditions that cause hypertropia or horizontal strabismus do not cause pseudoptosis.

Q1693
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 4-month-old boy does not fix or follow but has an otherwise normal eye examination. The child is re-examined when he is 6 months old and is noted to have normal responses to visual stimuli. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. delayed visual maturation
Rationale
The term delayed visual maturation (DVM) describes a condition wherein normal fixation and tracking do not develop within the first 3-4 months of life, but visual behavior subsequently normalizes.
Cerebral visual impairment (CVI) is caused by pathology posterior to the lateral geniculate nucleus. CVI can be congenital or acquired. Causes include structural central nervous system (CNS) abnormalities, intrauterine infection, periventricular leukomalacia, hypoxia, hydrocephalus, abusive head trauma, and encephalitis. Although some improvement in vision can occur, a complete normalization of vision is uncommon. Uncorrected refractive error and intrauterine infection also would not be associated with spontaneous normalization of vision.

Q1694
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What feature characterizes central fusion disruption?
Correct answer: B. misalignment of the visual axes
Rationale
Patients with central fusion disruption have misalignment of the visual axes and intractable diplopia. The angle of strabismus can be small or may vary. The patients do not have any fusion or fusional amplitudes. The patients have double vision because they lack sensory adaptations of suppression, or anomalous retinal correspondence.
Central fusion disruption can occur in a number of clinical settings: after disruption of fusion for a prolonged period; after head trauma; and, in rare cases, in long‑standing strabismus.

Q1695
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What method is recommended for assessing the refractive state in amblyopia?
Correct answer: C. cycloplegic retinoscopy
Rationale
Cycloplegic retinoscopy is the most objective and accurate method to determine the ocular refractive state in amblyopia. Due to the large accommodative capacity and tone in children, cycloplegia is necessary to accurately determine the full refractive error, especially in patients with hyperopia. Therapy for refractive amblyopia is predicated upon correcting the full refractive error of the amblyopic eye(s) and penalizing the least amblyopic or non-amblyopic eye. Because an amblyopic eye’s ability to control accommodation tends to be impaired, this eye cannot be relied on to compensate for uncorrected hyperopia as would a normal child’s eye.
Retinoscopy under anesthesia (but without complete cycloplegia), manifest refraction, and autorefraction are not satisfactory, because they may not determine the full optical refractive state in the highly accommodative pediatric eye.

DVD should be treated if it manifests frequently during the day and is noticeable (6 to 8 prism diopters). Treatment can involve changing fixation preference if it is unilateral, or it can involve surgery. DVD can occur with or without a horizontal component and usually involves a torsional component. DVD usually presents by the time a child is 2 years old, but age does not play a role in determining when a DVD should be fixed.

Dacryocystocele presents as a bluish swelling inferior and nasal to the medial canthus. Associated nasal mucocele can significantly compromise the airway, since infants are obligate nose breathers. Dacryocystoceles associated with acute respiratory distress require immediate surgical intervention. NLD probing in conjunction with nasal endoscopy and intranasal cyst removal is effective in more than 95% of infants. Surgical treatment of an infected dacryocystocele via a skin incision should be avoided because of the risk of creating a persistent fistulous tract.

Correct answer: A. amblyopia

Strabismus can be a later manifestation of amblyopia but is not caused directly by the plexiform neurofibroma. Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) is associated with cataract. Lisch nodules are common in NF1 patients but do not need to be monitored.

Q1701
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the most frequent cause of childhood visual impairment in developed countries?
Correct answer: A. retrogeniculate visual impairment
Rationale
Visual dysfunction in infants and children is classified into 3 major categories:
  • delayed visual maturation
  • pregeniculate visual impairment
  • retrogeniculate visual impairment
Cognitive impairment, though it can affect the language-learning ability and other visually oriented skills, is not a classification of visual dysfunction.
Delayed visual maturation occurs when normal visual fixation and tracking does not develop within the first 3 months of life. Pregeniculate visual impairment refers to visual deficits related to pathology anterior to the lateral geniculate nucleus. Retrogeniculate visual impairment (also termed cerebral visual impairment [CVI]) refers to visual deficits related to pathology posterior to the lateral geniculate nucleus. Retrogeniculate visual impairment is the most frequent cause of childhood visual impairment in developed countries.
Amblyopic visual deficits result primarily from visual cortical changes. With abnormal visual experience early in life, cells of the primary visual cortex can lose their ability to respond to stimulation of 1 or both eyes, and the cells that remain responsive show significant functional deficiencies, including abnormally large receptive fields. For this reason, amblyopia would be considered a retrogeniculate cause of vision loss.

Q1702
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A toddler with esotropia since infancy and severe amblyopia in the left eye develops a prominent, conjugate, horizontal jerk nystagmus that is right-beating in both right gaze and left gaze. What is this the most likely cause of this condition?
Correct answer: D. manifest latent nystagmus with infantile esotropia syndrome
Rationale
Latent nystagmus is a marker of fusional maldevelopment. Latent nystagmus can become manifest when only 1 eye is being used for vision, such as in amblyopia.
A null point in left gaze would be expected to dampen nystagmus in left gaze. Vestibular nystagmus is periodic alternating nystagmus, an unusual form of congenital motor jerk nystagmus that periodically changes directions. Infantile nystagmus syndrome would become manifest in infancy.

Q1703
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
Pseudoesotropia can be associated with what other finding?
Correct answer: D. prominent epicanthal folds
Rationale
Pseudoesotropia occurs when facial features cause tissue to obscure the nasal sclera, leading to the appearance that the eyes are directed inward. Pseudoesotropia is usually associated with a reduced interpupillary distance or prominent epicanthal folds. No real deviation exists, and the results of both corneal light reflex testing and cover-uncover testing are normal. As the child grows, the pseudoesotropia is usually reduced or resolves. Temporal retinal dragging may cause pseudoexotropia.

Q1704
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A patient undergoes a retrobulbar anesthetic injection just prior to glaucoma filtering surgery. What change in eye position is the surgeon likely to observe intraoperatively?
Correct answer: B. incyclotorsion and depression of the eye
Rationale
A retrobulbar injection introduces anesthetic into the intraconal space, an extension of the fascial planes of the annulus of Zinn. The annulus of Zinn is formed by the 4 rectus muscle insertions and their intermuscular fascia; it encompasses the optic canal and splits the superior orbital fissure into an intraconal and extraconal compartment (Figure 1). The intraconal compartment contains both divisions of the oculomotor (III) and abducens (VI) nerves. Also recall that the nerve to the inferior oblique muscle travels in the inferior branch of the oculomotor nerve. Therefore, abduction, supraduction, and excyclotorsion would not occur, as these motor nerves have been anesthetized by the retrobulbar block. The trochlear nerve (IV) lies outside the annulus of Zinn in the extraconal space, and is often spared during retrobulbar blocks, resulting in intact incyclotorsion and infraduction of the globe intraoperatively.
Figure 1. The four rectus muscles and their intermuscular fascial attachments form the annulus of Zinn. A: Optic canal. B: Superior division of the oculomotor nerve (III). C: The nasociliary nerve (V-1), supplying sensory innervation to the globe. D: The inferior division of III. E: The lacrimal nerve (V-1). F: The frontal nerve (V-1). G: The trochlear nerve (IV). H: The abducens nerve (VI). Note that the superior orbital vein (blue) is variably drawn as intraconal or extraconal, depending on the atlas.

Q1705
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What intracranial structural abnormality could account for new-onset downbeat nystagmus in a 4-year-old girl?
Correct answer: A. Arnold-Chiari malformation
Rationale
Less than 20% of childhood nystagmus is acquired and necessitates further imaging. Downbeat nystagmus is usually acquired secondary to Arnold-Chiari malformation. Pinealoma is associated with convergence-retraction nystagmus. Chiasmal tumors have been associated with spasmus nutans, a triad of nystagmus, head bobbing, and torticollis. Craniopharyngioma is associated with see-saw nystagmus.

Q1706
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 4-year-old boy presents with the fundus findings shown in the figures and cataracts in both eyes. What congenital infection did he most likely have?
Correct answer: C. rubella
Rationale
Congenital rubella syndrome is caused by rubella virus that is transmitted transplacentally to a fetus. Eye findings include a variable pigmentary retinopathy, ranging from a salt-and-pepper appearance to a pseudoretinitis pigmentosa. In this case, the patient has macular pigmentary changes, as well as peripheral pigmentary changes. Other eye findings in congenital rubella syndrome include cataract, glaucoma, and microphthalmia. Rubella has also been identified as a cause of Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis. Extraocular manifestations include hearing loss and cardiac abnormalities.
Congenital syphilis can present in the eye as a chorioretinitis with a salt-and-pepper retinopathy. However, cataracts are not seen with syphilis. Other eye findings include interstitial keratitis, uveitis and glaucoma. Other early manifestations include persistent rhinitis, rash, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and pneumonia. Late findings include peg-shaped teeth and deafness.
Toxocariasis is an infection resulting from ingestion of the nematode larvae of an intestinal parasite common to dogs and cats, through ascarid ova in soil contaminated by their feces. It presents in the eye as a typically unilateral posterior uveitis characterized by a large white granuloma in the retina that can cause retinal dragging. Cataracts are not seen.
Congenital toxoplasmosis can present in the eye with retinitis or uveitis. The retina is usually thickened and white with overlying vitritis. There may be a flat retinal scar at the edge of the lesion in the retina. Cataracts are not seen. Other findings include microcephaly, developmental delay, hepatosplenomegaly, and intracranial calcifications.

Q1707
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
An infant has a capillary hemangioma involving the right eyelid, as shown. This child is at greatest risk of developing what type of amblyopia?
Correct answer: D. deprivation amblyopia
Rationale
Ptosis can cause deprivational or anisometropic amblyopia. The eyelid can cover the visual axis or induce astigmatism in the affected eye, causing an anisometropic amblyopia. In this case, occlusion of the visual axis presents the greatest risk for visual deprivation amblyopia. The child may develop a chin-up head position in order to use the eye with ptosis.
Strabismic amblyopia would result from eye misalignment. Ametropic amblyopia would occur due to high refractive error. Meridional amblyopia refers to a specific variety of isoametropic amblyopia in which bilateral high astigmatic errors decrease resolving ability due to chronically blurred meridians.

Q1708
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
For patients with Duane syndrome, what is the preferred surgical procedure to treat upshoots and downshoots?
Correct answer: D. Y-splitting of the lateral rectus muscle
Rationale
Y-splitting of the lateral rectus muscle is the preferred surgical therapeutic option for upshoots and downshoots in patients with Duane syndrome. Additional options to address the upshoots and downshoots include large lateral rectus recession, retroequatorial fixation of the lateral rectus muscle, and more recently, deactivation of the lateral rectus muscle and reattachment to the lateral periosteum of the orbit with a subsequent transposition procedure.
Surgical therapy for strabismus from Duane syndrome depends upon the deviation pattern and includes transposition of the vertical rectus muscles and recession of the medial rectus muscle on the affected side with or without recession of the medial rectus muscle on the opposite side. Transposition procedures and recession of the medial rectus muscles, however, do not address upshoots and downshoots. Surgical intervention should not be performed in patients who have binocular vision with the eyes in primary position or for binocularity achieved with an acceptably slight head turn.

Q1709
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What extraocular muscle is responsible for elevation of the eye in adduction?
Correct answer: A. inferior oblique
Rationale
The movements of the vertical and oblique muscles are complex because in primary position, the muscle axes are not in alignment with the visual axis. Therefore, when an eye is adducted, the inferior oblique is the primary elevator. The superior rectus is the primary elevator in abduction. Neither the superior oblique nor inferior rectus muscles are elevators of the eye.

Q1710
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 23-year-old man was recently found to have convergence paralysis. In addition to diplopia at near, the patient notes blurred vision when focusing on near objects. What can be done to minimize the patient's symptoms?
Correct answer: A. a trial of plus lenses with base-in prisms for near work
Rationale
Convergence paralysis results in an exotropia at near. Base-in prisms will help move the images toward the apex of the prism to alleviate the diplopia. Blurred vision at near suggests an accompanying accommodative insufficiency component that can occur with convergence paralysis. Thus, plus lenses at near would be required in addition to the base-in prism. Surgery is not a good option, since this will alter the alignment in the distance. Usually, convergence paralysis occurs secondary to an intracranial lesion.
