Q1711
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A child presents for evaluation of allergic conjunctivitis. She continues to experience puffy, red, watery, itchy eyes despite using an oral antihistamine. What is the preferred management?
Correct answer: C. topical H1-receptor blocker
Rationale
After confirming the findings that support the diagnosis of allergic conjunctivitis, the ophthalmologist needs to modify this patient's treatment plan, because it is not effective. Seasonal allergic conjunctivitis tends to occur in the spring and fall and is triggered by environmental contact with specific airborne allergens such as pollens from grasses, flowers, weeds, and trees. Patients typically present with reddened, watery eyes, boggy-appearing conjunctiva, and complaints of itchy eyes. If scrapings of the conjunctiva are obtained in patients with allergic conjunctivitis, eosinophils are present. Management of allergic conjunctivitis involves removal of the offending allergens from the patient's environment and initiating systemic and/or topical medications. Cool compresses to the eyes can further increase patient comfort. In this case, the patient was started on oral antihistamines. Oral antihistamines tend to be less effective at relieving specific ocular symptoms but are especially useful in cases where other symptoms, such as nasal congestion, are present. In this case, an H1-receptor blocker or mast cell stabilizing drop is preferred. Mast cell stabilizing drugs are not offered as options here. Mild topical corticosteroid drops should be reserved for severe or recalcitrant cases. Patients, especially children, treated with topical corticosteroids need to be monitored closely for steroid adverse effects, such as cataracts or glaucoma.

Q1712
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
The patient shown is at greatest risk for developing what form of amblyopia at this stage?
Correct answer: B. anisometropic amblyopia
Rationale
This 2-month-old girl has a capillary hemangioma involving the right upper eyelid and orbit, which displaces the globe and induces an astigmatic refractive error (8 diopters of astigmatism in this case). This places the child at high risk for anisometropic amblyopia, which is a dissimilar refractive error in the 2 eyes. Isoametropic amblyopia, also known as bilateral ametropic amblyopia, is a bilateral decrease in visual acuity due to large, approximately equal, uncorrected refractive errors in the 2 eyes of a child.
Hyperopia exceeding 4.00 D-5.00 D and myopia exceeding 5.00 D-6.00 D carry a risk of inducing isoametropic amblyopia. Because capillary hemangiomas deform but do not shorten or elongate the globe, and more importantly, because the lesion is a unilateral process in this case, the patient is not at risk of isoametropic amblyopia. Strabismic amblyopia develops in children who have constant, nonalternating heterotropias. Visual deprivation amblyopia occurs because of an eye abnormality that obstructs the visual axis or otherwise interferes with central vision. Despite the large size of the hemangioma in this patient, the image shows that the visual axis is not yet obstructed.

Q1713
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A toddler presents with ptosis and a chin-up position. What is the most important determinant in choosing the surgical technique for repair?
Correct answer: B. levator function
Rationale
The levator function is the most important determinant of the type of surgical repair to employ. Moderate to good levator function can often benefit from a levator resection. Poor levator function requires a frontalis sling approach to recruit the brow musculature to lift the lid.
The age of the patient, the presence of amblyopia, and the presence of associated syndromes can be important determinants for the timing of surgical repair.

Q1714
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 6-year-old boy with neuroblastoma is found to have acquired Horner syndrome. What is the most likely site of the causative neuroblastoma?
Correct answer: D. primary cervical/apical sympathetic chain
Rationale
Horner syndrome can occur from a primary cervical or apical thoracic neuroblastoma that involves the sympathetic chain. While neuroblastoma is the most common cause of metastatic orbital malignancy in children, Horner syndrome does not occur from metastatic neuroblastoma. Neuroblastoma usually arises from the adrenal gland or sympathetic ganglion chain in the mediastinum or retroperitoneum.

Q1715
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
An infant is noted to have leukocoria, microphthalmos, and elongated ciliary processes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: D. persistent fetal vasculature (PFV)
Rationale
All of the listed conditions (ROP, Coats disease, retinoblastoma) can present with leukocoria, but only persistent fetal vasculature is associated with microphthalmia. PFV results from failed regression of the fetal hyaloid vasculature. Findings can vary from a retrolental membrane to a stalk connecting the lens and optic nerve. It is also associated with elongated ciliary processes, cataract and retinal detachment, and angle closure glaucoma.

Q1716
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A patient presents with transient episodes of convergence, accommodative spasm, and miosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. spasm of the near reflex
Rationale
Spasm of the near reflex is a condition with excessive convergence, excessive accommodation, and miosis. Patients often present with episodes of esotropia alternating with orthophoria. The etiology generally is thought to be functional, although it rarely can be associated with organic disease. Treatment consists of cycloplegic agents such as atropine and homatropine, hyperopic correction, bifocal glasses, and/or counseling to address underlying psychologic issues.
Cyclic esotropia has periods of esotropia and orthophoria, but it is not associated with miosis or accommodative spasm. Divergence insufficiency has esotropia worse at distance than near, and no pupillary abnormalities. Convergence insufficiency shows decreased convergence, not excess convergence.

Q1717
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
In a patient with epidemic keratoconjunctivitis, what is the most appropriate indication for treatment with topical corticosteroids?
Correct answer: D. subepithelial corneal opacities
Rationale
Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis is a highly contagious viral conjunctivitis that is usually self-limited. Treatment is usually supportive, with cold compresses and artificial tears. The complication of subepithelial corneal opacities is sometimes treated with topical steroids. 
Epiphora and periorbital pain are common symptoms that do not require steroid treatment. Periorbital ecchymosis does not require steroid treatment but may be a sign of preseptal cellulitis.

Q1718
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the most appropriate surgery to perform for a V-pattern esotropia with no inferior oblique overaction?
Correct answer: C. bilateral medial rectus recession with inferior transposition (inferoplacement)
Rationale
In a V-pattern esotropia, the medial rectus muscles can be recessed and moved toward the apex of the deviation, which would be inferiorly in this case. Lateral muscles should be moved away from the apex of the deviation. A useful mnemonic is MALE: medial rectus muscle to the apex, lateral rectus muscle to the empty space. When horizontal muscle recession-resection is performed, displacement should be in opposite directions, but this will cause symptomatic torsion if the patient has vision in the eye.

Q1719
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
For a child with optic nerve hypoplasia, what visual acuity would be consistent with the diagnosis?
Correct answer: D. 20/20 to no light perception correlating well to the integrity of the macular fibers
Rationale
Optic nerve hypoplasia (ONH) is characterized by small optic discs on fundus examination. Although a decreased number of optic nerve axons may be present histologically, this cannot be quantified premortem. Visual acuity can range from normal (20/20) to no light perception and is related to the integrity of the macular fibers, rather than disc size. Clinically, the disc is pale or gray and smaller than normal. This condition can be unilateral or bilateral and is often asymmetric, as shown. It may be associated with a yellow to white ring around the disc (double ring sign). Visual acuity in patients with optic nerve hypoplasia often does not correlate with the overall size of the disc or the amount of visual field constriction. Frequently, visual fields contain localized defects combined with visual field constriction but these do not correlate to disc size. Patients with ONH may have any combination of absence of the septum pellucidum, agenesis of the corpus callosum, cerebral hemisphere abnormalities, and pituitary gland abnormalities.

Q1720
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What type of exodeviation are orthoptic exercises the most appropriate initial therapy for?
Correct answer: C. convergence insufficiency
Rationale
Orthoptic training to stimulate convergence might improve the deviation in patients with convergence insufficiency, a type of convergence weakness exotropia. Patients with Duane retraction syndrome might present with exotropia due to decreased adduction. Dissociated strabismus might manifest with an exodeviation. Both Duane retraction syndrome and dissociated strabismus are treated surgically. Positive angle kappa is a form of pseudostrabismus, in which the eyes appear exotropic, but the visual axes are optically aligned.

Q1721
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 5-year-old boy has a history of bilateral superior oblique palsy. Cover testing would be expected to reveal what deviation and pattern?
Correct answer: B. V-pattern esotropia with excyclotorsion
Rationale
Bilateral superior oblique palsy occurs commonly after head trauma but is sometimes congenital. Unlike the unilateral superior oblique palsies, it is associated with a V-pattern esotropia and excyclotorsion greater than 10°.
V-pattern esotropia with incyclotorsion is seen in skew deviations, an important differential to exclude in cases of closed head injury. A-pattern strabismus is not typically seen in association with superior oblique palsy. It occurs most commonly in patients with exotropia and persons with spina bifida.

Q1722
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 68-year-old woman has a large esodeviation secondary to a complete sixth nerve palsy OD that has not resolved for 9 months. She cannot abduct past midline. What treatment would you recommend?
Correct answer: D. transposition of the vertical recti
Rationale
Surgery for the treatment of 6th nerve palsy is indicated when spontaneous resolution does not occur after 6 months or more of follow-up. In patients with some lateral rectus muscle function, a large recession of the antagonist medial rectus muscle, combined with resection of the lateral rectus muscle, is appropriate. However, in cases of total paralysis like this one, a vertical muscle transposition procedure is usually required. Botulinum toxin injection into the ipsilateral medial rectus muscle can be used initially to balance the paretic lateral rectus muscle while waiting for potential spontaneous improvement in 6th nerve function. Orthoptic exercises would not be useful.

Q1723
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A child is uncooperative during the eye examination. What is the most appropriate step to take?
Correct answer: C. Try a combination of rest periods, persistence, and, if necessary, a return visit.
Rationale
Most infants and children can be examined successfully in the office. A combination of persuasion, rest, playing, and in some cases rescheduling for a different day may be necessary. The practitioner needs to balance the emotional consequences of restraint for the patient and caregivers. An examination under anesthesia may become necessary if an adequate examination cannot be performed in the office.

Q1724
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 13-day-old infant presents with esotropia and poor suck reflex from bilateral facial weakness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: D. Möbius syndrome
Rationale
Möbius syndrome is a congenital dysinnervation syndrome presenting as combined cranial nerve VI and VII paresis, as well as limb, chest, and tongue defects. This syndrome produces facial weakness and esotropia with horizontal gaze palsies, due to aplasia of the CN VI nucleus and involvement of other pontine structures.
The main differential diagnosis is congenital myasthenia gravis. A transient neonatal form, caused by the placental transfer of acetylcholine receptor antibodies of mothers with myasthenia gravis, usually subsides rapidly. Ptosis is present in over 90% of these patients and would be seen more commonly than facial weakness.
Botulinum toxin could also be a cause of facial weakness and ophthalmoplegia, but is likely to produce bilateral ptosis and poor pupillary reactivity in addition.
Duane syndrome is another congenital innervational ophthalmoplegia syndrome; it affects CN III and CN VI, often causing esotropia with lid fissure narrowing on attempted adduction due to co-contraction of the medial and lateral recti. Duane syndrome is not associated with facial paresis.

Q1725
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the most common ophthalmologic manifestation of abusive head trauma?
Correct answer: D. bilateral intraocular hemorrhages
Rationale
Retinal hemorrhages are the cardinal manifestation of abusive head trauma (AHT, formerly termed shaken baby syndrome). The incidence of retinal hemorrhages in AHT is approximately 80%. Classically, children with AHT have retinal hemorrhages that are multilayered: preretinal, intraretinal, and subretinal. Papilledema occurs in less than 10% of cases of AHT. Cranial nerve paresis and exudative retinal detachment are not commonly associated with AHT.

Q1726
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What is the primary purpose of the 4-diopter base-out prism test?
Correct answer: C. It is used to document a facultative scotoma in a patient with no manifest deviation.
Rationale
The 4-diopter base out prism test is used to document the presence of a small macular scotoma in a patient with monofixation syndrome and either a microstrabismus or no manifest deviation. When the prism is placed over the nonfixating eye, there is no movement of the eye and no convergence movement of the contralateral eye.
This is the least reliable test to document a macular suppression scotoma because patients with monofixation syndrome might switch fixation and patients with bifixation might recognize the diplopic response, but make no convergence movements. While a normal patient (a patient with bifixation) would demonstrate the convergence behavior, it is not the purpose of the test to demonstrate this.

Q1727
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
A 5-year-old boy is found to have decreased vision in his left eye. The visual acuity is 20/25 in his right eye and 20/60 in his left eye. Cycloplegic retinoscopy is +1.00 sphere in the right eye and +1.75 sphere in the left eye. The sensorimotor examination is consistent with 25 prism diopters of esotropia. What is the most likely cause of the patient's decreased vision?
Correct answer: A. strabismic amblyopia
Rationale
Amblyopia is a unilateral or, less commonly, bilateral reduction of best-corrected visual acuity that cannot be attributed directly to the effect of any structural abnormality of the eye or posterior visual pathways. Etiologies include strabismic, anisometropic, isoametropic (high bilateral refractive error), or deprivation. In this case, the patient has an esotropia; thus, strabismus is the cause.

Q1728
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
Patients found to have gonococcal conjunctivitis should also be treated for what common coinfection?
Correct answer: D. chlamydia
Rationale
Up to one-third of patients with gonococcal conjunctivitis have been reported to have concurrent chlamydial venereal disease. Because of this frequent association, it is advisable to give patients supplemental oral antibiotics for treatment of chlamydial infection. The other 3 infectious agents (hepatitis C virus, herpes simplex virus, and syphilis) are not found with high coinfection frequency.

Q1729
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
What are the typical ocular findings in patients with the tubulointerstitial nephritis uveitis (TINU) syndrome?
Correct answer: B. anterior uveitis
Rationale
In addition to systemic manifestations necessary for this diagnosis (elevated blood creatinine levels, proteinuria, β2-microglobulinuria, normoglycemic glycosuria, abnormal liver function test results [LFTs], eosinophilia, fevers, arthralgias, myalgias, rash), patients with TINU present with an acute, often bilateral, nongranulomatous anterior uveitis. While the eyes can also become injected as a result of the iritis, this is not a scleritis. Posterior segment manifestations are atypical of this syndrome.

Q1730
Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus
In patients with aniridia, what is the most common cause of progressive corneal scarring?
Correct answer: D. limbal stem cell deficiency
Rationale
Aniridia is due to a mutation of the PAX6 gene and is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. Sporadic cases also occur and are associated with Wilms tumor. Patients with congenital aniridia can develop progressive corneal scarring within the first decade of life, necessitating corneal transplantation to restore vision. Adult patients with aniridia can also develop later-onset issues with non-healing epithelial defects and corneal neovascularization. The major underlying mechanism is related to limbal stem cell deficiency, although abnormal cell differentiation may play a role as well.
Herpes simplex keratitis can be a cause of progressive corneal scarring, but it is more common in atopic patients, not aniridic patients. Endothelial decompensation can be seen in Peters anomaly patients, but is not typical of aniridia. Patients with aniridia are more prone to have ptosis than exposure keratopathy.
